articles.title: Asia’s Economic Integration: A Roadmap for Peacebuilding in the Middle East
articles.full_text:
Economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific has been the key driver of peace since 1952.
When the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, ASEAN, was formed in 1967, the five founding states intended to produce a front against the spread of communism. The venture has since grown to include a total of 11 countries, producing a remarkable set of unforeseen consequences, from becoming the fifth-largest economy in the world to reinforcing peace across a swath of diverse and developing countries.
Instead of pursuing Cold War initiatives, the bloc has become increasingly integrated, tied together through manufacturing supply chains, trade infrastructure, and shared financial institutions like the Chiang Mai Initiative. ASEAN now produces over $4 trillion in GDP and has a population of 678 million people. The collaboration’s biggest success, however, has not simply been increased commerce. With economic integration comes regional stabilization and peace, a consequence further fostered by the signing of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) in 2020, which includes Australia, China, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea. Economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific has been the key driver of peace in the region ever since 1952 with the Treaty of San Francisco, and it serves today as a key example of how market mechanics can drive peacebuilding. In fact, it was ASEAN that eroded tensions from the Konfrontasi war in the early 1960s, and has solidified the climate of peace between the Southeast Asian members ever since.
Economists and politicians have often considered the question of whether trade contributes to peaceful relations between states. The affirmative answer is not novel; however, in the case of ASEAN and the Asia-Pacific, the specifics begin to clarify the theory. Peacebuilding through economic means is more a matter of building economic capacity and trade interdependence than of simply trading goods between nations. This crucial specification turns the Asia-Pacific from a successful case study into a model for peacebuilding elsewhere, and it is one that has been imitated by the Gulf Cooperation Council or, more recently, by the C5 in Central Asia.
Economic interdependence is a consequence of cooperation, occurring over time by building trust and relying on companies that diversify operations across countries. Daron Acemoglu, a Nobel Prize winner in Economic Sciences, has regularly argued for this by pointing out that both prosperity and stability mutually flow from systems or institutions that offer a broad stake in the economic growth of a nation. Thus, when firms create cross-border commerce, war becomes economically unviable and politically undesirable. The principle is not exclusive to the Asia-Pacific, and despite ASEAN’s success, it is clear that outliers perpetuate risks by building up economic barriers instead of interdependence. Examples include relations between North and South Korea or China and Taiwan. The question, therefore, remains: how can peace be built today through economic interdependence, or in other words, how can rivals begin working together in an economic capacity?
Answers learned in the Asia-Pacific could resound further away. In the Middle East, for example, diplomatic efforts for peace in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and Israel and the Palestinian Territories have worked through a long campaign of advocacy; however, it is only with the additional incentives that economic cooperation brings that peace efforts actually remain sustainable and enduring. For Israel and the Palestinian Territories, economic interdependence and a shared aspiration could enhance the ongoing international effort to ameliorate decades-long tensions. Syria offers an immediate test case as well. When the Assad regime fell in 2025 and the United States and the European Union both lifted sanctions, organizations began to move in, building relationships and supporting the fragile new state’s desire for peace. American companies have established power generation projects, the Gulf states and Turkey have signed dozens of economic memoranda of understanding with the new state, and startups like Behti Betak or nonprofit organizations like the Words of Isa are building grassroots relationships aimed at creating a newly integrated Syria, driving peace across the Middle East. Integration leads to interdependence. Interdependence self-reinforces peace.
Peacebuilding of this sort may be especially critical for Israel and the Palestinian Territories, where conflict and violence have persisted for decades before the Gaza War. Reconstruction and reconciliation efforts require that businesses spread their operations across the divide. Organizations like the Portland Trust, based in the United Kingdom, have focused on the region on the basis that economic co-operation and dialogue between the parties is inseparable from diplomatic peacebuilding efforts. And such economic development (alongside political will) can create hope, ambition, and opportunities for Palestinians. The founding Chief Executive of The Portland Trust, Lord Jonathan Kestenbaum, brings a personal history to the work of reconciliation. His family’s own flight from Nazi persecution ultimately led them to the UK, where he grew up, and whilst a student in London, he was General Secretary (mazkir) of Bnei Akiva UK, a branch of the global youth movement. He then studied at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem in the 1980s completing an MA in education, and thereafter helped to build an international training program for young educators. As a dual national at the time, Kestenbaum was conscripted to military service, with this experience influencing his life-long commitment to reconciliation between Palestinians and Israelis with a particular focus on building bridges through economic co-operation.
Lord Kestenbaum returned home to the U.K. after a few years in Jerusalem and gave up his dual nationality, retaining only British citizenship. He helped found the Portland Trust, and spent many years fostering peace efforts between Israelis and Palestinians. This history gave him a grounding in the region, a commitment to co-existence and a familiarity that exemplifies how peacebuilding through commerce is not abstract policy but is instead built through relationships and real-life experiences. The Portland Trust has to date worked extensively to support Palestinians and Israelis through projects like the Palestinian Agriculture Impact Fund and the building of the city of Rawabi.
Personal experiences bring markets together, and when they come together, they accelerate growth and integration among an increasing number of actors. Each of these actors learns to empathize with their business partners, regardless of historical or political differences. The process reinforces peace, builds harmony, and creates trust. In the case of Israel and the Palestinian Territories, the process is needed alongside reconstruction efforts like Trump’s Board of Peace, which aims to produce lasting peace but has yet to break ground.
Peace is not guaranteed through economics; however, throughout the last century, and in the case of the Asia-Pacific, it has become the most reliable mechanism of sustaining peace, cultivating the types of relationships that grow closer instead of farther apart. Private investment adds a financial tie to the process; however, intentional relationships with an empathetic desire for peace fundamentally secure the process. Southeast Asia’s history, compared to Syria’s cautious reopening or Gaza’s Board of Peace, shows that commerce can lay groundwork that politics otherwise cannot. The region will need institutional support, perhaps even at the level of an ASEAN, but the foundation is growing. More inter-state commerce will bring stronger relationships, paving the way forward to a future of peace, stability, and economic growth.

Peacebuilding of this sort may be especially critical for Israel and the Palestinian Territories, where conflict and violence have persisted for decades before the Gaza War. Reconstruction and reconciliation efforts require that businesses spread their operations across the divide. Organizations like the Portland Trust, based in the United Kingdom, have focused on the region on the basis that economic co-operation and dialogue between the parties is inseparable from diplomatic peacebuilding efforts. And such economic development (alongside political will) can create hope, ambition, and opportunities for Palestinians. The founding Chief Executive of The Portland Trust, Lord Jonathan Kestenbaum, brings a personal history to the work of reconciliation. His family’s own flight from Nazi persecution ultimately led them to the UK, where he grew up, and whilst a student in London, he was General Secretary (mazkir) of Bnei Akiva UK, a branch of the global youth movement. He then studied at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem in the 1980s completing an MA in education, and thereafter helped to build an international training program for young educators. As a dual national at the time, Kestenbaum was conscripted to military service, with this experience influencing his life-long commitment to reconciliation between Palestinians and Israelis with a particular focus on building bridges through economic co-operation.
Lord Kestenbaum returned home to the U.K. after a few years in Jerusalem and gave up his dual nationality, retaining only British citizenship. He helped found the Portland Trust, and spent many years fostering peace efforts between Israelis and Palestinians. This history gave him a grounding in the region, a commitment to co-existence and a familiarity that exemplifies how peacebuilding through commerce is not abstract policy but is instead built through relationships and real-life experiences. The Portland Trust has to date worked extensively to support Palestinians and Israelis through projects like the Palestinian Agriculture Impact Fund and the building of the city of Rawabi.
Personal experiences bring markets together, and when they come together, they accelerate growth and integration among an increasing number of actors. Each of these actors learns to empathize with their business partners, regardless of historical or political differences. The process reinforces peace, builds harmony, and creates trust. In the case of Israel and the Palestinian Territories, the process is needed alongside reconstruction efforts like Trump’s Board of Peace, which aims to produce lasting peace but has yet to break ground.
Peace is not guaranteed through economics; however, throughout the last century, and in the case of the Asia-Pacific, it has become the most reliable mechanism of sustaining peace, cultivating the types of relationships that grow closer instead of farther apart. Private investment adds a financial tie to the process; however, intentional relationships with an empathetic desire for peace fundamentally secure the process. Southeast Asia’s history, compared to Syria’s cautious reopening or Gaza’s Board of Peace, shows that commerce can lay groundwork that politics otherwise cannot. The region will need institutional support, perhaps even at the level of an ASEAN, but the foundation is growing. More inter-state commerce will bring stronger relationships, paving the way forward to a future of peace, stability, and economic growth.
When the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, ASEAN, was formed in 1967, the five founding states intended to produce a front against the spread of communism. The venture has since grown to include a total of 11 countries, producing a remarkable set of unforeseen consequences, from becoming the fifth-largest economy in the world to reinforcing peace across a swath of diverse and developing countries.
Instead of pursuing Cold War initiatives, the bloc has become increasingly integrated, tied together through manufacturing supply chains, trade infrastructure, and shared financial institutions like the Chiang Mai Initiative. ASEAN now produces over $4 trillion in GDP and has a population of 678 million people. The collaboration’s biggest success, however, has not simply been increased commerce. With economic integration comes regional stabilization and peace, a consequence further fostered by the signing of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) in 2020, which includes Australia, China, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea. Economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific has been the key driver of peace in the region ever since 1952 with the Treaty of San Francisco, and it serves today as a key example of how market mechanics can drive peacebuilding. In fact, it was ASEAN that eroded tensions from the Konfrontasi war in the early 1960s, and has solidified the climate of peace between the Southeast Asian members ever since.
James Wilson is an international affairs researcher focusing on economic development, regional integration, and peacebuilding. His research examines how trade, investment, and cross-border economic cooperation can contribute to stability in conflict-affected and emerging regions.
articles.summary: Economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific has been the key driver of peace since 1952.

articles.title: After the Bangsamoro Poll, Can Politics Maintain the Peace?
articles.full_text:
The peace process in the autonomous region will continue long after the votes have been counted and a new government formed.
The Bangsamoro Transition Authority votes on a proposed transition plan as an interim Bangsamoro Parliament in a special session on June 17, 2019.
On September 14, more than 2.3 million registered voters in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the southern Philippines will go to the polls for the first regular parliamentary election.
The immediate priority is that the elections should be peaceful, orderly, and credible, but beyond that there is another question that deserves attention: what will political competition look like in communities where political loyalties are changing, particularly in areas historically aligned with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF)? The answer could have important consequences for the peace process.
Election-related violence is not new to the Bangsamoro. It long predates the peace agreement with the MILF, and has often been associated with clan rivalries, private armed groups, and local political competition rooted in longstanding disputes. In many communities, elections can even appear relatively peaceful because political power is concentrated within a dominant family or network. The absence of violence, therefore, does not necessarily mean the absence of political contestation; sometimes, it simply reflects the absence of meaningful competition.
As I have argued previously, the movement’s political environment has become increasingly fragmented. Former allies now find themselves competing through different political formations, including the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) and the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP). Some may remain aligned with UBJP, while others have moved toward BFP or other competing parties and candidates. This raises the question of whether former allies who once operated within a common political and organizational framework can compete against one another without reproducing the patterns of conflict that the peace process was designed to transform.
There is a danger of interpreting every violent incident during the election period as evidence that the peace process is failing. This would overlook the longstanding nature of election-related violence in the Bangsamoro, which has long existed independently of the Muslim insurgency and the peace process. Thus, reports of localized violence that have appeared in recent weeks and months need to be examined carefully.  The important question here is where these incidents are occurring, who is involved, and whether they are connected to the emerging political dynamics that surround them.
At the same time, assuming that all such incidents are merely ordinary election violence could obscure emerging risks to the peace process. In this case, the important goal is whether local disputes can still be contained through the institutions and relationships established by the process.
The government of the Philippines and MILF have taken steps to maintain a ceasefire during the election period. The security mechanisms established under the peace process have coordinated arrangements for the polls, reflecting the recognition that political competition should not disrupt the cessation of hostilities.
But elections create challenges that cannot always be resolved through ceasefire arrangements alone. The difficulty becomes particularly apparent when communities that were previously aligned around the MILF become politically divided. At the community level, these divisions can cut across families, former comrades, and other longstanding relationships.
This is a normal feature of political transition. Former combatants are expected to become citizens and political actors with different choices and interests. However, it also represents a significant transformation. The peace process once depended in part on the ability of the MILF to maintain organizational cohesion and discipline among its forces and communities. Democratic politics, by contrast, requires the acceptance of political pluralism. Thus, the challenge is to ensure that the shift from political cohesion to political pluralism does not become a transition from one form of conflict to another.
The August 15 ambush of BARMM’s Interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua’s convoy has underscored the uncertainty in the pre-election environment.  The incident has been interpreted in a variety of ways, and there has been speculation on social media that individuals aligned with the BFP may have “staged” it, exposing deepening rifts within the MILF.  The MILF and Philippine government have condemned the incident, and authorities continue to investigate its circumstances. Nevertheless, this episode illustrates that in a fragile political transition, perceptions can themselves become consequential.
For a peace process built on confidence among former adversaries, this is a major concern. While a certain amount of violence may be inevitable, the important variable is whether political actors and communities continue to believe that disputes can be managed through legitimate institutions.
This is why the success of the September 14 elections will likely be gauged after election day. Will losing candidates accept the results? Will political parties trust the electoral institutions? Will communities regard the new parliament as legitimate? And will political disputes remain within the institutional arena, or will they spill into clan networks, armed structures, or other forms of coercion?
A credible election can strengthen these institutions by demonstrating that political authority can be acquired and contested through democratic means. But if political actors perceive the process as unfair, or if communities believe that political competition is being settled through intimidation or violence, distrust could extend beyond individual candidates to the institutions themselves, posing a more serious challenge to the peace process. Thus, the political system that emerges from them should be trusted enough to contain political competition peacefully.
The current fragmentation of the MILF’s political environment could also create opportunities for spoilers. An armed group could take advantage of a clan dispute, for example, or political actors could use a local incident to deepen divisions or challenge the legitimacy of an electoral outcome. A useful post-election assessment should examine whether any violent incidents involve former conflict actors, whether they spread across MILF communities, whether political actors mobilize around them, and whether existing peace mechanisms are able to contain them.
One encouraging development is that the Philippine government and MILF are already looking beyond election day. The joint implementing panels agreed to continue their engagement through a special meeting in Kuala Lumpur on September 25. This is important because whatever the electoral outcome, the peace process will remain unfinished.
If the election produces a result that one faction strongly dislikes, can the Philippine government and MILF still return to the negotiating table, and can disagreements over the emerging political order be managed without suspending cooperation on normalization? These may prove more consequential aspects of their agenda than whether the election itself is entirely free of localized incidents.
The first parliamentary election represents a significant milestone for the Bangsamoro peace process, but its ultimate success will be judged by the character of political competition after the ballots are counted.  The transition requires that, as political actors, former combatants accept that they can lose, that their former allies can become legitimate competitors, and that institutions must provide the arena in which those disagreements are settled.

articles.title: From 9/11 to Pahalgam: India’s Evolving Strategy in the Global War on Terror
articles.full_text:
The September 11 attacks reshaped how the world thinks about – and addresses – terrorism. India is no exception.
Soldiers pose for a photo with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at Adampur Air Force Base in Punjab on May 13, 2025, following Operation Sindoor.
Some incidents in world history not only leave deep scars on the soul of a nation but alter the nation’s trajectory irreversibly. The terror attack of September 11, 2001 was one such incident. A perfectly normal morning turned into a horrific nightmare when 19 al-Qaida terrorists hijacked four passenger planes, two of which crashed into the Twin Towers in New York and one into the Pentagon building outside of Washington, D.C. The Twin Towers came crashing down and the result was a death count of almost 3,000. 
The resultant national outrage and anger led to the United States leading its most extensive military mission since the Vietnam War, chasing al-Qaida and its leader Osama bin Laden into Afghanistan. In a military campaign lasting almost 20 years, al-Qaida was largely neutralized and Osama bin Laden was eventually tracked and killed in Pakistan on May 2, 2011. 
The 9/11 attacks led to profound changes in the United States as well, especially in matters of internal security. There was a clear mandate that no matter what, there cannot be another 9/11 type of incident on the American mainland ever again.  
In the Indian context however, it took decades of terror attacks before India similarly said, “no more.” Thanks to a policy crafted by Pakistan in the early 1990s to “bleed India through a thousand cuts” with cross-border terrorism, India endured a large number of terror attacks and losses, especially in Kashmir. But then one terror incident shook India like never before.
The terror attack in Pahalgam on April 22, 2025 killed 26 innocent civilians in a popular tourist spot in Kashmir. The attack was launched by terrorists belonging to The Resistance Force, an offshoot of the Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT). The anger and outrage in India were magnified many times over as the victims – all men – were specifically identified by their religion (Hindu, except for one Christian and one local Muslim who tried to intervene). The men were also shot dead in front of their wives.  
The resultant military operation, Operation Sindoor, launched by India into Pakistan on May 7, made clear India’s new resolve against terrorism.
While these two incidents – 9/11 and the Pahalgam attack – were separated by almost 24 years, they are united by two nations’ expressed resolve to fight terror to the ends of the Earth. But as the Pahalgam attack sadly showed, the war against terror has not been won. 
Al-Qaida may not be a force to reckon with in the form it was 25 years ago and it may no longer have leaders like Osama bin Laden who could attract and ideologically indoctrinate youth to join. But many smaller offshoots of al-Qaida still operate across the globe. In the Indian context, while LeT and other Pakistan-based terror groups may have been dealt a punishing blow by India, inputs from Pakistan indicate that there is a strong resolve to revive these groups. Therefore, the fight against terror isn’t over yet. 
It is therefore important to examine how terror is changing form and how nations are constantly evolving their strategies to stay ahead of the curve to counter and neutralize such threats before they manifest.
Over the past 25 years, the form terrorism has changed, as have the type of instruments used to carry out terror attacks. Naturally, the strategies to tackle terror have evolved as well. 
Unlike big terror groups like al-Qaida or the Islamic State (IS) in the past, terror groups have now morphed into smaller and more autonomous groups. Lone wolf attacks are now becoming the norm and technologies like drones, cyber, and even artificial intelligence are being used by terror groups. Indirect attacks like cyberattacks on key energy and banking infrastructure are complementing high-impact physical attacks on the population. 
Hierarchical organizations and organized training camps are increasingly giving way to more fluid structures, which operate through affiliations and franchises, encrypted communications, cryptocurrencies, social media, and loosely connected cells. Campaigns seeking territorial control like the IS in Iraq and Syria are being replaced by terror campaigns to disrupt social cohesion within a country and bleed nations financially.
And, accordingly, strategies to fight terror by countries too are evolving rapidly. Counterterrorism has evolved from a predominantly military campaign into a much broader strategy incorporating multiple instruments of state power like intelligence, financial surveillance, border control, cyber monitoring, deradicalization, and international cooperation. When military action is taken, it takes the form of precision operations through cutting-edge standoff weapon platforms.
The fight against terror in India had a frustrating beginning. In most cases, the response to terrorist attacks was limited to sectoral military operations, tightening border controls, and issuing warnings to Pakistan. In some cases, it also led to cutting off diplomatic ties for some time. 
The first such terror attack was the hijacking of Air India’s flight IC-814 on December 24, 1999, just a few months after the Kargil war. With very few options then and increasing public pressure, India agreed to release two Pakistan-based terrorists, Ahmed Omar Shiekh and Masood Azhar, in exchange for over 160 civilian hostages. Massod Azhar went on to establish Jaish-e-Mohammad (JeM), the Pakistan-based terrorist group that later launched a terror attack on the Indian Parliament on December 13, 2001. Caught by surprise, India ordered a full-scale military mobilization under Operation Parakaram, but it ultimately ended without a bullet being fired.
The 26/11 Mumbai terror attack in 2008 was a milestone in many ways. Widely considered as India’s 9/11 moment, it brought global attention to India’s war against terror. Although once again India did not end up punishing Pakistan for the attack, it did lead to a major security review and structural changes. The National Investigative Agency (NIA) was formed as a result, with sweeping powers on matters of internal national security. The NIA is now functioning as the central counterterrorism law enforcement agency in India. 
The mandate of fighting terror expanded to include stronger intelligence coordination, tighter coastal security and border surveillance, specialized forces to fight terror, and cooperation between central and state agencies. The overall responsibility for coastal security was placed under the Indian Navy. 
Tracking and monitoring terror finance too became a key instrument in the fight against terror.  The Multi Agency Center, which was established in December 2001 as a part of the key recommendations of the Kargil Review Committee, also became a key coordination platform for intelligence exchange and cooperation against terror. However, most of India’s anti-terrorism measures remained passive, reactive, and preventive.
It was only after 2014, when the Modi government came to power, that the intent to deliver a decisive response to any act of terror grew firm. Counterterrorism operations in Kashmir were given a new momentum and measures to block infiltration across the Line of Control were strengthened. 
A terror attack on September 18, 2016 by JeM terrorists against an army camp in Uri, Kashmir, led to the first cross-border surgical strikes by the Indian Army, which destroyed multiple terrorist camps and infrastructure in Pakistan. It was not only a strong reply to the terror attack but also signaled a major shift in India’s strategic policy and rules of engagement regarding cross-border terrorism. 
While it did deter Pakistan to some extent, it did not end its terror campaign. On February 14, 2019, JeM terrorists unleashed another terror attack, this time on a police convoy in Pulwama, Kashmir, killing 40 soldiers. Upping the ante, this time, the India Air Force launched strikes on a terror camp of JeM in Balakot, Pakistan on February 26. It was the first time that the Indian Air Force had crossed into Pakistani airspace to launch a strike against terror. 
However, it was the terror attack in Pahalgam on April 22, 2025 that outraged the nation like never before. Modi vowed to track the terrorists “to the ends of the Earth.” With an aim to deliver a decisive blow to the terror network in Pakistan, the Indian Armed Forces launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, hitting the heart of the Pakistan-based terror network. Within 96 hours, nine major terrorist camps destroyed and India had even hit key military assets like airfields and radar stations, forcing Pakistan to seek a ceasefire.
However, the Indian experience tells us that the fight against terror is far from over. With Pakistan unlikely to give up on its policy of state-sponsored terror against India, new forms of threats are likely to emerge. India therefore cannot think that Operation Sindoor is enough to deter any future terror attacks from across the border. In the fight against terror, no deterrence strategy can be absolute. It has to evolve, keeping pace with technology and terror tactics, and hope to stay one step ahead. 
A key to this constantly evolving thought is PRAHAAR, India’s first comprehensive National Counter Terrorism Policy & Strategy which was unveiled on February 23, 2026. This provides a national counterterrorism framework for prevention of, and responding   to terrorist activities and radicalization through coordinated “whole of government” and “whole of society” approaches.
As the world marks the 25 years of the 9/11 attack, the lesson is not whether terror has been defeated but whether nations are equipped well enough to disrupt and deter future terror threats. The success of any strategy is measured by its outcomes. Even if one major terror attack succeeds despite hundreds of potential terror attacks being thwarted, the strategy would still be termed a failure. 
The October 7, 2023 Hamas terror attack into Israel is an example: the best of intelligence and overwhelming military superiority could not preempt or prevent the attack. The events of October 7 not only killed almost 1,200 people in Israel but unleashed a brutal conflict in Gaza and West Asia, which still continues to this day. 
For India, the fight against terror predates 9/11. Over 25 years later, that fight continues, strengthened now with a new political-military resolve and constantly evolving methods of deterrence.
Some incidents in world history not only leave deep scars on the soul of a nation but alter the nation’s trajectory irreversibly. The terror attack of September 11, 2001 was one such incident. A perfectly normal morning turned into a horrific nightmare when 19 al-Qaida terrorists hijacked four passenger planes, two of which crashed into the Twin Towers in New York and one into the Pentagon building outside of Washington, D.C. The Twin Towers came crashing down and the result was a death count of almost 3,000.
articles.summary: The September 11 attacks reshaped how the world thinks about – and addresses – terrorism. India is no exception.

articles.title: From 9/11 to the Iran War, Pakistan-US Ties Remain Transactional
articles.full_text:
There’s a reason the nation’s relationship with the U.S. has fluctuated while India’s has largely held steady.
U.S. President Donald Trump is presented gifts from Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir in the Oval Office of the White House, Washington D.C., Sep. 25, 2025.
Twenty-five years ago, the September 11 attacks transformed Pakistan’s relationship with the United States. Almost overnight, Pakistan went from facing American sanctions and limited diplomatic attention to becoming a frontline partner in the U.S.-led war in Afghanistan.
In its counterterrorism cooperation, Pakistan offered vital ground-and air-based logistical transit to Afghanistan as well as intelligence and military action. In return, the United States provided financial reimbursement and military assistance in the form of subsidized sale of military hardware and technology. 
The relationship became increasingly strained as the two sides accused each other of failing to deliver what had been promised. Yet the two sides remained close as long as Washington needed Pakistan for the war in Afghanistan.
When the U.S. military withdrew from Afghanistan in August 2021, much of the urgency behind the relationship disappeared. Washington’s political attention declined, although counterterrorism, trade, health, and other forms of engagement continued at the institutional level.
Twenty-five years after 9/11, Pakistan and the United States appear to have entered another period of warm relations. Pakistan has again presented itself as a useful partner through mediation between Washington and Tehran, alongside cryptocurrency deals, critical mineral investments, and counterterrorism cooperation.
As Pakistan mediates in the Iran-U.S. war, given the difficulties of reaching a truce, there’s a constant fear of Pakistani leaders becoming the eventual fall guys. To avert that outcome, Islamabad has been investing significant time and resources to the success of the mediation efforts. The outcome has been far from assured.
Some see this as another example of Pakistan over-promising and falling short of delivering. But there’s a bigger question behind recent events: Why does every revival of Pakistan-U.S. relations require another geopolitical crisis?
The problem is that Pakistan-U.S. relations lack enough independent commercial, institutional, academic, and professional connections to maintain political engagement when the immediate geopolitical transaction ends. 
The contrast with India-U.S. relations helps explain this problem.
During the early 2000s, India-U.S. ties were largely driven from the top. President George W. Bush and Prime Minister Manmohan Singh pushed through the civil nuclear agreement despite serious opposition within both countries. Over the following two decades, the relationship created its own institutional and economic constituencies. Technology companies, universities, defense manufacturers, investors, and the Indian diaspora now have their own reasons for sustaining it. Daniel Markey described this as “a reversal of the motive forces behind U.S.-India ties: from top-down to bottom-up.”
This explains why India-U.S. relations have survived serious political headwinds during current U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term. The two countries disagreed over trade, immigration, Russia, Pakistan, and the war with Iran. Yet their military, economic, and technological engagement has continued. 
The clearest evidence is the new ten-year Framework for the U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership signed in October 2025 and the expansion of the Biden-era iCET (initiative on Critical and Emerging Technologies) mechanism into TRUST (Transforming Relations into Utilizing Strategic Technologies) in February 2025, covering artificial intelligence, semiconductors, quantum computing, biotechnology, energy, space, critical minerals, and pharmaceutical supply chains. 
When it comes to China, the Trump administration’s narrower focus on denying Beijing control of the First Island Chain arguably reduces India’s direct operational relevance compared with Japan and the Philippines. India’s relevance in the U.S. strategic competition with China will therefore depend on whether Washington continues to see the Indian and Pacific oceans as disjointed theaters and whether India remains restricted to its immediate neighborhood.
Pakistan faces different conditions. For one, it is a close strategic and defense partner of China. Although democratic credentials are not attracting as much U.S. attention under the Trump administration, there are other constraints on the relationship. Pakistan’s security problems discourage tourism, investment, and academic exchange. Its universities and think tanks have fewer sustained partnerships with American institutions. Pakistan also lacks India’s economic scale, technological capacity, and purchasing power.
This does not mean that Pakistan lacks bottom-up ties with the United States. The United States is Pakistan’s largest single export market and one of the largest FDI sources. American companies operate profitably in sectors of Pakistan’s economy – franchising, fast-moving consumer goods, agribusiness and financial services – with growing interest in information technology, renewable energy, and healthcare. 
The Karachi-based American Business Council has more than 55 member companies, most of them Fortune 500 firms. The Lahore-based American Business Forum has 23 founding members and 22 associate members. Moreover, thousands of Pakistani healthcare professionals, STEM professionals, and academics actively bridge the economic and educational landscapes of both societies. 
Yet these connections remain demonstrably insufficient to determine the overall direction of the relationship. Political leaders, military officials, and regional events continue to provide the ballast for Pakistan-U.S..
Pakistan has apparently sought new ways to demonstrate its utility to Washington. Critical minerals, cryptocurrency, counterterrorism, and mediation with Iran all form part of this effort. While these initiatives can produce real economic and diplomatic gains, they could also reproduce the old transactional cycle if they remain agreements among senior officials or a small number of political- and military-linked businesses.
It is difficult for Pakistan to reproduce India’s bottom-up relationship with the United States, given India’s relative economic scale and its geopolitical position vis-à-vis China. 
Still, Islamabad can become less dependent on its temporary geopolitical utility. This would require producing high value-added textile exports and diversifying the overall export supplies. Pakistan can also do more to attract U.S. grassroots engagement by improving domestic security, ensuring constant energy supply, sustaining the current simplified tariff and tax regime to attract investment, protecting contracts and intellectual property, and building stronger links among universities, think tanks, and businesses. 
Pakistan should also use its diaspora for professional, technological, and commercial cooperation instead of viewing it mainly as a source of remittances and political support.
Pursuing these policies will ensure Pakistan-U.S. integration beyond just economic diplomacy. Instead of announcing deals and foreign visits to catch ephemeral attention, Islamabad must commit toward building industries and relationships with the U.S. that continue after the leaders leave office or the geopolitical focus shifts. Doing so will give the partnership a stronger foundation.

When the U.S. military withdrew from Afghanistan in August 2021, much of the urgency behind the relationship disappeared. Washington’s political attention declined, although counterterrorism, trade, health, and other forms of engagement continued at the institutional level.

articles.title: Tashiev and the Letter of 75: Charges Reclassified, Sentences Lessened, Confusion Reigns
articles.full_text:
Both Tashiev’s lawyers and the prosecutors filed appeals after the July verdict, the former seeking complete acquittal and the latter harsher sentencing. Neither has gotten what they asked for.
When the trial of the former head of Kyrgyzstan’s State Committee for National Security, Kamchybek Tashiev, ended in July the judge delivered what appeared to be a damning verdict followed by an absurdist reprieve. 
Tashiev – alongside former Speaker of the Zhogorku Kenesh Nurlanbek Turgunbek uulu, former Member of Parliament Kurmankul Zulushev, and five others – was found guilty of a coup attempt under Article 326 (“Violent seizure or retention of power, as well as an attempt to violently change the constitutional order”) of the Kyrgyz criminal code and acquitted of abuse of office charges.
Tashiev and the rest were sentenced to four years in prison – the prosecutors had sought nine. The judge immediately replaced the prison terms with three years of supervised probation.

The court apparently reclassified the charges from a coup attempt under Article 326 to “obstruction of the exercise of electoral rights,” Article 195.

Latypbek Nuralimov, a lawyer representing Turgunbek uulu, told TASS, “They sentenced him to four years in prison, but they applied probation [for two years] because the crime is less serious.”
Chinara Dzhakupbekova, a lawyer representing Kursan Asanov, a former deputy minister of internal affairs charged in the case, expressed confusion over how Article 195 could even apply to the case. articles.title: What the AfD’s Rise in Germany Means for China-EU Relations
articles.full_text:
China’s economic success is bringing industrial disruption that empowers populist groups in Europe. That could lead to significant long-term challenges for the Chinese government and businesses.
The September 6 state election in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, resulted in a decisive victory for Alternative for Germany (AfD), which secured nearly 44 percent of the vote. It marked a stunning rise for the party, which is widely considered to belong to the far-right of the political spectrum.
While the AfD’s performance is fundamentally a domestic political development driven by local grievances, energy costs, and other factors, this outcome offers an important, often overlooked perspective on the economic policy dialogue between the EU and China. 
The rapid ascent of Chinese firms in key sectors like automotive and chemicals has accelerated pressure on legacy European manufacturers. The subsequent corporate restructuring and job losses fuel public anxiety that political groups can leverage to gain ground. If this trend continues, short-term commercial gains for Chinese players could later give way to long-term operational hurdles, forcing them to navigate an EU defined by more political fragmentation and regulatory unpredictability. 
While not a silver bullet, adopting a more sustainable, localized engagement strategy in Europe offers Chinese enterprises a way to protect their market access while ensuring European host regions benefit as well.
In the September 6 regional elections, the AfD won more than 40 percent of the votes, falling short of an outright majority but securing a win that signifies a crushing victory over incumbent Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union, the popularity of which collapsed from above 37 percent in 2021 to below 18 percent. 
On the surface, a regional election in eastern Germany may seem distant from the EU’s foreign trade policy. A closer look, however, suggests otherwise. The AfD’s success draws attention to an often overlooked dimension in the ongoing China-EU economic debate: the impact on European political dynamics. 
For years, bilateral economic discourse between Brussels and Beijing has revolved around familiar claims. The EU points to Chinese industrial subsidies, market access barriers, and product dumping as unfair distortions that hurt European competitiveness. The Chinese narrative counters that Europe’s struggles are self-inflicted and stem from factors like high energy prices and regulatory burdens.
The election results in Saxony-Anhalt suggest that another critical element belongs in this conversation: the feedback loop between rapid market shifts and domestic political volatility.
While local factors remain key drivers of the AfD’s rise, industrial disruption acts as a catalyst. In the lead-up to the election, announcements of massive layoffs and structural adjustments at Volkswagen became “political rocket fuel” on the AfD campaign trail. These cutbacks were driven in part by intense competition from Chinese automakers, which have rapidly seized market share in China and the EU. Similar market penetration is unfolding across other industries, including chemicals and technology, which later down the line may turn into catalysts for broader socio-economic friction. 
The commercial success of Chinese companies in Europe is built on a variety of factors, such as strong price competitiveness, high quality, and supply chain efficiency. Offering quality goods well below European price points yields immediate market share gains. Yet focusing exclusively on rapid volume growth creates secondary risks. When aggressive market entry coincides with local manufacturing contraction, the indirect spillover effects may feed voter anxiety that turns into support for populist platforms, accelerating political shifts across the continent.
Political movements like the AfD tend to be eurosceptic and nationalistic. The AfD, for instance, has demonstrated strong rhetoric against the EU, even raising the possibility of Germany leaving the bloc, dubbed Dexit. Regardless of the prospect of the plan, the tone is indicative of the movement’s attitude toward the EU.
Such sentiments may gain ground in the future, as the political shift seen in Saxony-Anhalt mirrors broader continental trends, where the AfD and similar political movements continue to build momentum. Within the European Union, where trade measures, retaliatory tariffs, and foreign policy decisions rely on qualified majority voting or complete consensus, the proliferation and strengthening of such political movements could make reaching coherent policy decisions far more difficult than it is today.
While the EU is already pursuing de-risking strategies and anti-subsidy duties against certain Chinese imports, the rise of euroscepticism threatens to further deepen existing divisions between member states, resulting in an EU that is even more erratic, protectionist, and unpredictable, marked by policy gridlock and inconsistent domestic regulations. Ultimately, such a scenario would make it significantly more difficult for Chinese companies to navigate the EU market.
As the EU and China gear up for the second meeting of the trade and investment consultation mechanism in the autumn, the fundamental takeaway is that a more durable, collaborative framework for economic engagement is urgently needed. Unchecked business expansion powered by aggressive pricing yields short-term benefits in the form of increasing market share. However, it risks longer-term challenges if it exacerbates host economies’ industrial distress.
While no single strategy solves every structural challenge, adopting a more sustainable market-entry model offers a path forward. Chinese businesses that prioritize joint ventures, technology transfers, localized manufacturing, and direct job creation for European workers can help stabilize China-EU economic relations while safeguarding their own long-term commercial investments. 
Beyond traditional equity partnerships, co-developing green transition infrastructure, establishing joint research and development initiatives, and crafting shared compliance benchmarks that bolster supply chain resilience offer promising avenues for cooperation. To realize these goals, it is imperative to explore the specific mechanics of such market entry through close collaboration among researchers, corporate executives, and policymakers.

articles.title: Can Southeast Asia Benefit From the China-US AI Race?
articles.full_text:
As Washington and Beijing compete to turn technology into influence, the region needs to negotiate what it gains and what it is expected to give up.
Southeast Asia’s familiar predicament – being asked to choose between Washington and Beijing – is acquiring an artificial intelligence dimension. In August, Reuters reported that a draft U.S. State Department letter warned partners against combining participation in Pax Silica, the U.S.-led technology initiative, with competing arrangements. The letter didn’t include specific names, but the obvious inference was that Washington was trying to discourage participation in China’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO).
The draft was undated, and Reuters could not establish if it would be sent or whether it would change. Even so, its political ambition was clear: Washington wanted cooperation on AI to carry a stronger expectation of alignment.
For Southeast Asian governments, the danger extends beyond an uncomfortable diplomatic decision. Technology agreements made today can shape which choices remain affordable tomorrow. If a country’s businesses and public services become heavily dependent on one foreign supplier, resisting that supplier’s government may become more costly even without a formal demand to take sides. The region therefore needs to negotiate development benefits and political room for maneuver together, while competing powers still have reasons to court Southeast Asia.
Separate U.S. and Chinese initiatives are drawing countries into different bargains. Pax Silica, launched in December 2025, brings together countries seeking closer cooperation across technology supply chains, from critical minerals to AI systems. Its appeal lies in the prospect of investment, industrial partnerships, and advanced American technology.
WAICO began with 29 countries signing its founding agreement in Shanghai on July 16. By August 12, Foreign Minister Wang Yi reported 38 founding members. Its purpose is to “promote international cooperation and global governance on AI,” with a particular focus on making sure Global South countries have equitable access to this pivotal technology.
These parallel arrangements have not yet divided the world into exclusive camps. Kazakhstan joined both, as Reuters noted. Uzbekistan joined WAICO and is actively seeking membership in Pax Silica. Singapore described the Pax Silica declaration as non-binding and presented its participation in terms of mutual economic benefit. 
The reported U.S. letter matters precisely because it would narrow that flexibility. Whether Washington can actually get its partners to make a binary choice depends on the benefits it offers, the costs it can impose, and the willingness of partners to accept its terms.
Beijing’s offer speaks to governments worried about being left behind. WAICO presents developing countries with a place in discussions about AI governance, alongside promises of training and practical cooperation. In July, Chinese president Xi Jinping pledged 5,000 training opportunities for developing countries over five years and AI application cooperation centers with regional organizations, including ASEAN. Such promises address a concern that great power debates often neglect: how countries with limited resources can put AI to productive use.
This also serves China’s strategic purpose. Bringing more governments into a Shanghai-based institution strengthens Beijing’s claim to speak for countries poorly represented in existing technology governance. Its emphasis on access makes U.S. restrictions easier to portray as an effort to preserve privilege. Yet WAICO’s inclusive nature does not settle who will influence the agenda or capture the commercial gains. Southeast Asian participants should judge China’s offer by the capabilities it helps them acquire and the influence they gain over the cooperation itself.
Washington has a different source of bargaining power: the ability to restrict access to advanced computing equipment. U.S. guidance issued in May reaffirmed that exports of certain equipment to companies based in China and their overseas subsidiaries can require American approval. For a Chinese company operating in Malaysia, this means its access to equipment may still depend on decisions made in Washington. Kuala Lumpur’s diplomatic friendships cannot, by themselves, settle that question.
The American offer also increasingly combines access with a broader commercial relationship. The American AI Exports Program is designed to promote packages that bring hardware, software, and services together, backed by possible financing and government support. U.S. development finance officials have explicitly tied their ambitions to trusted suppliers and American strategic interests. For a recipient, an attractive investment package could therefore influence a much wider range of future technology purchases.
The political effect need not begin with coercion. A well-integrated system may work well, attract investment and win support from domestic businesses. As those benefits accumulate, however, the cost of changing suppliers rises. Governments may eventually face pressure from employers, investors, and public agencies to preserve access, even when relations with the supplier’s home government deteriorate. Commercial success can thus give a foreign partnership political staying power. That is one route through which an AI bloc could develop before countries formally agree to belong to one.
Not every foreign dependency is automatically bad, however. Southeast Asian economies can gain from American investment, Chinese technology, and partnerships with both. Rejecting those opportunities in pursuit of complete technological independence would impose substantial costs. The more real test is whether cooperation leaves local firms and institutions better able to make their own decisions, or simply better equipped to keep buying from the same partner.
Singapore shows that some choices remain open. Its participation in Pax Silica has coexisted with the use of Chinese-origin technology. AI Singapore’s SEA-LION models draw on both Alibaba’s Qwen and Google’s Gemma, adapting them to Southeast Asian languages and contexts. Local expertise allows Singapore to select and adapt foreign tools for regional purposes. 
Other governments can exercise influence through the resources and permissions investors need. Thailand’s reported September 4 pause on 166 data center projects, covering both projects under construction and those awaiting approval, came amid efforts to establish rules on resource use and economic benefits. It illustrates a development question often hidden by the geopolitical contest: how much should a host country gain in return for supplying land, electricity, water, and public support? Foreign investment can be welcome while its terms remain negotiable.
That bargaining power has limits. Investors can look elsewhere, governments face different fiscal pressures, and access to the most advanced technology is uneven. A country seeking basic, affordable AI services faces a different negotiation from one trying to become a regional technology hub. Not every country in Southeast Asia enjoys Singapore’s expertise or commands the same level of commercial interest. But those differences make clear national priorities more necessary: governments need to know what benefits they will receive for making certain commitments. 
If Washington is going to attempt to force the question of alignment, it needs to make clear what the returns will be. Southeast Asian governments should press for clarity about access, financing, and the circumstances under which cooperation could be restricted. Restrictions directed at particular security risks should not automatically become demands to abandon unrelated partnerships. If the United States asks countries to bear the economic costs of excluding Chinese suppliers, it should be prepared to offer dependable and competitive alternatives.
Beijing should face equally concrete questions. Promises of shared development need to produce sustained training, affordable services, and opportunities for local businesses. WAICO’s participants should seek a meaningful role in setting priorities, alongside clear commitments about what cooperation will deliver. An expanding membership gives China diplomatic standing; members are entitled to expect benefits beyond attending Chinese-hosted meetings.
ASEAN can help governments negotiate from better information. Its existing AI governance work provides a starting point for sharing expertise and comparing how foreign partnerships serve regional needs. Members could coordinate expectations on training, local participation, and the continuity of essential services, while retaining different diplomatic relationships. Such cooperation would make it harder for suppliers to benefit from governments negotiating in isolation.
The emerging AI rivalry will test Southeast Asia’s capacity to turn external attention into lasting advantage. Refusing to choose sides remains a defensible diplomatic position, but it needs material support: capable domestic institutions, worthwhile alternatives and agreements that preserve future choices. articles.title: Another New Job for Saida Mirziyoyeva: Manager of the Tashkent International Financial Center
articles.full_text:
The daughter of the Uzbek president is head of the presidential administration and now also manager of Tashkent’s ambitious gambit to attract foreign investors.
Saida Mirziyoyeva has another new job. By presidential decree – that is, by order of her own father, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, whose administration she heads – Mirziyoyeva has been appointed manager of the Tashkent International Financial Center (TIFC). 
The TIFC was proposed in a March 2026 presidential decree as part of an effort to bring in long-term foreign direct investment. The financial center aims to attract investors in a range of industries from banking, investment, and insurance services to digital assets, Islamic finance, and green tech, in addition to professional services like auditing, legal counsel, and fintech. 
Signed into law in July, the TIFC will operate under a special legal regime, based on English law, with a unique regulatory framework and an independent commercial court.  With this arrangement, Uzbekistan seeks to address long-standing concerns foreign investors have had by carving out a legal space that isn’t governed strictly by Uzbek law.
In pursuit of attracting foreign investors, those engaged in the TIFC will reportedly be able to hire foreigners without obtaining the usually required work permits and take advantage of special entry visa options. They will be allowed use foreign currency or cryptocurrency for payments and other monetary obligations and will benefit from tax and customs breaks until 2076.
In announcing the signing of the law in July by Mirziyoyev, Mirziyoyeva said on social media, “This is one of the most important pieces of economic news of the year and the result of reforms that we pursued for almost ten years.” She went on to argue that the TIFC’s special structures “are the mechanisms to which global investors, banks, investment funds and international financial companies are accustomed. This new regulatory ecosystem should make the country more attractive for capital, modern financial services and major international projects.”
According to a Telegram statement posted by presidential press secretary Sherzod Asadov, as manager, Mirziyoyeva will organize the agenda and preside over meetings in the absence of the financial center’s chairman – the chairman is, by law, Mirziyoyev. She will coordinate the TIFC’s launch and represent the financial center in dealings with international organizations, investors and partners – both those abroad and in Uzbekistan. She will have the authority to conclude agreements, establish working groups and “engage experts.”
In June 2025, Mirziyoyeva was appointed head of the presidential administration, effectively becoming her father’s chief of staff. Uzbekistan’s government does not have a vice president post, making Mirziyoyeva the highest-ranking official after her father. In August 2026, Uzbekistan adopted a new law regulating the presidential administration that granted Mirziyoyeva sweeping new powers – everything from judicial reforms to anti-corruption, and an automatic seat on the Security Council – and lifetime immunity to boot. She holds an extraordinarily wide range of power while being subject to no accountability outside of her father’s opinion. 
Now she’s also in charge of Tashkent’s ambitious gambit to attract foreign investment.
Uzbekistan is not unique in turning to family to consolidate power. In neighboring Tajikistan, President Emomali Rahmon’s son, Rustam Emomali, holds a variety of important positions – he’s chairman of the National Assembly and also mayor of the capital, both posts he was appointed to by his father, in 2020 and 2017, respectively. As chairman of the Nation Assembly, Emomali is constitutionally next in line for the presidency, should his father resign or otherwise vacate the post. In Turkmenistan, Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov passed the presidency on to his son Serdar in 2022 before government changed its structure to give the elder Berdimuhamedov a new position technically above that of the president.
Nepotism may be political comforting for those in power, but’s not necessarily comforting for investors.

The TIFC was proposed in a March 2026 presidential decree as part of an effort to bring in long-term foreign direct investment. The financial center aims to attract investors in a range of industries from banking, investment, and insurance services to digital assets, Islamic finance, and green tech, in addition to professional services like auditing, legal counsel, and fintech. 
Catherine Putz is managing editor of The Diplomat.
articles.summary: The daughter of the Uzbek president is head of the presidential administration and now also manager of Tashkent’s ambitious gambit to attract foreign investors.

articles.title: East Asia’s Quiet Race to Find the Universe’s Missing Mass
articles.full_text:

Scientists at work at the China Jinping Underground Laboratory in Sichuan Province.
On September 1, 2026, physicists with the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, a ten-ton liquid xenon detector buried nearly a mile underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota, announced they had recorded a single particle interaction that standard background processes struggle to explain. The event, drawn from 220 days of data collected between March 2023 and April 2024, sits at a statistical significance of about 2.6 sigma, far short of the 5-sigma threshold physicists require to claim a discovery, but it’s the strongest hint LZ has produced to date that a weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) may have grazed its xenon target. It’s potentially a step forward in LZ’s main goal: to detect dark matter.
LZ’s spokesperson, Professor Rick Gaitskell of Brown University, was careful to frame it as intriguing rather than conclusive. “With only one event, we don’t want to get ahead of ourselves,” he said. “We are not claiming to have seen dark matter. But we have seen something interesting that we want to share with the scientific community for their input.” His collaborators similarly stressed that unexpected backgrounds have fooled sensitive detectors before.
Beyond the scientific question itself, it’s notable where the result was unveiled: not in the United States, but at the TeV Particle Astrophysics (TeVPA) 2026 conference in Japan. That is a small but telling sign of how central East Asia has become to the global effort to identify dark matter, the invisible substance thought to make up roughly 25 percent of all matter in the universe. Dark matter’s existence is inferred from galactic rotation and gravitational lensing, but it has never been directly observed.
While LZ, Europe’s XENONnT, and Italy’s DarkSide-20k dominate headlines in the West, China, South Korea, and Japan run their own parallel programs, some of them world-leading in sensitivity, others aimed at settling decades-old controversies that Western experiments cannot resolve alone.
China’s dark matter program is anchored at the China Jinping Underground Laboratory (CJPL) in Sichuan Province, shielded by 2,400 meters of rock, making it the deepest operational underground laboratory in the world, with a cosmic-ray flux roughly two orders of magnitude lower than shallower European sites.
The flagship experiment there is PandaX-4T, a dual-phase liquid xenon time-projection chamber holding 3.7 tons of ultra-pure xenon, run by a consortium including Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Peking University, and the University of Science and Technology of China. Its most recent full-exposure result, published in Physical Review Letters in January 2025 using 1.54 ton-years of data, set the tightest limit yet on spin-independent WIMP-nucleon interactions for dark matter particles above 100 giga-electronvolts (GeV) putting it on a par with or ahead of LZ and XENONnT in that mass range. PandaX has also pushed into more exotic territory, setting the strongest constraints to date on hypothetical dark photons and axion-like particles using low-energy data from the same detector.
A second, complementary Chinese effort, the China Dark Matter Experiment (CDEX), also based at CJPL, uses ultra-sensitive germanium detectors rather than xenon to hunt for lighter dark matter candidates in the 1-10 GeV range. Its CDEX-1B result, published in 2019, excluded the parameter space claimed by two earlier controversial signals (DAMA/LIBRA and CoGeNT) at high confidence for low-mass WIMPs. The collaboration is now building CDEX-50, a 50-kilogram germanium array, at the newly expanded CJPL-II site.
China also pursues dark matter from orbit. The DAMPE satellite (known as Wukong, launched in 2015 from Jiuquan) measures cosmic-ray electrons and positrons up to several tera-electronvolts (TeV), looking for the kind of spectral anomalies that dark matter annihilation might produce. Its first Nature paper in 2017 reported an unexplained break in the electron-positron spectrum around 0.9 TeV, a result the mission continues to refine with larger datasets.
South Korea’s contribution is narrower in scope but scientifically pivotal. The COSINE-100 experiment, run at the Yangyang Underground Laboratory by a South Korea-U.S.-U.K.-Brazil collaboration under South Korea’s Institute for Basic Science, was built specifically to test that claim using the same sodium-iodide crystal technology as DAMA/LIBRA. A companion study combining COSINE-100 with Spain’s ANAIS-112 experiment pushed the exclusion of the DAMA/LIBRA claim even further. It is one of the clearest examples of an Asian experiment resolving, rather than merely contributing to, a foundational debate in the field.
Japan’s Kamioka Observatory, run by the University of Tokyo’s Institute for Cosmic Ray Research, has a long pedigree in underground physics, best known internationally for the Super-Kamiokande neutrino detector. Its dedicated dark matter effort, XMASS, operated an 832-kilogram liquid xenon detector from 2013 until it ceased data-taking in 2019; its results, like those of most direct-detection experiments, found no confirmed WIMP signal but helped rule out large regions of parameter space and cross-checked earlier claims of annual modulation.
Since then, Japanese efforts have shifted toward a different technique: directional detection. The NEWAGE experiment, led by Kobe University and also housed at Kamioka, uses a gaseous time-projection chamber designed not just to detect a WIMP interaction but to reconstruct the direction it came from – a capability that could, in principle, distinguish a genuine dark matter signal from background radiation, since dark matter should appear to stream from a consistent direction as the Earth moves through the galactic halo. The collaboration reported in 2025 that it had installed a new, lower-radioactivity detector module at Kamioka and begun final commissioning, with results expected in the coming cycle.
Japan’s more understated role, however, may be as convener. By hosting TeVPA 2026, the conference where LZ chose to unveil its most significant result to date, Japan positioned itself, if only for a week, at the center of the global conversation on dark matter, alongside its own domestic research base.
None of the Asian efforts described here has found a dark matter particle; nor has anyone else. But it is clear that East Asia’s research ecosystem has matured well past a supporting role. China Jinping Underground Laboratory is arguably the best-shielded laboratory on the planet; PandaX and CDEX post limits that rival or beat their American and European counterparts. articles.title: What Kazakhstan’s New Unicameral Parliament Means for Its Foreign Policy
articles.full_text:
Although Kazakhstan’s Senate rarely exercised its influence over the country’s foreign policy, its abolishment has left the country without the diplomatic expertise and sequential vetting that the upper chamber once provided.
In early June, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed enabling laws, putting into effect the new constitution passed via referendum in March 2026. Among the most significant changes was the abolishment of the bicameral parliament and its replacement with a new unicameral body, the Kurultai, whose 145 deputies were subsequently elected through party lists on August 23.
While the domestic consequences of the changes to the legislature have been debated widely, the question of how they will affect Kazakhstan’s foreign policymaking remains underexamined.     
With the abolishment of the bicameral parliament – comprising an upper house, the Senate, and a lower house, the Mazhilis – the number of committees under the new legislature was reduced to eight, down from 13 (seven in the former Mazhilis and six in the Senate).
Under Article 61 of the prior constitution, the dual-committee structure provided checks and balances within the legislative branch. The Mazhilis’s Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defense, and Security served as the primary chamber for drafting, amending, and holding preliminary readings for security and international agreements, while the Senate’s Committee on International Relations, Defense, and Security acted as a second layer of technical and diplomatic vetting. Treaties and defense pacts moved sequentially through both chambers and both committees. The Senate could approve, return for revisions, or reject a bill passed by the Mazhilis.
Another structural change lies in how deputies are selected. In the previous bicameral parliament, the president could appoint a certain number of deputies, and often appointed seasoned diplomats such as former ambassadors, ex-ministers, and career officials. The most prominent example is the current president, Tokayev, who was twice appointed as Senate speaker. Under the previous constitution, the Senate speaker was designated to become acting president if a sitting president stepped down or could not perform their duties – that’s what happened in 2019 when Nursultan Nazarbayev resigned. When Nazarbayev resigned, that arrangement delivered the presidency to an experienced diplomat, an outcome read at the time as a signal that Nazarbayev considered foreign policy the greatest challenge of the transition.
Although the previous Senate could reject the Mazhilis’ bills, it rarely rejected one outright. A strong presidency in Kazakhstan mostly sets direction of foreign policy, and the upper and lower chambers were typically aligned with the president’s objectives and policies. There was a case in 2011 when the Senate rejected a Mazhilis bill on the planned deployment of military personnel to Afghanistan. Most of the time, however, the two chambers did not come into conflict, and international agreements and treaties passed smoothly.
Under the new Kurultai, all foreign policy affairs fall to the Committee on International Relations, now chaired by Marat Kozhayev. The committee will be responsible for legislative review and preliminary scrutiny of international treaties, security pacts, and bilateral agreements. Given how much further the presidency has been consolidated under the new constitution, the Kurultai’s foreign policy outlook is likely to align closely with Tokayev’s. And with all deputies now elected through party lists, the Kurultai may lack experience in international law and negotiation that the previous Senate held via presidential appointments, as mentioned above. 
Tokayev has framed these constitutional and structural reforms as a modernization, an answer to the turbulence in world politics. The changes are supposed to push the agenda of creating an “effective, transparent and responsive” system. Ambitious as it is, this path poses several risks to foreign policy. First, with no second layer of review, the risk of ratifying rushed or flawed agreements increases.
Second, the new system further consolidates executive power. The president holds the right to dissolve the Kurultai if it repeatedly rejects the presidentially nominated parliamentary chairman, further weakening the legislature. Moreover, according to Article 42 of the new constitution, the president, as the head of state, holds the authority to determine the primary directions of foreign policy, as well as negotiate and sign treaties. A newly created advisory institution, the People’s Council (Halyk Kenesi), will also “possess the right of legislative initiative and will be empowered to introduce bills to parliament,” as well as “the power to prepare legislation for the Kurultai and, on the same basis as parliament, to propose nationwide referendums.” Notably, the People’s Council consists of 126 members drawn from three categories – ethnocultural organizations, local governments (Maslikhats), and civil society – but all approved by the president. 
To minimize the risks to Kazakhstan’s foreign policy now that the Senate, its chamber of sober second thought, has been abolished, the country should consider introducing minimum review windows to avoid rushed decisions, empowering the Kurultai’s Committee on International Relations, and ensuring that the newly created People’s Council remains strictly an advisory, consultative forum.
