articles.title: Why Is China Less Active in the 2026 Ebola Epidemic?
articles.full_text:
Ten years ago, China was a prominent source of Ebola aid. Today, China’s more powerful but its response is less than many expected – especially as the U.S. steps back.
An Ebola treatment center in Bunia, the DRC, constructed by the World Health Organization.
The Ebola epidemic spreading through the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) could become the largest Ebola outbreak on record if infections continue at their current pace. More than 6,700 people had been infected and more than 3,200 had died by September 2026. The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, a form of Ebola for which there is currently no licensed vaccine or approved treatment.
The crisis is unfolding at a remarkable moment for global health. The United States is retreating from the global health system it once led. Beijing is the world’s second-largest economy and holds substantial interests in the DRC’s copper and cobalt industries. That matters not because Beijing has an obligation to replace Washington. Rather, the outbreak offers a test of whether, as the United States pulls back from global institutions, China will step forward.
During the 2014-2016 West African Ebola outbreak, which caused approximately 11,325 deaths and more than 28,600 cases, China emerged as an unexpectedly prominent donor. By late 2014, Beijing had provided assistance valued at 750 million yuan, including laboratories, food aid, and health personnel. What was particularly striking, however, was the speed with which China’s aid arrived. Ebola was first detected in Guinea in March 2014, and by April, China had sent 4 million yuan worth of assistance. This was quickly followed by several firsts for Beijing, including the use of chartered flights to deliver humanitarian relief and the deployment of its first overseas infectious-disease field hospital.
Western countries, on the other hand, were slower to react. It was not until the outbreak had expanded dramatically during the summer of 2014 that the United States, Britain, and other major donors mounted large-scale responses. By then, China had already been providing assistance for months. Although Western countries would ultimately contribute more money, the significance of China’s early response went beyond its dollar value. It demonstrated Beijing’s growing willingness to assume a visible role in international affairs, foreshadowing a decade of intensifying geopolitical competition. 
Humanitarian concerns were not the only interests at stake. Officially, Chinese authorities talked about South-South cooperation, multilateralism and subtle criticism of Western indecisiveness. Western analysts, however, saw additional strategic interests, such as reducing the risk that Ebola would reach China and testing Beijing’s capacity for overseas power projection. 
The response offered scientific benefits as well. The crisis gave Chinese scientists rare access to outbreak data and field specimens. Chinese teams gained valuable experience establishing and operating mobile biosafety laboratories, capabilities that would later become increasingly important as China expanded its role in infectious-disease preparedness.
China today is wealthier, more diplomatically influential, and far more technically capable than it was a decade ago. Yet as of late August 2026, Beijing had provided $4.5 million – around 30.2 million yuan – in direct support to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and sent a few teams of medical experts. All assistance is valuable. But the level of support from China remains far smaller than many would have expected.
On the American side, despite the Trump administration’s broader retreat from foreign aid and its “America First” approach to global health, the United States has committed more than $512 million directly to Ebola response. Furthermore, the administration has requested more than $1.4 billion in additional funding from Congress. This suggests something more complicated than a simple transfer of global health leadership from Washington to Beijing.      
One explanation is that China simply faces less pressure to prove itself. In 2014, China was still establishing its identity as a major global actor. Ebola offered an unusually visible opportunity to demonstrate that Beijing could provide international aid at a moment when Western governments appeared hesitant. Today, China’s global status is no longer in question. It finances infrastructure across much of the developing world, sits at the center of global manufacturing, and has built deep diplomatic relationships throughout Africa.  
A second explanation is that the scientific incentives have changed. During the 2014-2016 outbreak, China could pair humanitarian assistance with an expanding research agenda, such as developing a vaccine against the Zaire Ebolavirus that was ravaging Western Africa. The current scientific landscape is different. Many of the vaccine and therapeutic candidates prioritized by the WHO are being developed outside China. With less obvious scientific ownership, Beijing may have fewer incentives to pair humanitarian assistance with a high-profile research agenda.
A third explanation may be the differing geopolitical environment. China in 2026 is operating amid slower economic growth and a more difficult geopolitical environment. Chinese citizens may want to see resources focused on issues at home. Further, an expansive intervention in eastern DRC would also carry operational and security risks. Lastly, Ebola competes for attention with wars, economic instability, and other international crises that are defining 2026. 
China’s own rhetoric creates an important test. Its June 2026 white paper on global governance argued that major countries should assume greater responsibility and that international cooperation should produce concrete results. Ebola provides an opportunity to put those principles into practice. 
The current Ebola crisis also presents areas where China could make distinctive contributions. Its strong manufacturing and logistical capacities could make it an important surge supplier of diagnostics, protective equipment, and other medical goods. On the diplomatic front, China can mobilize its strong relationships with African partner countries to become a multiplier of African and WHO capacities, assisting with the continent-wide response. 
Greater transparency could help. More detailed public reporting on the scale, timing, and purpose of Chinese assistance would make Beijing’s contribution easier to assess. Western governments, for their part, should avoid treating Chinese participation reflexively as a geopolitical threat. Both sides should look for areas where cooperation is possible. 
The larger lesson extends beyond Ebola. The decline of American leadership does not necessarily mean that another power will automatically fill the void. China may have the resources to do so, but whether – and where – it chooses to deploy them is a different question. 
For the people confronting Ebola on the frontlines, however, geopolitics is secondary. The immediate objective is simpler: preventing as much suffering as possible. The test for Washington and Beijing is not which country replaces the other, but whether both can use their considerable capabilities to bring the outbreak under control.

Yet as of late August 2026, Beijing had provided $4.5 million – around 30.2 million yuan – in direct support to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and sent a few teams of medical experts. All assistance is valuable. But the level of support from China remains far smaller than many would have expected.
On the American side, despite the Trump administration’s broader retreat from foreign aid and its “America First” approach to global health, the United States has committed more than $512 million directly to Ebola response. Furthermore, the administration has requested more than $1.4 billion in additional funding from Congress. This suggests something more complicated than a simple transfer of global health leadership from Washington to Beijing.      
One explanation is that China simply faces less pressure to prove itself. In 2014, China was still establishing its identity as a major global actor. Ebola offered an unusually visible opportunity to demonstrate that Beijing could provide international aid at a moment when Western governments appeared hesitant. Today, China’s global status is no longer in question. It finances infrastructure across much of the developing world, sits at the center of global manufacturing, and has built deep diplomatic relationships throughout Africa.  
A second explanation is that the scientific incentives have changed. During the 2014-2016 outbreak, China could pair humanitarian assistance with an expanding research agenda, such as developing a vaccine against the Zaire Ebolavirus that was ravaging Western Africa. The current scientific landscape is different. Many of the vaccine and therapeutic candidates prioritized by the WHO are being developed outside China. With less obvious scientific ownership, Beijing may have fewer incentives to pair humanitarian assistance with a high-profile research agenda.
A third explanation may be the differing geopolitical environment. China in 2026 is operating amid slower economic growth and a more difficult geopolitical environment. Chinese citizens may want to see resources focused on issues at home. Further, an expansive intervention in eastern DRC would also carry operational and security risks. Lastly, Ebola competes for attention with wars, economic instability, and other international crises that are defining 2026. 
China’s own rhetoric creates an important test. Its June 2026 white paper on global governance argued that major countries should assume greater responsibility and that international cooperation should produce concrete results. Ebola provides an opportunity to put those principles into practice.
articles.summary: Ten years ago, China was a prominent source of Ebola aid. Today, China’s more powerful but its response is less than many expected – especially as the U.S. steps back.

articles.title: Why Have Indians Become a Regular Target of Hate in Singapore?
articles.full_text:
Popular resentment toward the city-state’s Indian community and Indian nationals has been building for some time.
Shops on Serangoon Road in Singapore’s Little India quarter, Apr. 3, 2016.
When Lee Kuan Yew took Singapore out of the Malaysian Federation on August 9, 1965, he made English the new nation’s primary language of government and education, rather than Chinese, despite the fact that 75 percent of the population was ethnic Chinese. Ensuring that other ethnic minorities did not feel alienated, he also gave Malay, Mandarin, and Tamil official status.
After the race riots in 1964 that left 36 people dead, Lee dismantled the city’s deeply segregated colonial setup, where different ethnic groups lived in isolated enclaves, and introduced the Ethnic Integration Policy. This ensured that every building must have a mix of Chinese, Malay, and Indian residents that matches the country’s actual population.
These steps played a major role in remaking Singapore from a colonial city-state into a developed nation. For more than 50 years, the edifice Lee erected remained intact.
Given this background, the rise in racial attacks and derogatory slurs against the Indian community in the last few years look surprising, but the discontent against them has been simmering for a long time. The internet and social media have merely brought it to the fore. Suddenly, videos going viral about Indians littering beaches, misbehaving in public, or clashing with locals have circulated widely, sparking outrage and fueling stereotypes. For a country that prides itself on racial harmony, the intensity of this reaction is both striking and concerning.
A number of recent incidents show that things have gone a bit too far. When reports came about nine Singaporeans missing in the recent Nepal flash floods, some social media posts started that they were “not our own” because most of those missing were ethnic Indians. One post even referred to them as “ABNN,” a derogatory term for Indians.
Temasek chief executive Dilhan Pillay Sandrasegara, who is of Indian origin, was similarly attacked after Air India announced that it was seeking fresh capital from its shareholders. Singapore Airlines (SIA) owns about 25 percent of Air India. Social media posts claimed that since Sandrasegara is of Indian origin, he will favor Air India and put SIA money into the loss-making airline.
SIA’s net profit fell 57.4 per cent to S$1.2 billion in the year ended March 2026. Its annual report attributed the decline partly to its share of Air India’s full-year losses. This is an important issue on which the government should be questioned, not the city’s Indian population, who have no role in it.
Another catalyst was the Singapore-India Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement (CECA), which has been misinterpreted online as a mechanism for “Indians taking local jobs,” despite repeated clarifications from the government that CECA does not grant automatic employment or citizenship rights. This has blurred the distinction between Indian expatriates and Singapore-born Indians, making all Indians potential targets of hostility.
For the first time in the history of Singapore, the country is facing a challenge which has the potential to tear apart the social fabric. That is why the government has come heavily down on such campaigns. In June of this year, Singapore authorities took action against 14 social media platforms targeting the Indian community and restricted access to these posts for users in Singapore.
As far as recent incidents are concerned, the government has launched an investigation. Singapore Senior Minister K. Shanmugam said that police were ”investigating ‘shameful’ and ‘totally unacceptable’ comments posted online.”
Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also said that the country must never allow prejudice against any community to become accepted or normalized.
“We can and should have robust debates. But we should never use seemingly legitimate arguments as a cover to fuel prejudice against any community or hostility towards foreigners,” Channel News Asia quoted Wong as saying.

Many times, Singapore ministers have blamed external forces for sowing tension in society. The question is why such propaganda gains the support of locals. Or is it a sign of the success of Lee’s policy that Indian expats are occupying top corporate positions which Singaporeans are not getting?

articles.title: Al-Qaida: 25 Years After 9/11
articles.full_text:
The current threat from al-Qaida is diffused. It relies on homegrown, lone-actor terrorists to carry out low-end attacks, such as stabbing and vehicle ramming.
Twenty-five years after the fateful terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon on September 11, 2001, the fraternity of terrorism scholars and practitioners is divided over al-Qaida’s status. Some believe that al-Qaida still poses a potent threat to global peace and security, albeit of a different nature, while others think it has lost its mojo.
Indeed, al-Qaida failed to create the Sunni global Caliphate it promised its followers. In fact, the global jihadist movement split between al-Qaida and the Islamic State (IS), which weakened the former. IS has superseded al-Qaida as the dominant global jihadist actor. The ideological tussle and inter-group fighting between al-Qaida and IS have helped security and intelligence agencies around the world to cut them to size.
The strategic defeat that al-Qaida desperately wanted to inflict upon the United States has not materialized. Indubitably, the U.S. is struggling to retain its global hegemony in the face of China’s meteoric rise, but it is for a different set of reasons. Attributing power challenges to the U.S.-led unipolar system to al-Qaida would be a gross exaggeration and distortion of facts.
In terrorism, violence is the central benchmark of evaluating the success or failure of a terrorist group. Al-Qaida Core, operating out of Afghanistan, has not carried out an international terrorist attack in more than a decade.
The majority of al-Qaida’s top leaders, barring the current de facto chief Saif al-Adel and his deputy Abd al-Rahman al-Maghrebi, have been eliminated by the U.S. in drone strikes and targeted assassinations. Saif al-Adel likely lives in a safe house in Iran and is dependent on Iranian intelligence for his own security. This has undermined his credibility and capacity to command loyalty and obedience from various al-Qaida affiliates.
Of al-Qaida’s various affiliates, Somalian al-Shabab, al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) in Yemen, and Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) in Mali are the strongest, while al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS), notwithstanding its proximity to the core group, is the weakest.
AQIS has been trying to grow its network in India, especially in Indian-administered Kashmir, Bangladesh, and Pakistan. Barring some nominal successes, it has miserably failed to make an impression since its emergence in September 2014. Nevertheless, it regularly issues a flagship propaganda magazine, “Nawai Ghazwa-e-Hind,” which articulates al-Qaida’s official stance on critical developments. AQIS has been embedding its fighters with various Pakistani jihadist groups to obfuscate its involvement in terrorist attacks, which is consistent with al-Qaida Core’s strategy of focusing on the near-enemy, as discussed below.
Al-Qaida is currently facing a serious leadership crisis, and it will not be surprising if various affiliates still loyal to the mother group adopt the pathway of IS and Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS). The former’s defection made it the most feared jihadist group and leader of the global jihadist movement, while the latter’s rebellion eased its path to victory in Syria and helped it gain international recognition.
Al-Qaida’s Malian affiliate, JNIM, which has made great territorial strides in Mali, is contemplating following HTS’ footsteps and disassociating from al-Qaida to avoid isolation and reprisals ahead of its complete victory.
At its peak, al-Qaida funded and strategically guided different jihadist groups around the world, including the Taliban regime in Afghanistan. Ironically, it is now dependent on the Taliban both for its finances and security. Al-Qaida Core has been reduced to a former shadow of itself; it inspires no confidence in the younger generation of jihadists who self-radicalize online and engage in lone-actor terrorism.
Those who believe al-Qaida continues to be a threat to international peace and security argue that after two decades of the war on terror, the U.S. left Afghanistan by handing back power to the Taliban. Al-Qaida successfully weathered the U.S. strategic pressure and retained its presence in Afghanistan, which constitutes a victory even if it is a pyrrhic one, they claim.
In five years of Taliban rule, al-Qaida has reconstituted itself by embedding with local jihadist movements in Pakistan. It is actively supporting an umbrella militant alliance, Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP). The resurgence of militant violence in Pakistan since August 2021 has increased al-Qaida’s footprint, especially in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. Likewise, al-Qaida affiliates in Yemen, Somalia, and Mali have made substantive territorial, financial, and organizational gains.
The threat al-Qaida poses today is qualitatively different from the security challenges it posed to international peace in 2001. The absence of an international mass casualty attack does not make al-Qaida less relevant. Rather, there is a need to take a more nuanced view of the threat it poses.
The terror group has not changed its goal of creating a global Sunni Caliphate or carrying out attacks in the West. However, as the international security environment has evolved, al-Qaida has also changed its trajectory and modus operandi. Now, it is focusing on the near-enemy, i.e., Muslim democratic states that it deems apostate, instead of the “far-enemy,” meaning the United States.
Al-Qaida is no longer investing its time and focus in high-profile attacks like 9/11; rather, it is creating space for itself by aligning with local jihadist movements and obscuring its presence to avoid counterterrorism pressure. It is adopting emerging technologies like drones and 3D-printed technology to build weapons, investing in maritime capabilities, and striving to achieve financial self-sufficiency. All these elements make al-Qaida a potent threat in the long run.
Over a period of 25 years, al-Qaida has shown resilience. It has survived by adapting, decentralizing operations to regional franchises, and moving ideological indoctrination to encrypted social and digital media platforms.
The current threat from al-Qaida is diffused. It relies on homegrown, lone-actor terrorists to carry out low-end attacks, such as stabbing, vehicle ramming, and shootings in the West. This threat, due to its low intensity, is more manageable but less detectable and preventable because people are self-radicalizing online. Furthermore, al-Qaida is engaging in hybrid warfare tactics where violence is one of several elements it is using to achieve its objectives.
So, the singular fixation with al-Qaida’s violent credentials is flawed. Al-Qaida engages in information, ideological, and cognitive warfare alongside violent extremism. It has advised its affiliates to focus on governance by moderating their aggressive jihadist postures.
On balance, al-Qaida has survived the war on terror, and it is far from a spent force; however, the threat it poses is now manageable. At the same time, it is facing credibility and leadership crises that are not likely to subside anytime soon.
On the one hand, for the Taliban regime, al-Qaida is a liability. It can neither own the group nor disown it. The former will result in international diplomatic and security pressure, and the latter will dent the Taliban’s ideological legitimacy in the jihadist world. Likewise, for flourishing regional affiliates like Al-Shabab, JNIM, and Al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), al-Qaida Core is more of a nuisance than an ideological mothership.
Al-Qaida remains relevant, but it has evolved and the threat it poses has also evolved. Putting this fact in perspective will help both practitioners and scholars to develop a better understanding of the terror group.

articles.title: Vietnam’s To Lam Concludes State Visit to Russia, Departs For France
articles.full_text:
The Vietnamese leader and his counterpart Vladimir Putin identified trade and energy as important areas of future bilateral cooperation.
Vietnamese President To Lam shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin during their meeting in Moscow, Russia, Sept. 9, 2026.
Vietnam’s top leader To Lam yesterday wound up a state visit to Russia during which he and Russian President Vladimir Putin pledged to develop their cooperation in the realms of trade, energy, and defense.
Lam arrived in Russia on Monday for a three-day visit, before departing yesterday for France, where he was scheduled to meet with President Emmanuel Macron and attend the International Space Summit in Paris.
During the visit, Lam, who serves both as president and general secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV), held talks with Putin, Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, Chairman of the State Duma Vyacheslav Volodin, and other high-ranking officials.
Ahead of their meeting, Putin praised Vietnam’s “impressive results” under the CPV’s rule, and said that he was “delighted” to welcome Lam and his delegation to the Kremlin. In turn, the Vietnamese leader described Putin as “a great friend of our country,” and said that Hanoi views its relationship with Moscow as “a priority, a consistent pillar of our foreign policy, and a strategic choice of enduring significance.” Both sides made ample reference to the Cold War-era cooperation between communist North Vietnam and the Soviet Union.
Addressing the media after the meeting, Putin described the talks as “very meaningful and substantive” and said that the two sides had signed an “impressive package” of bilateral agreements. These included MoUs in areas such as justice, finance, investment, transport, ethnic affairs, energy, nuclear safety, science and technology, education, and mineral resources, Vietnamese state media reported.
Putin said that economics and trade was a particular focus of talks. He noted that while trade had increased by more than 5 percent last year, progress that he attributed to the free trade agreement between Vietnam and the Russia-dominated Eurasian Economic Union, “the overall volume of trade in absolute terms does not yet match the potential.” The two sides agreed to target $15 billion in two-way trade by 2030.
Another priority was cooperation in the energy sector, which has been a recent priority for both governments. In a joint statement released yesterday, the two sides described energy as an area of “strategic breakthrough in Vietnam-Russia relations” that would help shore up energy security for both countries. Both sides “agreed to improve the efficiency of ongoing projects and continue to expand cooperation in the oil and gas sector in Vietnam and Russia,” the statement said. It also referenced the March 2026 agreement with Russia that will likely make Vietnam the first Southeast Asian nation to achieve a civilian nuclear energy capacity, stating that it had “opened a new chapter” in the two countries’ partnership.
Specifically, Vietnam’s state energy firm Petrovietnam signed a framework agreement with the Russian state-owned oil and gas company Zarubezhneft on ‌cooperation in a project to set up a strategic oil reserve in Vietnam.
“The Russian side has proposed that its partners ​consider the idea of jointly establishing ​strategic fuel reserves in Vietnam,” Putin ‌told the media after his meeting with Lam. “Our companies are also interested in establishing transit energy supplies through Vietnamese territory to neighboring countries.”
Lam said that Vietnam “welcomes more active investment by Russian corporations and enterprises in the development of renewable energy, oil and gas sector and the development of deep-sea resources.” He added that the Russian side would strive to “create favorable conditions for Vietnamese enterprises to expand their investment and business activities in Russia in such areas as agriculture, forestry, fisheries, and seafood.”
Above all, Lam’s visit testifies to the energy that Vietnam has invested in its foreign partnerships since he took over the leadership of the CPV just over two years ago. In that time, Lam has paid official visits to China, Russia, Belarus, India, and Cuba, as well as the U.S., France, South Korea, and the United Kingdom, and regional partners including Indonesia, Thailand, Singapore, Malaysia, and the Philippines.
He has also spearheaded a rapid expansion of Vietnam’s circle of Comprehensive Strategic Partnerships, welcoming France (October 2024), Malaysia (November 2024), New Zealand (February 2025), Indonesia (March 2025), Singapore (March 2025), Thailand (May 2025), the U.K. (October 2025), and the European Union (January 2026) to the top tier of Hanoi’s diplomatic hierarchy.
In recent weeks, Lam supplemented this to state visits to Australia and New Zealand and met with Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing in Hanoi. According to Reuters, he is also expected to address the U.N. General Assembly in New York later this month, and to make a state visit to Canada. In October, the news agency added, the Vietnamese leader “is expected to return to Europe, where he could meet ​EU leaders in Brussels as part of a broader trip, according to three people informed about the plans.”
The varied political hue of Vietnam’s key partnership, and its ability to maintain good relationships with them is the essence of its doctrine of “bamboo diplomacy.” Judging by Lam’s crowded travel schedule, Hanoi is doubling down on this approach as the world enters a period of global perturbation and flux.

articles.title: Is Indonesia’s 100 GW Solar Plan Realistic?
articles.full_text:
Whether or not the goal is achievable, it sends a strong signal that Jakarta is serious about putting more resources toward clean energy.
An aerial view of a solar power station in Bali, Indonesia.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has set an extremely ambitious target of building 100 GW of solar capacity by 2029. Naturally, many people are wondering if this a realistic goal. I’ll spare you the suspense. The answer is no. But it does send a strong signal that the government is serious about putting more resources toward cleaner energy.
People often look at Indonesia’s energy sector, dominated by coal and other fossil fuels, and the extremely slow progress on renewables to date, and conclude that clean energy is a non-starter. I don’t agree. The government has been signaling for some time that it is willing to pivot toward clean energy. The catch is that it wants to do so on its own terms, without simply opening Indonesia up as a market for private developers and investors where the state-owned utility PLN ends up on the hook for expensive purchase agreements. This, in my estimation, was the major flaw with how Indonesia’s Just Energy Transition Partnership was originally designed.
The actually important question is not whether Indonesia can build 100 GW of solar power – obviously, it cannot do so in three years. The question is whether we are getting closer to an approach that can actually be implemented and scaled given the peculiarities of Indonesia’s political economy. I think the answer is a tentative yes. Prabowo recently unveiled the first stage of the 100 GW plan, announcing 5.3 GW of solar power projects under development or which will soon be opened for bidding.
The first thing we need to do is unpack the headline figure. 5.3 GW of new solar capacity would be a very significant step forward in Indonesia’s clean energy ambitions, but only eight of these projects are actually in an advanced stage of development. The bulk of the announced capacity, some 4.5 GW worth of projects, are still in the early stages without financing or confirmed project developers. However the eight projects that are further along tell us a lot about how to build clean energy in Indonesia.
Two of the announced projects are small off-grid solar facilities, designed to replace diesel generators in remoter areas. One of these is being developed by a subsidiary of state-owned oil and gas giant Pertamina, and the other by PLN itself. Together they account for under 2 MW of capacity. The other six projects are larger utility-scale solar and battery storage facilities mainly using floating arrays built on top of reservoirs. They range in size from 46 MW to around 133 MW and, once completed, will add almost 670 MW of solar generating capacity to the grid.
These six projects are in various stages of development, with some quite far along or nearly operational. They feature a range of financial backers including state-owned infrastructure fund PT Sarana Multi Infrastruktur, development banks as well as European lenders. Private sector developers include local firm TBS Energi, as well as Saudi Arabia’s ACWA Renewables, China’s GCL, and Singapore-based Vena Energy. The 92 MW Saguling facility in West Java is one of the few projects to be developed under the JETP framework.
The really important observation is that in all of these projects, state-owned electric utility PLN is not just the off-taker. They are an active equity partner, in most cases holding 51 percent ownership of the project. This is the same model, and equity split, we saw in the Cirata floating solar project in West Java, the first really successful large-scale solar power plant in Indonesia that went into operation in 2023. The new wave of solar power projects is clearly using the Cirata model.

PLN operates a large fleet of Indonesia’s coal-fired power plants, and has been reluctant to simply act as a market-maker and off-taker for private renewable energy developers. Involving PLN in these projects as an equity partner provides the utility with an incentive to actually support them. Is it the most efficient design, or the one private developers and financers would ideally want? Probably not. But it is a model that can scale in Indonesia. We are seeing proof of that now.

That we don’t know. The state-directed model may very well need to change as the scale and pace of investment changes. I’ll spare you the suspense. The answer is no. But it does send a strong signal that the government is serious about putting more resources toward cleaner energy.

articles.title: El Niño, Climate Catastrophe, and the Coming Financial Showdown
articles.full_text:
Pablo Berrutti discusses Nepal’s glacial collapse, Indonesia’s wildfires, and why efforts at climate mitigation are falling short.
Mud covers buildings and properties following devastating floods in Trishuli, Nuwakot District, Nepal, Aug. 27, 2026.
Pablo Berrutti is founder and managing director of Altiorem, a sustainable finance library, and a strategic advisor with a background in the integration of artificial intelligence, measuring the impact of climate change and its impact on business.
This includes banks and insurance companies and their awkward relationships with factoring in the challenges of climate change and confronting their responsibilities, which have recently been sorely tested by the arrival of a super-charged El Niño weather phenomena.
In recent weeks the glacial collapse in Nepal, wildfires in Indonesia, the haze, droughts, and typhoons across East Asia have taken horrible toll on human life and racked up damage bills that will be measured in the tens of billions of dollars.
Governments and financial institutions were warned. The potential for this year’s El Niño was first raised in May and formally announced on June 16. The World Meteorological Organization says the current conditions are expected to last until February.
But Berrutti told The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt that wealthy countries like Australia had spent very little on preparation and building in resilience into assets. Instead, about 95 percent of disaster funds went to recovery.
“Whereas other countries, sadly, who aren’t as wealthy as Australia, a lot of Southeast Asian countries, clearly aren’t in a position to be able to build that resilience to these types of events,” he said.
He added that it’s not only the big events that made headlines for causing destruction and loss of life that matter, but also the chronic effects of extreme heat. More than 30,000 people had died this year from back-to-back European heatwaves.
“It’s also an economic productivity perspective or a human health perspective, the knock on effects from fires and what that means from a lung disease and heart disease perspective,” Berrutti said.

articles.title: Philippine Court Acquits Former First Lady Imelda Marcos of Corruption
articles.full_text:
In 2018, the mother of the current president was accused of using Swiss foundations to transfer at least $200 million abroad during her 1975-1986 term as Manila governor.
A portrait of former Philippine First Lady Imelda Marcos at the Marikina Shoe Museum in Manila, Philippines, May 10, 2026.
The Philippine Supreme Court yesterday overturned a corruption conviction against Imelda Marcos, the mother of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., more than three decades after the initial charges were filed.
In November 2018, the Sandiganbayan, the Philippines’ special anti-corruption court, convicted the former first lady, now 97, of seven counts of graft and sentenced her to sentenced her six to 11 years imprisonment for each charge. It also barred her from holding political office for life.
In a decision dated June 10 but made public yesterday, the 1st Division of the Supreme Court overturned the Sandiganbayan’s ruling, Rappler reported. In a 50-page ruling, Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda said that the prosecution had failed to prove her guilt “beyond reasonable doubt” and said that the key testimony and documentary evidence used against her were “inadmissible and lacked sufficient probative weight.”
The cases stemmed from allegations that Marcos and her late husband, deposed President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., used a network of Swiss foundations to hold and transfer at least $200 million abroad during her 1975-1986 term as Manila governor.
The Supreme Court decision did not dispute that the transactions had taken place, but ruled that the prosecution failed to meet the evidentiary requirements necessary to sustain criminal convictions.
In its 2018 ruling, the Sandiganbayan claimed that Imelda Marcos had “a direct or indirect financial interest” in the Swiss foundations and had “participated in the management of the same.” It attempted to substantiate this using documents retrieved from Swiss banks that, according to Rappler, were “authenticated in accordance with Swiss legal procedure.”
In his ruling, however, Zalamenda argued that the Swiss documents “were not properly authenticated” and that the prosecution “was not able to present any credible witness who could have attested to the genuineness and due execution of the documents.” As a result, prosecutors failed adequately to demonstrate that the Marcos-linked foundations in Switzerland were businesses as required by Section 3(h) the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.
As a result, Zalamenda said that he had no choice but to overturn the convictions.
The case is just one of many against Imelda Marcos stretching back to her husband’s years in office. Ferdinand E. Marcos was first elected in late 1965, but placed the Philippines under martial law in 1972, after which thousands of opponents were jailed, killed, or “disappeared.” During these years, Marcos was accused of amassing more than $10 billion that the Presidential Commission on Good Government has since spent decades trying to recover, and Imelda become an international byword for corrupt extravagance. She amassed a collection of shoes so large that they are now housed in a purpose-built museum in Metro Manila.
In February 1986, a campaign of mass public demonstrations brought down the “conjugal dictatorship” of the Marcoses and they fled into exile in the United States, where Ferdinand died in 1989. Two years later, Imelda Marcos was allowed to return to the Philippines, but continues to face criminal and civil charges dating back to her husband’s years in power. The charges overturned by the Supreme Court in June were first announced in December 1991, shortly after Imelda’s return to the Philippines.
In practice, however, these charges have been little more than a legal headache for the Marcos family. Far from facing accountability for widespread corruption and human rights violations, the Marcos family has since the early 1990s been allowed to rebuild its power and influence, first in its home province of Ilocos Norte and then on a national level. This process that culminated in Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s conquest of the presidency in 2022.
Given this backdrop, and the extremely technical nature of the Supreme Court’s ruling, it is hard to see the acquittal as anything less than a setback for accountability in the Philippines and a proof that if one has enough wealth and prominence, it is possible to evade punishment for virtually anything.

articles.title: North Korea’s Nicaragua Courtship
articles.full_text:
At a time when Pyongyang is restructuring its foreign relationships, its diplomatic focus on the Central American nation stands out.
Since emerging from its self-imposed COVID-19 isolation, North Korea has closed a number of its diplomatic missions overseas while reshaping others. The government has concentrated on relationships it sees as strategically useful, focusing heavily on deepening ties with Russia, its burgeoning relations with Belarus, and, most recently, the rekindling of engagement with China. Yet, amid this diplomatic retrenchment, one unexpected country has received particular outreach and attention from the Kim Jong Un regime: Nicaragua.
At a time when North Korea is restructuring its foreign relationships, its decision to court Nicaragua stands out, both for its geographic position and the fact that it came at the invitation of the Kim regime. While the two countries seem like natural partners given the nature of their authoritarian systems of government and long-standing history, the outreach is nevertheless a notable deviation from North Korea’s baseline behavior. Ultimately it could signal increased cooperation between the two countries as well a new trajectory for North Korea’s foreign policy designs going forward, one that exists outside China’s and Russia’s immediate orbit.
Background on the Nicaragua-North Korea relationship
North Korea’s relationship with Nicaragua has ebbed and flowed with changes in Managua’s government.
Pyongyang avoided diplomatic relations with the U.S.-backed Nicaraguan government until 1979, when the Sandinista National Liberation Front took power. At the time, the Kim regime’s connections to the Sandinistas largely ran through its Cuban partner, although North Korea had reportedly provided military training to the group’s personnel in the lead-up to the revolution.
Bilateral engagement between the two countries peaked in the 1980s. This included North Korean military assistance with the delivery of four patrol vessels valued at $8 million, as well as mutual diplomatic support. In 1986, Daniel Ortega, the Sandinista leader and then president of Nicaragua, traveled to Pyongyang for a first-of-its-kind summit between the two nations. Nicaragua followed this up with a show of solidarity by deciding to boycott the 1988 Olympics hosted in Seoul.
Bilateral ties cooled after the Sandinistas fell out of power in 1990. This eventually led to the closure of the North Korean embassy in Managua in 1995. 
It was not until Ortega returned to power in 2006 that the two governments reestablished diplomatic relations. But it would still take another decade before the next notable development.
In January 2017, a North Korean delegation headed by Choe Ryong Hae – one of Kim Jong Un’s top officials – attended the inauguration of Daniel Ortega for his third term as president of Nicaragua. There, the two governments lauded nearly 40 years of friendship and mutual diplomatic support.
However, the practical depth of the relationship remained shallow. In 2017, North Korea’s exports to Nicaragua were reportedly worth just $1.8 million, while reciprocal trade was minimal. There were no indications of military cooperation, and diplomatic engagement remained surface-level. Beyond the ceremonial nature of Choe Ryong Hae’s visit, there was little indication that the relationship was poised to deepen.
The COVID-19 pandemic marked a substantial turning point for North Korean foreign relations. The border lockdowns and restrictions on movement of overseas personnel sharply curtailed diplomatic activities. All but a handful of embassies in Pyongyang closed owing to movement restrictions and resource depletion, reducing contact between foreign diplomats and North Korea government officials.
This self-imposed isolation enabled the Kim regime to reset its policy designs going forward. The Eighth Party Congress in January 2021 produced a five-year policy roadmap for North Korea. The implications for foreign policy began to manifest when emerging from the COVID-19 lockdown period.
As North Korea began reopening in 2023, evidence of this restructuring of foreign partnerships became increasingly visible. Pyongyang closed its embassies in Angola (2023), Bangladesh (2023), Democratic Republic of the Congo (2023), Guinea (2023), Libya (2024), Nepal (2023), Senegal (2023), Spain (2023), Syria (2024), and Uganda (2023).
Although North Korea’s government did not give a specific reason for these closures, it signaled a reallocation of resources that went toward other relationships it wished to cultivate further. North Korea opened additional consulates in Russia, pursued deeper engagement with Belarus – culminating with Alexander Lukashenko’s March 2026 visit – and, curiously, invited Nicaragua to open an embassy in Pyongyang.
In July 2023, the Kim regime sent a delegation to Nicaragua to propose that Managua set up an embassy in the North Korean capital. Pyongyang’s state media did not publicize the initiative; rather, it was the Nicaraguan government that revealed the invitation. Within a year, Managua had inaugurated its diplomatic mission in Pyongyang and presented ambassadorial credentials to the North Korean government.
Since then, North Korea has increasingly referenced Nicaragua in its state media reporting. In the official news wire service, KCNA, Nicaragua has been the subject of 12 reports so far in 2026, after 15 in 2025 and eight in 2024. This compares to only two in 2023.
There are still unanswered questions as to why Pyongyang extended this outreach. Does North Korea see potential for trade (arms or otherwise)? Is Pyongyang seeking to expand its own work in the region?
Part of the answer may lie in Cuba, a longtime partner of both governments. At the same time that North Korea was seeking to advance ties with the Nicaraguan government, South Korea was moving to normalize diplomatic relations with Cuba. Cuba had long maintained close ties with the North while keeping its distance from South Korea, but that changed in February 2024 when Havana and Seoul formalized ties.
This move was a diplomatic setback for Pyongyang, which had up to that point maintained its third-largest embassy in Havana (behind Moscow and Beijing). In essence, Seoul’s encroachment in Cuba marked the potential weakening of a key regional partnership for the Kim regime.
Notably, Nicaragua closed its embassy in South Korea in April 2024. Although Managua cited budget constraints as its reason for the closure, the timing was notable: it came just two months after the Cuba-South Korea normalization of relations and amid Pyongyang’s continued courtship of Nicaragua. Whether the events were connected, however, remains unclear.
But finding a regional partner is only part of the equation. Other Central American countries maintain friendly relations with North Korea, raising the question of what makes Nicaragua stand out for Pyongyang.
In practice, North Korea’s preferred relationships have been with those countries that satisfy three prerequisites. First, they are looser in their adherence to the rules-based international order. Second, they are not closely aligned with the United States, South Korea, or their allies and partners. Third, the country lacks something that North Korea can provide, giving Pyongyang a potential source of leverage. 
Nicaragua satisfies those three criteria. The United States strongly opposes the Sandinista government, and Nicaragua no longer maintains a diplomatic mission in Seoul. Further, Nicaragua’s traditional security relationships with Cuba and Venezuela have become less reliable, creating potential space for another source of military equipment or training.
From Managua’s perspective, North Korea offers a like-minded partner with a similarly personalized, family-centric political system. This is in part why Nicaragua has earned the moniker the “North Korea of Latin America.” 
For governments run by families like the Ortega-Murillo regime, North Korea offers an example of how an under-resourced authoritarian government can survive sustained pressure from much larger powers. This only reinforces the legacy of extremes that Nicaragua has faced under both the Ortega-Murillo government and the Somoza government that preceded it. Authoritarianism has been the dominant force in Nicaragua for most of its political history, and North Korea offers a useful example both to tout and follow.
But the similarity between systems of government is only a starting point for solidarity, as there are practical considerations as well. The relationship can also facilitate cooperation when other economic and security channels become constrained by international pressure. For a regime that prioritizes survival, North Korea offers capabilities that may matter despite the country’s relatively small economic footprint. Pyongyang has decades of experience operating under sanctions and maintaining security relationships with similarly isolated governments.
These capabilities may expand into the military realm. For years, Russia has been the principal supplier of arms and training to the Nicaraguan military, but Managua has recently signed agreements with Beijing to deepen China-Nicaragua security ties. North Korea provides another potential source of equipment and know-how for the Ortega-Murillo regime.
For all the diplomatic activity, tangible economic and security cooperation still remains limited. For example, the primary recorded exports for the two countries in 2024 were rolled tobacco from Nicaragua and delivery trucks from North Korea. 
That could change as Russian demand for North Korean equipment and personnel necessary for the Russia-Ukraine War draws down.
articles.summary: At a time when Pyongyang is restructuring its foreign relationships, its diplomatic focus on the Central American nation stands out.

articles.title: Shifting Poles and Power 35 Years After the End of the Soviet Union
articles.full_text:
For many post-Soviet states, multipolarity is nothing new. Navigating between competing powers has been an important part of their security strategy since independence.
Since late August, seven of the 15 republics of the former Soviet Union celebrated the 35th anniversary of the declaration of their independence. Some marked the occasion in spectacular fashion, such as Uzbekistan and others with more sedate celebrations. But all sought to display and embrace the national identities they have developed since attaining sovereignty. 
In 1991, the Soviet Union collapsed and the bipolar world of the time came to an end. In the post-Cold War period, widely described as a period of U.S. unipolarity, when there was no power that could seriously challenge U.S. supremacy, the new republics worked hard to strengthen their national identities. 
The rise of China, and Russia’s resurgence under President Vladimir Putin, changed the balance of power in the late 2000s. 
Today, the dominant narrative – not only in countries of the Global South in general and in the post-Soviet space in particular but increasingly in Western discourse, too – is that the world is shifting toward a different system, a multipolar one. 
This multipolarity is on display across the post-Soviet space. The Baltic states, for example, became NATO members in the early 2000s. In Eastern Europe, while Belarus became a close ally of Russia, Ukraine hedged and then inched toward the West. In Russian discourse, Ukraine’s desire to join NATO was a threat to Moscow’s security. Other states in the South Caucasus and Central Asia continue to hedge among the various poles in the emerging multipolar world. 
What does security look like for the current post-Soviet states? Has the world indeed become multipolar for these states or has it been multipolar for them all along? There is a plethora of alliances, blocs, and various other groups in the world today, many which border or reach into the post-Soviet space: From the Western-led NATO, to BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and the Collective Security Treaty Organization, each built around the perceived national interests of states, their history and power politics in the region. More recently, one could argue, such groups have formed around religious identity, such as the Mecca Pact involving Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye. The world is transitioning toward an international system with several centers of power. Whether we call it a multipolar world or something else, the emergence of different poles seems clear.
In the post-Soviet space, over the past three decades, these poles have largely been centered around Russia, China, and the United States. Chinese expansion in the region has reached unprecedented levels in particular. China has replaced Russia as the main trading partner of most of the Central Asian states. While Russia has pursued an alternative Eurasian security order in the post-Soviet space, China’s economic power and the scale of its economic engagement have made it increasingly dominant through its geoeconomic programs, including the Belt and Road Initiative and other credit and assistance schemes. 
Until Russia’s war in Ukraine, security and international relations scholars were broadly discussing and researching how interstate war had declined since the Second World War, with more casualties coming from civil wars and domestic unrest. 
In my security and international relations classes, we mostly focused on internal conflicts, conflicts involving non-state actors, and terrorism. This thinking changed in 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, followed by Israel’s war in Gaza in 2023 and, more recently, the U.S. war in Iran. None of these active wars appears to be ending soon. Multiple conflicts and ongoing Cold War-like rivalries indicate that there are several powers fighting for what they believe is their sphere of influence.
While countries in the Global South have been talking about multipolarity for some time, it was only after U.S. President Donald Trump’s shift towards a more isolationist foreign policy for the U.S., as well as his demands for NATO members to look after their own security, that the topic of multiple poles and spheres of influence has became more serious.  This was reinforced by the Canadian prime minister’s reference to the importance of middle powers working together in the new world, presented in a speech to the World Economic Forum in Davos in January. The transition toward multiple spheres of influence is accompanied by a shift toward nationalist and isolationist policies.
More recently, Türkiye has emerged as a new pole for the Central Asian states. Four Central Asian states share a common Turkic identity. Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan ,and Türkiye are members of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), which brings these countries together around their Turkic identity, while Turkmenistan is an observer. It is perhaps the first organization that unites these states based on their local Turkic languages and culture rather than the prior regional lingua franca, Russian.

Nationalist tendencies are on the rise in many societies today, for example the rise of Reform U.K. in the United Kingdom, the recent victory of Germany’s far-right AfD, and the growing influence of One Nation in Australia. In this changing global system, we see not only an ideological dimension, reflected in the Western and non-Western divide, but also an identity-driven dimension, as illustrated by the recent Mecca Pact and the OTS. For many states in Central Asia, it remains important to maximize their national interests while coexisting with multiple poles competing for influence in the region – something that has always been the case.
Since late August, seven of the 15 republics of the former Soviet Union celebrated the 35th anniversary of the declaration of their independence. Some marked the occasion in spectacular fashion, such as Uzbekistan and others with more sedate celebrations. But all sought to display and embrace the national identities they have developed since attaining sovereignty. 
In 1991, the Soviet Union collapsed and the bipolar world of the time came to an end. In the post-Cold War period, widely described as a period of U.S. unipolarity, when there was no power that could seriously challenge U.S. supremacy, the new republics worked hard to strengthen their national identities. 
The rise of China, and Russia’s resurgence under President Vladimir Putin, changed the balance of power in the late 2000s. 
Today, the dominant narrative – not only in countries of the Global South in general and in the post-Soviet space in particular but increasingly in Western discourse, too – is that the world is shifting toward a different system, a multipolar one. 
This multipolarity is on display across the post-Soviet space. The Baltic states, for example, became NATO members in the early 2000s. Other states in the South Caucasus and Central Asia continue to hedge among the various poles in the emerging multipolar world. 
What does security look like for the current post-Soviet states? Has the world indeed become multipolar for these states or has it been multipolar for them all along? There is a plethora of alliances, blocs, and various other groups in the world today, many which border or reach into the post-Soviet space: From the Western-led NATO, to BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and the Collective Security Treaty Organization, each built around the perceived national interests of states, their history and power politics in the region. articles.title: North Korean Elites and Regime Weakness
articles.full_text:
North Koreans pay their respects before the 20 meter tall Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il statues at the center of the Mansu Hill Grand Monument located at Mansudae, Pyongyang, North Korea.
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy.  This conversation with Dr. Jieun Baek – author of “Privileged but Powerless: How North Korean Elite Grievances Reveal the Regime’s Greatest Weakness” (Yale 2026) – is the 525th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
Describe the key characteristics of North Korea’s elites.
North Korea officially rejects the idea that it has an elite class, yet it is one of the world’s most stratified societies. Its elites include Korean Workers’ Party cadres, intellectuals, senior military and security officials, and individuals personally close to Kim Jong Un. The traditional elite largely inherits status through favorable songbun [North Korea’s hierarchical classification system], family history, and proven political loyalty. A newer unofficial elite – the donju, or “masters of money” – derives influence from capital, markets, and connections.
These groups are not monolithic, but they share one defining characteristic: their positions help maintain the regime. In return, they may receive Pyongyang residency, superior housing and education, better food, prestigious employment and education, overseas opportunities, and access to luxury goods – European watches, imported cosmetics, pet poodles. 
None of this is discreet. The regime stages elite reward deliberately. When the Kyongru-dong neighborhood opened, officials framed the new housing not as a public good but as the deserved inheritance of those whose loyalty had earned them “the best of civilization.”
Yet every privilege is conditional. Elites must continuously demonstrate political reliability, professional usefulness, and personal loyalty to Kim. And the most privileged are also the most closely watched: privilege and surveillance rise together.
Examine why North Korean elites are “privileged but powerless.”
North Korean elites possess influence, wealth, and access unimaginable to most citizens, but they lack the most basic power over their own lives. They cannot safely criticize policy, organize independently, protect their families from guilt by association, or know whether today’s privilege will survive tomorrow’s purge. Even the most senior officials can be demoted, imprisoned, or executed without due process, like Jang Song Thaek in 2013.
Their proximity to power actually creates additional danger. Elites face intense surveillance, mandatory ideological activity, extractive “loyalty” contributions, workplace rivalries, and constant evaluation. Thae Yong Ho, the most senior North Korean diplomat to defect in years, put it with characteristic economy: “The closer you are to the Sun, the higher the chances you will burn.” Several escapees told me middle-ranking posts felt safer than the apex.
They may supervise institutions or control substantial resources, but they cannot challenge the system that grants those privileges. As one elite escapee told me, they are “disposable slaves to Kim Jong Un.” They are powerful downward, toward those beneath them, but powerless upward, before the Leader.
Analyze the correlation between North Korean elite “feigned fealty” and the erosion of elite loyalty to Kim Jong Un’s regime.
North Korean public life is a carefully directed performance. Elites attend rallies, recite ideological texts, participate in self-criticism sessions, and display intense devotion. But visible obedience should not be mistaken for sincere belief.
One interviewee described this perfectly through an anecdote. Inspectors would arrive at his home in white gloves to check the portraits of the Kim leaders, hunting for a speck of dust that could bring serious consequences down on his family. He cleaned those portraits, he told me, not out of reverence but out of self-preservation.
As depicted in the table below, “Feigned fealty” describes that widening gap between low inward loyalty and high outward loyalty. Many elites perform devotion because doing so protects their careers, families, status, and lives. This is preference falsification under extreme coercion: everyone plays a role, while few can know what others truly believe.
The gap appears to be widening under Kim Jong Un. Elite defections have increased dramatically; younger elites prioritize money, business, foreign study, and opportunities for their children over service to the Party; and many privately favor economic reform and greater access to information. The regime’s elaborate demands for loyalty reveal not confidence, but anxiety. A system sustained by genuine conviction is resilient. One sustained by surveillance, rewards, and fear may look stable until a shock exposes how shallow its support has become.
Identify the five options for North Korean elites with grievances.
Aggrieved elites have five primary options.
First, they can maintain the status quo and do nothing. This is the least immediately dangerous and most rational choice, but it allows resentment and distrust to accumulate beneath the surface.
Second, they can defect and seek asylum abroad. Defection is an unequivocal rejection of the regime, but it carries extraordinary risks for escapees and their families.
Third, they can erode the regime’s monopoly over resources by building alternative power structures. Markets, private food production, solar energy, informal finance, tutoring, communications, housing, and healthcare can gradually reduce dependence on the state.
Fourth, they can engage in dissent – from coded criticism and hidden transcripts, to use James C. Scott’s concept, and subtle defiance to clandestine information sharing or organized resistance.
Fifth, they can push for democratization and systemic reform. This is the most ambitious and dangerous option because it requires trust, coordination, and first movers willing to confront enormous barriers to collective action.
Assess the role of North Korean elite grievances in revealing the regime’s greatest weakness and its implications for U.S., European, and Asian policymakers and geopolitical strategists.
The regime’s greatest strength and greatest weakness are the same: its dependence on elites. Elites are its architects, administrators, financiers, enforcers, and protectors. The broader population can be controlled through isolation and terror, but the regime must continuously manage elites through a delicate combination of privilege, surveillance, and coercion. If elite allegiance fractures, the system’s foundation begins to crack.
Policymakers should therefore look beyond missile tests and leadership imagery to study elite incentives, generational change, defections, market activity, information consumption, and signs of preference falsification. They should avoid assuming that elite dissatisfaction will automatically produce reform; North Korea’s barriers to trust and collective action remain formidable.
They should also avoid inadvertently improving the regime’s capacity to reward loyalty. Hard-currency access, prestige projects, and engagement channels the state can capture are redirected into patronage for insiders. Sanctions design and diplomatic sweeteners deserve to be tested against that standard.
The United States, Europe, South Korea, Japan, and other partners should expand secure access to outside information, combining radio and portable media with technologies that circumvent censorship. North Korean escapees should lead content creation so that it is credible, tailored, and safe for intended audiences. Governments should also protect escapees, strengthen pathways for asylum, document elite testimony, and support decentralized economic and information networks that reduce the state’s monopoly over daily life.
Finally, strategists must prepare for multiple futures, including gradual liberalization, elite-led reform, succession instability, or sudden internal shock. North Korea may appear immovable, but a regime that requires constant performances of loyalty is revealing its fear: that when people are finally free to choose, many of its most privileged citizens may choose something else.

articles.title: The Ultimate Hedger: Why Vietnam Is Thriving Amid Global Disorder
articles.full_text:
Vietnam is deeply committed, for strategic and historic reasons, to respond to uncertainty and global geopolitical tensions by hedging. And it’s working.
To Lam, general secretary of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Vietnam and president of Vietnam, delivered the Keynote Address at the 23rd IISS Shangri-La Dialogue, May 29, 2026.
Vietnam has emerged as a leading strategic hedger in a global order undergoing major power transition. In other words, it has engaged in “repeated, diverse, sustained, and complementary actions to engage with all major powers without reaching a formal alliance with any and without restrictions on possible actions with others.”
On April 2, 2025, Vietnam’s strategy faced a massive test: on so-called “Liberation Day,” U.S. President Donald Trump targeted Vietnam with a punishing 46 percent tariff, accusing the country of conniving with China on transshipment and treating the United States unfairly. Totaling $123.5 billion, the U.S. trade deficit with Vietnam was the third largest after its deficits with China and Mexico. It attracted attention. 
On April 14-15, Chinese President Xi Jinping was in Hanoi, pressuring Vietnam not to give in too much to the United States. With pressure from both sides, the future of Vietnam as a connector country in global supply chains was under great stress.
Fast forward 16 months, and Vietnam has not just survived in the disorder; it has thrived. 
Overall exports increased by 17 percent in 2025 overall (and exports to the U.S. increased 28 percent, to $153 billion). In the first seven months of 2026, the U.S. imported $104.7 billion worth of goods from Vietnam, a 23 percent year-on-year increase. Vietnam’s GDP growth rate reached 8 percent in 2025 and 8.18 percent in the first half of 2026, despite trade tensions and the Iran war, and in contrast to the prediction of 5.6 percent for 2025 made by the IMF Outlook in September 2025. 
To accomplish this economic feat, Vietnam did not throw its lot in with one great power or join an alliance. In fact, it doubled down in its strategic behavior as a hedger. Vietnam is deeply committed, for strategic and historic reasons, to respond to uncertainty and global geopolitical tensions by hedging.
Amazingly, it has worked so far. Vietnam seems particularly able to succeed in hedging and resist the formidable pressures of three great powers – not only China and the U.S., but Russia – due to three key advantages. First, Vietnam’s crucial geopolitical position means that no great power can let another dominate, forcing them to show some forbearance. 
Second, Vietnam has built a position of structural indispensability in supply chains as the recipient of investments linked to businesses’ “China plus one” or out-of-China strategy. For many Western firms, Vietnam is hard to replace. Vietnam has also started to diversify its markets. 
Third, Vietnam has shown tactical genius in handling each of the three great powers and their leaders.
With the United States, Vietnam negotiated intensely and directly, the day after the tariffs were announced. Getting ahead of ASEAN solidarity, it engaged intensely with Washington and on July 2, 2025, became the third country to reach a deal with the Trump administration, after the United Kingdom and China. The deal reduced U.S. tariffs to 20 percent (and 40 percent on transshipments, although the term is not well defined) and committed Vietnam to across-the-board opening to U.S. exports. These conditions were reconfirmed in a formal White House Fact Sheet in October. But, crucially, Vietnam refused to accept poison pill restrictions and commitments to follow U.S. sanctions on China, unlike Malaysia and Cambodia at the time. 
Even the lowered tariffs led to painful supply chain adjustments and automation, but Vietnam’s efforts mitigated the worst of the damage.
At the same time, Vietnam went out of its way to signal opening to Trump’s own priorities. In May 2025, the Ministry of Finance led the largest-ever Vietnamese corporate delegation to the Select USA fair in Maryland. They enlisted some U.S. corporate support in fending off further tariffs. The same month, on May 16-21, Vietnam fast-tracked a $1.5 billion real estate investment by the Trump Organization, with events attended by Eric Trump. 
On February 18-20, 2026, Secretary General of the Communist Party of Vietnam To Lam traveled to the United States to attend the opening ceremony of the Trump Board of Peace for Gaza and sign a flurry of cooperation agreements.
Yet, Vietnam would not cross certain boundaries with the U.S. Hanoi’s willingness to compromise did not prevent a strong push to resume the war legacy remediation program, which had been disrupted by the dismantlement of USAID. The United States gave in – Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth came to Hanoi and committed another $130 million to the fund, but he could not persuade Vietnam to sign an arms deal. Vietnam also refused to take measures that would antagonize China or Russia and refused to join the Pax Silica initiative.
At the same time, Vietnam underwent intensified engagement with China. As mentioned earlier, Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited Hanoi in April 2025 and Vietnamese leader To Lam reciprocated with a visit to Beijing on April 14-17, 2026, leading to the conclusion of a joint statement and 32 cooperation agreements. Foreign ministers also visited each other, as well as Vietnam’s former prime minister and president. The increased cooperation resulted in new MOUs between Chinese and Vietnamese media that include content co-production terms and the promotion of people-to-people ties. In terms of sheer number of agreements, Vietnam signed more with China than the United States over the past year and half.
On AI governance, Minister Vu Hai Quan led a delegation to the Shanghai World AI Conference, butinitially refused to join the 29 founding members of the World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO) created by China, unlike Indonesia and Malaysia. Here again, Vietnam kept to its hedging playbook, apparently refusing to cross a U.S. red line. However, on July 31, Vietnam ended up joining WAICO in a low-key manner, along with seven other new members. But the Vietnam scholarly community does not interpret this as a making a choice between Pax Silica and WAICO.
Vietnam similarly intensified its long relationship with Russia. No fewer than seven Vietnamese leaders have visited Russia since January 2025, including top leader To Lam on May 9-12, 2025. During that visit, the two leaders signed a major joint statement that accelerated energy cooperation. In March 2026, Vietnam reached a nuclear deal with Rosatom to fast-track the building of one nuclear reactor in Khan Hoa province, leaving Japanese, French, Korean, and U.S. companies disappointed. Vietnam and Russia regularly discuss maritime issues, with General Phan Van Giang’s visit to Moscow in May 2025 offering Vietnam some support in the South China Sea.
Over the past 18 months, Vietnam also upgraded and intensified its relations and economic engagement with Japan, India, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, the U.K., France, and the EU. In fact, since January 2025, Vietnam has deepened its strategic partnerships with existing partners, while adding six comprehensive strategic partners (the U.K., the EU, Indonesia, New Zealand, Singapore, and Thailand), nine new strategic partners, and two new comprehensive partners.
In sum, Vietnam has managed so far to do well in the midst of a trade war, geopolitical tensions, and global uncertainty, all through the mastery of the art of hedging. This art is a risky one over time, with countless necessary adjustments. The question remains whether Vietnam will manage to jump all the hoops ahead.
This article has been updated to note Vietnam’s membership in WAICO.
