articles.title: Russia Is Helping Supercharge North Korea’s Military Drones
articles.full_text:
North Korea, already receiving Russian drone technology, could eventually gain access to more advanced capabilities like autonomous AI‑enabled and jet‑powered drones.
In this photo provided by North Korean state media, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attends tests of “various kinds of reconnaissance and suicide drones” developed and produced by the Unmanned Aerial Technology Alliance, Mar. 18, 2025.
Russia’s expanding military partnership with North Korea has become one of the most significant proliferation risks of the Ukraine war. Since Pyongyang began actively supporting Russia’s campaign, Moscow is believed to have transferred sensitive technologies such as naval reactors for nuclear‑powered submarines, air defense systems, and other advanced capabilities in exchange for North Korean weapons and troops. Russia has already provided drone technology to Pyongyang, and the rapid evolution of Russian battlefield innovations now raises concerns that North Korea could, in time, gain access to far more sophisticated systems, including new versions of autonomous AI–enabled and jet–powered drones.
In a war that began as an artillery‑heavy conflict, drone usage and tactics have evolved rapidly. One of the most consequential developments is Russia’s experimentation with autonomously controlled AI‑enabled drones. Earlier iterations required a human operator to confirm targets, with AI used primarily to counter radio‑jamming and ensure the drone reached its destination. In recent months, however, Russia has begun allowing onboard AI systems to make independent strike decisions. This shift toward autonomous targeting represents a significant technological leap and raises concerns that North Korea, already receiving Russian drone technology, could eventually gain access to these more advanced capabilities.
As with much of the evolution of technology in the Ukraine war, Russia’s has equipped its autonomous AI drones with off-the-shelf technology, specifically commercial grade Nvidia Jetson Orin computers designed to create AI-enabled devices. Using such tools, Russia is training the drone AI to identify specific targets such as gas stations.
Russia has also begun modifying drones with jet powered engines. Jet powered drones are more expensive than the propellor powered models that have been heavily utilized during the war, but they are also more difficult to shoot down. The Geran-5, a Russian version of the Shahed drone, also has a China connection: Its 200 kilogram-thrust turbojet engines are believed to have Chinese origins.
North Korean Drone Cooperation With Russia
Since becoming active in the war against Ukraine, North Korea has transferred over 15 million artillery shells and provided Russia with an estimated 15,000 troops. Reports suggest that Moscow agreed to provide drone technology to Pyongyang in exchange for the troop deployment, but North Korea’s decision to provide Russia with cluster bombs for its suicide drones was likely also a factor. 
The partnership that has developed between Russia and North Korea has allowed Pyongyang to rapidly advance its drone development program. Prior to the Ukraine war, North Korea only possessed outdated reconnaissance drone technology despite development efforts dating back at least to the early 2010s, including initial efforts to develop a strike drone based on U.S. technology. The war in Ukraine, however, has allowed Pyongyang to not only undertake rapid technological advances in its drone technology but to also gain battlefield experience in utilizing them.
When Russian President Vladimir Putin met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in September 2023, Russia provided North Korea with four suicide drones and one reconnaissance drone. More significantly, Russia is believed to have transferred the technology behind Iran’s Shahed-136 drone, the template for Russian drone advances, to North Korea, as well as equipment to enable production. 
North Korea has also unveiled its Geumseong series tactical attack drones, which closely resemble Russia’s Lancet‑3 loitering munition and Israel’s HERO‑30, a similarity that strongly suggests additional technology transfers from Moscow. Pyongyang claims the Geumseong series is already AI–enabled, a capability it has not previously demonstrated. Given North Korea’s limited domestic experience with autonomous guidance systems and Russia’s active development of AI‑driven loitering munitions, this initial integration of AI was almost certainly achieved with Russian assistance.
Pyongyang has additionally benefited from its partnership with Russia beyond the transfer of technology. Unconfirmed reports suggest that North Korean laborers were being recruited through the Jihyang Technology Trading Company to support production of Shahed/Geran drones at Russia’s Yelabuga drone production facility in Tartistan. The North Korean workers were expected to assist in production and handle secondary and itinerary assembly, practical skills that would over time enhance North Korea’s own ability to produce drones.
North Korean troops have also gained practical tactical experience in drone warfare on the battlefield. North Korean tactics quickly evolved during their deployment to Russia to the realities of drone warfare. This includes the deployment of troops in smaller groups to evade enemy drones and adoption of tactics in long-range strike missions. 
Pyongyang’s participation in the war is also giving it access to real world data on the success of North Korean drones and ballistic missiles against Western defensive systems, and access to Russian operational tactics for electronic warfare. Taken together the knowledge gained from North Korea’s combat experience will enhance its ability to utilize drones and evade defensive systems.
Will North Korea Produce AI-Enabled or Jet-Powered Drones?
In 2025, the General Staff Department ordered the North Korean military to integrate AI into both manned and unmanned systems, including drones. With AI integration part of North Korea’s weapons development policy, advances in the field from Russia are likely to be adopted in time. 
The Jetson Orin computers in Russian drones are commercial grade parts and had circuit boards printed with “Made in China.” Russia is likely procuring them from illicit Chinese supply chains; North Korea will be able to as well. The kits are also relatively cheap. Some versions cost less than $300. 
Given the battlefield experience that North Korea has gained in Russia using drones and the technology cooperation between the two, including initial usage of AI, it would seem only a matter of time before Pyongyang integrated autonomous AI strike drones into its arsenal. This will enhance its ability to hit targets in the South, including civilian infrastructure, and overwhelm traditional missile defense systems over time. 
Jet powered drones would require North Korea to make modifications to its production lines that go beyond those needed for AI adoption or other iterative advances drone technology from the war. While Pyongyang could likely acquire the engines from China or develop its own version, doing so would raise the cost of its drones but not to an extent that it would be prohibitive using off-the-shelf technology.
Strategic Challenges for the United States and South Korea
As Russia continues to push the boundaries of drone technology, we should expect those innovations to make their way to North Korea with implications for security on the Korean Peninsula. Notably, South Korea’s own drone technology, especially drone interceptors, is still in an early stage of development. 
In the current conflict, the use of drones in combination with traditional ballistic missiles has overwhelmed missile defense systems with sustained attacks. Drones are both cheaper and more easily produced than ballistic missile interceptors. They also have rendered tanks useless and hindered the advance of ground troops. Because these systems are highly mobile and easy to hide, they are difficult for even militaries with air superiority to eliminate, as the Iran-U.S. war has demonstrated. 
Autonomous targeting drones and jet-powered drones will provide North Korea with increasingly capable asymmetric tools to counter the United States and South Korea during a conflict. While they will not provide North Korea with a decisive advantage, they will complicate allied operations and increase the cost to civilian infrastructure and military systems that will be required to win a conflict.
This shift to cheaper, more mobile, and increasingly autonomous systems is a trend that will reshape conflict for the foreseeable future and one that the United States and South Korea must adapt to more quickly.

Jet powered drones are more expensive than the propellor powered models that have been heavily utilized during the war, but they are also more difficult to shoot down. The Geran-5, a Russian version of the Shahed drone, also has a China connection: Its 200 kilogram-thrust turbojet engines are believed to have Chinese origins.
North Korean Drone Cooperation With Russia
Since becoming active in the war against Ukraine, North Korea has transferred over 15 million artillery shells and provided Russia with an estimated 15,000 troops. Reports suggest that Moscow agreed to provide drone technology to Pyongyang in exchange for the troop deployment, but North Korea’s decision to provide Russia with cluster bombs for its suicide drones was likely also a factor.
articles.summary: North Korea, already receiving Russian drone technology, could eventually gain access to more advanced capabilities like autonomous AI‑enabled and jet‑powered drones.

articles.title: Which Document Proves Indian Citizenship? There Isn’t 1 Answer
articles.full_text:
Indian laws never specified any single document as proof of citizenship, but the Modi government’s citizenship screening drive has turned it into a big question.
In August 2026, two former Indian bureaucrats faced a challenge they never expected: they were asked to prove their Indian citizenship.
Navdeep Suri was India’s ambassador to the UAE and Egypt, while Ramesh Chander had served as ambassador to Belarus, among their other assignments. However, amid the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral roll, their names were missing from the 2003 voter list, which is being considered as the baseline of the last “pure roll.”
Their names are missing from the 2003 roll because they were serving India abroad at that time. But the voter roll revision mechanism flagged them as suspected doubtful citizens. They were told that ordinary identity documents like Aadhaar and Voter ID will not do; they will have to support their claim with more solid documents like passports, birth certificates or old land records.
The government has said the ongoing SIR is nothing but a routine electoral roll revision process, but in a country where no single document serves as proof of citizenship — and citizenship is essential for voting rights — the electoral roll revision has led to a rush for a range of documents, from birth and school-leaving certificates to land records.
Many applied for passports even though they have no plan for travelling abroad, only because they considered a passport to be unquestionable proof of citizenship.
However, a Ministry of External Affairs official said in June that an Indian passport is a “travel document” and not itself a document of Indian citizenship and that it had never been regarded as conclusive proof of citizenship.
Others have contested this claim, citing how the government’s own material on Overseas Citizens of India (OCI) says that an Indian passport is given only to an Indian citizen.
In any case, only about 7 percent of India’s population currently holds a passport, meaning the very document many now treat as the gold standard is one most citizens have never needed and don’t have.
As recent statements by different ministers and government officials, as well as court rulings, reveal, there is no single document that alone can prove one’s Indian citizenship. It is not an issue as long as one’s citizenship is not challenged. However, as soon as one’s citizenship is challenged, the burden of proof lies on that person.
The Citizenship Act recognizes citizenship principally through birth, descent, registration, naturalization and incorporation of territory. People belonging to the last three categories usually have citizenship certificates. However, for people belonging to the first two categories — who form the overwhelming majority of Indians — citizenship has to be proved through other documents.
According to a Q & A on a government website, “citizenship can be proved by any documents related to date and place of birth.” The government has not yet clearly notified any specific document. However, it has repeatedly rejected common identity documents like Aadhaar, PAN (tax ID), voter ID, driving license, ration cards and bank records as proof of citizenship.
Recently, a Calcutta High Court ruling said that possession of a voter card, Aadhaar card, bank account documents and PAN card does not automatically constitute conclusive proof of Indian citizenship.
A Guwahati High Court order in 2022 had echoed a similar view:  there is not a single document that can prove the citizenship of a person. Documents, including passport, ration card and voter ID, can constitute supporting evidence, but citizenship had to be assessed from the totality of evidence.
Recent government policies indicate that the government is increasing emphasis on birth certificates; they are being made mandatory in several aspects like admission in educational institutes and for driving licenses. The Union government has tightened rules for delayed registration of birth certificates, prioritizing integrity of the document for its importance in official purposes, including identity and citizenship-related documentation.
Over the past year and a half, when thousands, mostly Bengali-speaking Muslims, were detained in different states as suspected illegal Bangladeshi migrants, the police had mostly insisted on passports, birth certificates or school leaving certificates
The citizenship screening drive to ensure a voter roll free from illegal foreigners has led to problems due to multiple factors. Many people, especially of an older generation and from the marginalized sections of society, do not possess land records, birth certificates or school-leaving certificates.
Birth certificate possession has risen sharply for the younger generation, but remains genuinely rare for the old. The national birth registration rate was just 56.2 percent as recently as 2000 and had reached only 84.9 percent by 2017. National Family Health Survey data shows only 26.9 percent of children under five had a birth certificate in 2005-06. As registration systems improved, this share more than doubled to 62.3 percent by 2015-16.
All this means a meaningful share of adults, particularly those born before the early 2000s, have no registered record of their own birth.
Similarly, Census 2011 data put literacy among Indians aged 60 and above at just 28 percent for women and 59 percent for men nationally. This rate is lower in rural areas.
Taken together, the electoral roll revision process imposes a heavy burden of proof on older, poorer and rural Indians — the population least likely to have the paper trail the government now demands. This is why there is widespread apprehension that the voter roll revision may end up disenfranchising millions of Indians.
Given that recent months have seen a series of deportations, including wrongful ones, the disenfranchised will have reason to feel anxious about greater harassment.

articles.title: Why the South Korea-US Alliance Needs the Dark Eagle
articles.full_text:
Focusing strictly on China’s anxieties misses a far more urgent reality: South Korea faces an existential threat from North Korea.
Soldiers with 7th Infantry Division (Multi-Domain Command – Pacific) train with the Dark Eagle Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon during exercise Valiant Shield, June 6, 2026.
Rumors about the United States potentially deploying its Multi-Domain Task Force (MDTF) and the “Dark Eagle” hypersonic weapon to the Korean Peninsula are sparking predictable anxieties. Given the fierce economic and political backlash South Korea endured after hosting the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system in 2016, it is easy to see why critics are sounding the alarm. They argue that bringing in offensive hypersonic missiles will simply turn South Korea into a pawn in the broader China-U.S. rivalry. 
But focusing strictly on China’s anxieties and possible reaction misses a far more urgent reality: South Korea faces an existential, rapidly accelerating threat from North Korea’s evolving military capabilities.
War is no longer just fought on land, at sea, or in the air; it spills over into space, cyberspace, and the electromagnetic spectrum. The MDTF is built for this new reality. The task force is not just another conventional weapon to park on a base. It is a theater-level tool designed to blind an adversary’s radars, sever their communications, and seize control of the battlefield almost instantly.
The star of the MDTF is the Dark Eagle. According to the U.S. Army, this hypersonic glide vehicle boasts a range of over 3,500 kilometers (2,175 miles). What makes it genuinely disruptive is not just its speed – exceeding Mach 15 – but its unpredictability. Unlike traditional ballistic missiles that follow a standard, trackable arch, the Dark Eagle skims the upper atmosphere at altitudes of 30 to 50 kilometers. By flying this low and fast, it slips beneath the sightlines of ground-based early warning radars and easily bypasses legacy air defense systems.
For the Korean Peninsula, this technology rewrites the rules of deterrence. Over the past few years, North Korea has aggressively shifted toward solid-fuel ballistic missiles and mobile launchers. This means Pyongyang can roll a missile out of a tunnel and fire it in roughly 10 to 15 minutes. Older weapons, like Tomahawk cruise missiles, simply fly too slowly to eliminate these targets before they launch.
The Dark Eagle solves this timing crisis. If stationed in South Korea, it could obliterate command bunkers in Pyongyang or missile sites across the country in minutes. Even if launched from bases in Guam or Japan, the weapon would reach its target in roughly 10 minutes. This speed fundamentally shifts the strategic calculus. Knowing that a U.S. hypersonic weapon can strike the origin point of an attack almost instantly guts the logic of a surprise launch. It renders North Korea’s deeply buried nuclear bunkers highly vulnerable, serving as a visceral deterrent against miscalculation by leadership in Pyongyang.
Naturally, positioning an offensive weapon like a hypersonic missile in Northeast Asia is going to ruffle feathers. If THAAD was a shield, the Dark Eagle is undoubtedly a spear. But Seoul cannot afford to abandon the precise, asymmetric deterrence that modern weapons provide simply because of diplomatic friction with China.
Furthermore, the deployment of the MDTF would offer a strategic benefit: silencing the recurring political chatter in Washington about drawing down U.S. Forces Korea (USFK). Committing a flagship, next-generation asset to the peninsula would be ironclad proof that the United States is willing to project its most advanced military capabilities to defend South Korea.
The conversation needs to move past the rigid binary of either unconditionally hosting the MDTF forever or rejecting it out of sheer geopolitical panic. Washington and Seoul need a strategy that bolsters defense while managing diplomatic fallout. Instead of rushing into a permanent deployment, the two nations should establish a joint working group of experts and military officials to map out the logistics and political implications.
A smart first step would be a limited, rotational deployment of the MDTF during upcoming combined military exercises. This would allow both militaries to test how the Dark Eagle integrates into existing defense networks without the permanence that triggers regional crises. A phased, transparent approach buys Seoul the time it needs to build public consensus while offering diplomatic space to reassure neighbors that the weapon is meant to stabilize the region, not upend it.
Ultimately, the debate over the Dark Eagle is about much more than a single weapon system. It is a crucial test of how the U.S.-South Korea alliance is adapting to the unpredictable, multidomain threats of the 21st century. It is time approach the situation with strategic clarity, ensuring both the strength of the alliance and lasting peace on the Korean Peninsula.

articles.title: Turkish, Kazakh, and Malaysian Companies Hit With New US Sanctions Over Iran
articles.full_text:
In addition to sanctioning 27 Iranian airlines, the U.S. designated Turkish, Kazakh, and Malaysian companies for serving as general sales agents for long-sanctioned Iranian airline Mahan Air.
On September 8, the U.S. Treasury Department announced new sanctions aimed at grounding Iranian airlines, as part of the Trump administration’s “Operation Economic Outcast.” The sanctions hit 36 entities, including cargo service providers and general sales agents based in Turkiye, Kazakhstan, and Malaysia.
The Trump administration’s war against Iran has stretched into its seventh month. Although the U.S. government claims to be in control of the vital Strait of Hormuz, traffic remains low. Reuters reported that six ​commodity vessels passed through the strait on September 8, “down from ‌nine a day earlier and below the 10-day average of about 12.” In 2025, before the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, more than 100 commodity vessels passed through the strait each day on average.
In late August the Treasury Department announced an “economic D-Day.” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent explained: “In the Second World War, D-Day marked the historic beginning of a campaign with our allies to target and drive the enemy from its positions, including those in third countries. Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe. Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”
The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on September 8 designated 27 Iranian commercial airlines “for operating in the aviation sector of the Iranian economy.” 
In addition, OFAC took aim at a number of companies tied to Mahan Air, a privately owned Iranian airline. It was first sanctioned back in 2011 for providing “financial, material, and technological support to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force (IRGC-QF).” The Treasury Department at the time alleged that Mahan Air secretly ferried IRGC operatives, weapons, and funds. 
In 2020, OFAC designated two UAE-based companies, Parthia Cargo and Delta Parts Supply FZC, “for their material support of Iranian airline Mahan Air.” At the time, the Treasury Department outlined how the sanctioned companies helped Mahan Air “sustain its fleet of Western-manufactured aircraft.” The Treasury Department alleged that Mahan Air transported “terrorists and lethal cargo to Syria” and also “ Iranian technicians and technical equipment to Venezuela…”
In its latest round of sanctions, the Treasury Department designated several UAE-based companies it claims were involved in the transfer of three B-777 aircraft to Mahan Air.
The sanctions also designated a pair of Turkiye-based companies – S Sistem Lojistik Hizmetler Anonim Sirketi and Mes Cargo Transportation Tourism and Foreign Trade Limited Company – for coordinating shipments and serving as a general sales agent for Mahan Air. Similarly, Malaysia-based Icargo SDN BHD and Kazakhstan-based Tour Invest LLC were designated for acting as general sales agents for Mahan Air.

articles.title: Rethinking Russia, Re-evaluating Risk: The Changing Face of Kyrgyz Migration
articles.full_text:
The war in Ukraine has produced a much longer-term transformation of the institutional and political environment in which migration takes place.
Labor migration to Russia has traditionally played a central role in Kyrgyzstan’s economy. Between 2012 and 2021, average remittance inflows were the equivalent of  30 percent of Kyrgyzstan’s GDP. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the share of remittances in GDP has fluctuated, falling to approximately 17.6 percent in 2024. Despite this instability, remittance inflows have remained historically high in absolute terms. The volatility of recent years nevertheless points to a broader shift in the relationship between remittances and the Kyrgyz economy, suggesting that the country’s long-standing dependence on migration income is becoming more complex and potentially less predictable.
Russia’s war in Ukraine has contributed to changes in migration flows from Kyrgyzstan to Russia. According to estimates based on Kyrgyzstan’s 2022 National Population Census, approximately 854,000 Kyrgyz citizens were working in Russia. By 2026, the Kyrgyz Ministry of Labor reported that around 502,242 Kyrgyz citizens were engaged in labor migration in Russia. While differences in methodology and timing mean that these figures should not be treated as a precise measure of the decline, the overall trend is significant. Russia has not ceased to be the dominant destination for Kyrgyz labor migrants, but the changing scale of migration suggests that the long-standing Russia-centered migration system is undergoing a broader transformation.
Kyrgyzstan’s citizens have benefited from relatively open access to the Russian labor market through membership in the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) since 2015. Problems certainly existed: migrants frequently encountered arbitrary treatment by police, informal payments, document checks, and other forms of everyday insecurity. Yet the basic institutional framework remained relatively stable, and migration continued to be understood primarily as an economic and labor-market issue.
The  system has experienced crises before. Since the mass development of labor migration to Russia in the early 2000s, migrants have experienced several major disruptions, including the 2008-2009 global financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic. Yet the current crisis is fundamentally different. Earlier shocks were primarily economic or epidemiological and, after a period of disruption, the established migration system largely recovered to its prior state. The war in Ukraine, by contrast, has produced a much longer-term transformation of the institutional and political environment in which migration takes place.
The most important change since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine has been the securitization of migration in Russia. This involves more than simply tightening migration controls; migrants are increasingly treated as objects of national security governance, with migration policy becoming more closely linked to counterterrorism, border control, and internal security.
 In addition, Russia has increasingly sought to draw Central Asian migrants into its wartime manpower system, as the prolonged war in Ukraine created sustained demand for military personnel. Since 2022, Russian authorities have offered foreign nationals simplified access to citizenship in exchange for military service, while police raids and other forms of administrative pressure have increasingly been used to identify and recruit migrants and recently naturalized citizens of Central Asian origin. 
This has created a striking duality in Russia’s approach to migration: migrants remain economically important because of persistent labor shortages, yet their precarious legal status also makes them a particularly accessible population for military recruitment. In this sense, migration governance has become intertwined not only with border and internal security, but also with the state’s efforts to sustain wartime manpower.
For migrants from Kyrgyzstan the significance of these changes extends beyond the immediate risk of detention or deportation. The rules governing everyday life in Russia have become more complex and restrictive, including requirements relating to registration, documentation, medical examinations, language testing, and other forms of administrative control. Migration is therefore becoming not simply more difficult, but less predictable.
This unpredictability is particularly important because the traditional Russia-Central Asian migration system depended on predictability. Families could plan around seasonal migration, circular movement, and the expectation that migrants would return to Russia after spending time at home. When the rules governing entry, employment, and residence become uncertain, the entire household migration strategy becomes harder to sustain.
This ongoing transformation is also likely to change the gender composition of migration. Historically, men dominated migration to Russia, particularly in construction, transport and other physically demanding sectors. The prospect of increasingly restrictive migration controls, detention, military recruitment, and uncertainty over legal status changes the calculation. Women have become a significant part of Kyrgyzstan’s migration system. Kyrgyzstan has historically had a relatively high proportion of female migrants compared with other Central Asian countries and war has accelerated this feminization of migration. 
The gender implications of the current transformation require more attention. If young men increasingly avoid Russia while women become more visible in migration corridors, the social organization of migration, and potentially household roles and care responsibilities, will change as well. For women especially, these may include more precarity. Recent research from the International Organization for Migration (IOM) shows that female migrants from Kyrgyzstan continue to experience significant vulnerabilities throughout the migration cycle.
The asymmetric risks facing men in wartime Russia – specifically military mobilization and targeted security sweeps – are accelerating the structural feminization of Kyrgyz migration. This shift changes not only domestic division of labor and remittance flows within households, but also transfers the burden of economic survival onto female workers who navigate highly precarious service sectors.
One of the most consequential developments is that the new restrictions increasingly affect not only workers but also their families. A particularly important example is education. Since 2024, foreign children seeking admission to Russian schools have been required to demonstrate sufficient knowledge of Russian through testing, alongside requirements concerning their legal status in the country. Children who do not meet the language requirement cannot be enrolled in school. In June 2025, the State Duma approved a bill requiring schools to report information about migrant children and their parents to the Ministry of Internal Affair. In August, a draft amendment to the Law on Education prohibiting free education for migrant children was submitted to the State Duma for discussion.
The significance of this change should not be underestimated. For many migrant families, migration to Russia was not simply an individual labor strategy. It was a family strategy in which children could live with their parents and attend Russian schools. The new rules therefore challenge one of the assumptions on which family migration had been built.
The Kyrgyz government has subsequently had to wrestle with  how to provide education and social support to children whose parents work abroad.
In March 2025, the Kyrgyz government established the Tunguch online school as a pilot state institution for 2025–2028. The school provides education for students in grades 5-11 and was explicitly designed to expand access to education for children who cannot attend conventional schools because of geographical distance. By September 2025, the school had 43 classes – 28 in Kyrgyz and 15 in Russian – and children from more than 15 countries were studying through the online school, with Russia housing the largest group.
Tunguch represents an important change in the way the Kyrgyz state approaches migration. For more than two decades, the economic contribution of migrants was treated as a given, while many of the social costs of migrant children left behind, fragmented families, access to education, and reintegration were largely managed by households themselves.
By targeting the educational access and legal standing of migrant dependents, Russian policy has dismantled the “family migration” model. This systemic exclusion has forced the Kyrgyz state to pivot from passive economic beneficiary to active social mediator. Initiatives like the Tunguch online school mark the institutionalization of state-supported transnational living, signaling the state’s growing need to build infrastructure to mitigate its social externalities.
A potentially more consequential shift in Kyrgyzstan’s migration policy is emerging around the question of what happens when migrants return. On May 14, 2026, the Cabinet of Ministers approved the Program for the Reintegration of Returning Migrants for 2026–2030. This is the first national policy document specifically dedicated to migrant reintegration and signals an important change in how the state is beginning to understand migration: not only as a mechanism for absorbing domestic labor-market pressures and generating remittances, but also as a process that can reshape the country’s labor force, skills base, and economic development.
For much of the post-Soviet period, Kyrgyzstan’s migration policy was largely oriented toward managing outward mobility. Labor migration offered an important pressure valve in an economy with limited employment opportunities, while remittances became a major source of household income and foreign exchange. The policy challenge was therefore primarily how to facilitate migration, protect citizens abroad, and channel its economic benefits home. The new reintegration program suggests a different policy problem is now being centered: how to absorb and make use of the human, professional, and financial capital accumulated through migration when migrants return.
The program includes measures to support employment and self-employment, provide economic assistance, expand vocational retraining, and develop mechanisms for recognizing qualifications acquired abroad. Yet the adoption of the program should not be confused with evidence that Kyrgyzstan is prepared for a large-scale return. A policy framework is a first step; implementation capacity will determine whether reintegration becomes a viable alternative to renewed migration. The more fundamental question is whether the Kyrgyz economy can generate sufficient productive employment, wages, and opportunities for entrepreneurship to make staying economically meaningful for returnees. If these conditions are absent, reintegration programs may end up functioning primarily as short-term assistance schemes while migrants continue to view re-migration as the most viable livelihood strategy.
Diversification Beyond Russia, A Migration Crisis Unlike Any Before
The changing environment in Russia is also pushing Kyrgyzstan to diversify migration destinations. The United Kingdom has become one of the most visible alternatives. Kyrgyzstan began participating in the U.K.’s Seasonal Worker visa program in 2022. The quota available to Kyrgyz citizens increased from around 1,500 places in 2022 to 10,000 in 2025.
South Korea represents another increasingly important destination. Under the Employment Permit System, the quota for Kyrgyz workers increased by approximately 18 percent between 2023 and 2024, reaching more than 3,000 places. At the same time, South Korea has also been accessible through another route: Kyrgyz citizens who acquired Russian citizenship could take advantage of Russia’s visa-free arrangement with South Korea, which allow Russian passport holders to enter the country for short stays without a visa. This created an additional channel of mobility for some Central Asian migrants holding Russian passports, although visa-free entry should not be equated with legal authorization to work. Taken together, these developments illustrate how migration system is becoming more diversified, combining formal labor-migration programs with alternative mobility channels.
The current migration system crisis should therefore not be understood simply as another temporary decline in migration to Russia. The post-2022 crisis is different because it affects the foundations of the system. Russia is not simply becoming a more difficult labor market. It is becoming a more securitized environment in which migrants face greater uncertainty over entry, residence, employment, education for their children and personal security. 
This is a profound shift. For more than two decades, Russia occupied a particular place in the social imagination of Kyrgyzstan as the most accessible foreign labor market, a familiar destination connected through networks and post-Soviet institutions, and a place where generations of Kyrgyz citizens had built their livelihoods. That perception is now changing. The significance of this transformation may ultimately extend far beyond migration statistics. 
Labor migration to Russia has traditionally played a central role in Kyrgyzstan’s economy. Between 2012 and 2021, average remittance inflows were the equivalent of  30 percent of Kyrgyzstan’s GDP. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the share of remittances in GDP has fluctuated, falling to approximately 17.6 percent in 2024. Despite this instability, remittance inflows have remained historically high in absolute terms. The volatility of recent years nevertheless points to a broader shift in the relationship between remittances and the Kyrgyz economy, suggesting that the country’s long-standing dependence on migration income is becoming more complex and potentially less predictable.
Russia’s war in Ukraine has contributed to changes in migration flows from Kyrgyzstan to Russia. According to estimates based on Kyrgyzstan’s 2022 National Population Census, approximately 854,000 Kyrgyz citizens were working in Russia. By 2026, the Kyrgyz Ministry of Labor reported that around 502,242 Kyrgyz citizens were engaged in labor migration in Russia. While differences in methodology and timing mean that these figures should not be treated as a precise measure of the decline, the overall trend is significant. Russia has not ceased to be the dominant destination for Kyrgyz labor migrants, but the changing scale of migration suggests that the long-standing Russia-centered migration system is undergoing a broader transformation.
Kyrgyzstan’s citizens have benefited from relatively open access to the Russian labor market through membership in the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) since 2015. Problems certainly existed: migrants frequently encountered arbitrary treatment by police, informal payments, document checks, and other forms of everyday insecurity. Yet the basic institutional framework remained relatively stable, and migration continued to be understood primarily as an economic and labor-market issue.
articles.summary: The war in Ukraine has produced a much longer-term transformation of the institutional and political environment in which migration takes place.

articles.title: Lee and Macron Pledge Deeper Security Ties After Paris Summit
articles.full_text:
South Korea and France agreed to advance defense cooperation and coordinate on Hormuz Strait security following a summit in Paris.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and French President Emmanuel Macron wave before entering Élysée Palace for a summit, Paris, France, Sep. 8, 2026.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and French President Emmanuel Macron pledged on September 8 to deepen defense cooperation and coordinate on securing free passage through the Hormuz Strait. Their summit was the centerpiece event of Lee’s two-day state visit to France, which also produced new agreements on artificial intelligence, nuclear energy, and trade.
Lee laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier beneath the Arc de Triomphe and took part in an official welcome ceremony before a one-on-one lunch with Macron at the Élysée Palace. An expanded summit followed, and the two leaders then addressed reporters together.
“We agreed to achieve a genuine leap forward in defense and security cooperation in order to jointly respond to the uncertainties of the international order,” Lee said in the joint press conference after the summit, adding that the two governments would move quickly toward signing a reciprocal military logistics support agreement. South Korea and France also signed an amended protocol to their existing pact on protecting military secrets, expanding the list of French officials with access to classified material and tightening rules on its handling.
Hormuz Strait security featured prominently in the talks. 
“South Korea and France agreed to continue close coordination so that freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the stability of global supply chains can be restored as soon as possible,” Lee said. 
Meanwhile, Seoul officials cautioned that the discussion should not be read as a decision on troop deployment. South Korea has been weighing a range of contributions, including military options, but officials say no decision has been made. Any deployment, even of a small number of personnel, would require National Assembly approval under South Korean law.
On the economic side, Lee said the countries agreed to pursue $20 billion, or about 27 trillion won, in two-way trade by 2030. Roughly 20 Korean and French companies took part in a business roundtable on new investment opportunities, and trade promotion agencies KOTRA and Business France signed a cooperation document meant to expand support for companies entering each other’s markets.
The visit also produced a private investment agreement between Samsung Electronics and French AI startup Mistral, announced alongside government-level memorandums on artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and quantum technology. Samsung led a 3 billion euro funding round for Mistral, valuing the company at more than 21 billion euro. The investment gives Samsung a strategic stake as the two work on an in-house AI model for the Korean firm’s chipmaking operations.
Nuclear cooperation advanced too. Lee said the countries would sign further documents on nuclear research and fuel supply to push forward next-generation reactor development and diversify long-term supply chains, building on a nuclear fuel cycle cooperation agreement KHNP and French firm Orano signed during Macron’s April visit to Seoul. The two governments also agreed to open a high-level dialogue channel for private-sector nuclear cooperation.
Biotechnology cooperation also expanded. The Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology signed three memorandums of understanding with French research institutions and companies covering eco-friendly materials, climate-resilient crops, and quantum-computing-assisted drug discovery, agreements Lee said would help Korean biotech firms gain a foothold in the European market.
Lee added that the two sides modernized a bilateral aviation agreement dating to 1974, concluding talks that began in 2016. The updated pact adds fair-competition protections for consumers, expands code-sharing routes, strengthens mutual assistance during emergencies, and sets environmental standards for flight operations.
The countries also expanded people-to-people exchange programs. An agreement widening eligibility for their working holiday program, reached in April, takes effect October 1, and Korean teaching assistants will be dispatched to France starting in October under a language-exchange agreement also signed in April. The two sides also signed a memorandum expanding research ties between Korean scholars and Paris-Saclay University, whose mathematics and physics researchers have produced 12 Fields Medalists, along with a police cooperation agreement targeting transnational crime.
On Ukraine, Lee said France has played a central role in rallying European support for ending the war and restoring peace. He added that South Korea has backed Ukraine in various ways and would keep working with the international community on its recovery and reconstruction. Lee also thanked Macron for inviting South Korea to this year’s Group of Seven summit, saying the invitation allowed Seoul to add its voice to discussions on rebuilding international solidarity and restoring balanced, sustainable economic growth. He pledged that South Korea would keep contributing responsibly to challenges facing the international community through its cooperation with the G7.
Macron, in turn, reaffirmed French support for Lee’s approach to the Korean Peninsula. The two leaders agreed to keep cooperating on regional peace and stability, citing close links between security in Northeast Asia and in Europe. Macron also criticized North Korea’s military support for Russia’s war in Ukraine, saying Paris and Seoul share a commitment to upholding an international order based on law.
The peninsula was a recurring theme of Lee’s visit. Le Monde published a written interview with Lee on September 6 in which he said he wants to serve as a “pacemaker” in reviving dialogue between the United States and North Korea. Lee’s hope is that North Korea-U.S. diplomacy could lead to concrete and effective measures to halt Pyongyang’s nuclear buildup. The president acknowledged that “the wall of distrust built up over many years” cannot be torn down overnight. Still, he said he would keep working toward peaceful coexistence, a concept he laid out last month in his Liberation Day address.
The September 8 summit came five months after Macron’s state visit to Seoul in April, when the two governments upgraded their relationship to a global strategic partnership. This year also marks the 140th anniversary of diplomatic ties between South Korea and France.
Before arriving in Paris, Lee spent two days in southern France. He and Macron co-chaired the inaugural Lumière Summit on Monday at the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, a gathering on the future of film and video that drew about 150 participants from more than 30 countries. The two governments launched a Lumière Partnership worth a total of 1 billion euro, aimed at promoting the growth and globalization of the film and video industry. Lee opened the summit with remarks on cultural cooperation. He later met with Korean film figures – including directors Lee Chang-dong and Jung Ju-ri and actors Sul Kyung-gu and Jeon Do-yeon – before chairing a roundtable with executives from CJ ENM, Naver, Netflix and other companies.
Lee is scheduled to meet French National Assembly President Yaël Braun-Pivet on September 9, hold a luncheon with the Korean community in France and meet with OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann before concluding his four-day state visit.

articles.title: The Debate About New Provinces in Pakistan
articles.full_text:
The real question is not simply how many provinces Pakistan needs, but whether its political system can make smaller units more accountable, representative and effective.
Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has stirred debate in the country over the question of carving out new provinces. “The system we are living under has collapsed,” he said in July. “The only solution is to take [the matter of] administrative units, provinces or whatever you may call it, to the public.”
Others have spoken on the matter as well. While Defense Minister Khawaja Asif has called for greater decentralization and devolution of power to the grassroots, the director general of Inter-Services Public Relations, Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, pointed to Pakistan’s dramatic population growth even as the country continues to operate with only four provinces. He added that any administrative “reset” should be undertaken through constitutional methods, legal procedures, and political representatives.
The timing and personalities involved make the debate politically significant. It touches on Pakistan’s military-civilian relationship, its hybrid political system, inter-provincial relations and the historical forces that have shaped the country.
Naqvi is often seen as a figure with close ties with the military establishment — the latter is perceived as central to his political rise. Given his political trajectory and the military establishment’s immediate and subtle reinforcement of his statement, it is widely believed that the military is broadly sympathetic to, if not supportive of, the position that Naqvi articulated.
Proposals have ranged from around a dozen units to as many as three dozen. However, the question is not simply whether Pakistan has too few provinces, but whether its administrative map adequately reflects its demographic, linguistic, and regional diversity.
Supporters of new provinces point to Pakistan’s poor social development indicators. With a population of around 250 million, a literacy rate of only 63 percent, some 28 million children out of school and widespread child stunting, the argument for more decentralized and accountable governance is compelling. Smaller administrative units, advocates argue, could bring decision-making closer to citizens and improve the delivery of education, health, and other basic services.
Pakistan’s provinces are highly unequal in population, geography, and administrative complexity. Punjab alone has more than half the country’s population, while Balochistan is much larger geographically but sparsely populated. A provincial government in Lahore, Karachi, Peshawar, or Quetta inevitably faces difficulties administering remote and diverse regions. The demand for a separate South Punjab province illustrates this problem. Southern districts have long complained that political and administrative power is concentrated in Lahore and central Punjab.
Yet creating new provinces could also have explosive political consequences, particularly in Sindh. Any proposal involving Karachi would reopen sensitive questions of ethnicity and political power. The 2023 census put Karachi Division’s population at about 20.4 million. It is a deeply multi-ethnic city, with Urdu, Pashto, Sindhi, Punjabi, Baloch, and other communities living there. The violence that engulfed Karachi in the 1990s, particularly amid confrontations involving the Muttahida Qaumi Movement, which claimed to represent the Mohajirs, and the state and rival ethnic and political groups, remains embedded in the city’s political consciousness.
For this reason, redrawing Sindh’s boundaries would not be viewed simply as administrative reform. It could become a struggle over ethnic identity, resources, and control of Pakistan’s economic center. Demonstrations against new provinces have consequently often been framed as resistance to attempts to alter Sindh’s political balance.
There is also a formidable constitutional obstacle. Under Article 239(4) of Pakistan’s Constitution, an amendment altering the limits of a province cannot be presented to the president for assent unless it has first been approved by that province’s assembly by at least a two-thirds majority. Constitutional amendments also require two-thirds majorities in both houses of parliament.
This makes provincial reorganization fundamentally different from ordinary administrative boundary changes. A provincial assembly would effectively be asked to approve a reduction in its own territory, political influence, and potentially its share of resources. In Sindh, where the Pakistan People’s Party derives much of its political strength, such consent would be particularly difficult.
Some proposals, however, have a stronger institutional foundation. The demand for a separate Hazara province has been endorsed by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Assembly, while proposals for a Saraiki-speaking province in southern Punjab have received support in Punjab and the National Assembly. Neither has been implemented. Disagreements over boundaries, political interests, and the required constitutional majority have repeatedly stalled them.
Pakistan’s history also explains the suspicion surrounding attempts to redraw its map. The 1955 One-Unit scheme merged the provinces and princely states of West Pakistan into a single province, partly to create parity with East Pakistan (subsequently Bangladesh). The arrangement was abolished in 1970. The political crisis surrounding the 1970 election and the subsequent breakup of Pakistan left a lasting sensitivity about administrative arrangements being used to manipulate political representation.
Creating a new province does not necessarily bring the government closer to citizens. A new provincial capital can simply become another distant center of power. If the objective is better garbage collection, policing, schools, hospitals, municipal planning, and roads, the relevant institution may be a city or district government rather than a provincial government.
This is particularly important after the 18th Amendment, which devolved substantial powers to the provinces while local governments have often remained politically and financially weak. Decentralization without accountability can simply replace distant elites with new local elites.
The debate over Pakistan’s provinces raises fundamental questions about federalism, representation, fiscal distribution, regional identity, and the balance between the federation, provinces, and local governments.
It also has a wider South Asian dimension. India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and other countries in the region share many challenges in managing linguistic, ethnic, and regional diversity. India’s experience with state reorganization on linguistic lines, Bangladesh’s experiments with administrative decentralization, and Pakistan’s own history of provincial and local governance offer valuable comparative lessons.
Unfortunately, decades of tensions, particularly between India and Pakistan, have severely constrained such exchanges. South Asia has consequently lost opportunities for economic integration as well as institutional learning.
The real question is not simply how many provinces Pakistan needs, but whether its political system can make smaller units more accountable, representative, and effective. If provincial reorganization becomes merely another contest for territory and political power, it may deepen existing fault lines. If it forms part of a broader program of genuine decentralization, stronger local government, and accountable institutions, it could instead help address some of Pakistan’s longstanding governance problems.
In that sense, the question of new provinces is also a question about whether South Asia can learn from its own remarkably interconnected history rather than allowing political boundaries and enduring rivalries to prevent the exchange of ideas and institutional experience.

articles.title: Japan-Korea: Working Together as Like-Minded Countries?
articles.full_text:
Japan and South Korea share more than enough to work together on North Korea — but less than is often assumed.
Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae and South Korean President Lee Jae-myung attend a summit meeting in Andong, South Korea, May 19, 2026.
It is frequently argued that “Japan and South Korea are like-minded countries who share values and ought to strengthen their cooperation in dealing with North Korea.” The question worth asking is what the two countries are actually “like-minded” about — and what they are not.
There is no settled definition in international politics of “like-minded countries” — a concept increasingly prominent in Japanese diplomatic discourse as dōshikoku —, but the term generally refers to countries that share objectives or an understanding on specific issues. The two countries are not automatically like-minded simply because they are both democracies, nor do their policies automatically align across diverse fields because they are both U.S. allies. The degree of alignment has to be assessed issue by issue.
Japan-South Korea relations on the North Korean issue do have an evident duality. On the “threat” dimension, the two are quite robustly like-minded: both are concerned about North Korea’s growing nuclear and missile capabilities, and there is considerable room for cooperation in countering cyberattacks and cryptocurrency theft. The importance of Japan-South Korea security cooperation is also growing as the Russia-North Korea military relationship deepens. In managing relations with an unpredictable U.S. president, too, the bilateral Japan-South Korea framework has become if anything more important than the broader trilateral one.
The differences become apparent, however, the moment North Korea is treated not as a “threat” but as a potential “negotiation partner.” In South Korean eyes, North Korea is simultaneously a military threat and one half of a divided nation sharing a common language. Depending on the administration, the emphasis varies, but Seoul can never entirely set aside the questions of peaceful coexistence and eventual reunification.
Japan, by contrast, regards North Korea as a foreign country across the sea. Drones do not fly over from North Korea to Japan as they do to South Korea, and Japan’s North Korea policy is heavily constrained by the abduction issue — a factor absent for every other country in the region. Even if progress were made on nuclear and missile issues, it would be politically impossible for Tokyo to move toward normalization without meaningful progress on abductions.
Even if both Tokyo and Seoul were to support “dialogue” and “diplomacy” with Pyongyang, the underlying expectations would differ. Seoul values dialogue that eases inter-Korean tensions; Tokyo requires dialogue that advances its outstanding issues with Pyongyang. Even on denuclearization, where the ultimate goal may appear aligned, the two sides diverge over whether to treat a freeze of North Korea’s nuclear capabilities as an intermediate  milestone, and over when sanctions should be eased — Japan still insisting on CVID (complete, verifiable, irreversible denuclearization).
And then there is the Chinese variable. It is difficult to consider the efficacy of sanctions or future diplomatic negotiations without involving China, North Korea’s foremost economic partner. Yet Japan and South Korea often view China quite differently. Japan perceives China primarily as a long-term security threat, while South Korea sees it as both a concern and an indispensable partner for managing the Korean Peninsula. Even conservative South Korean presidents have at times prioritized ties with Beijing over alignment with Tokyo. The geopolitical weight of sharing a land border with China is not something Seoul can ignore.
These differences, however, hardly make cooperation impossible. On the contrary, the right approach is to treat cooperation as necessary precisely because interests and priorities diverge. If U.S. President Donald Trump were to pursue a summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un for legacy purposes, both Japan and South Korea would seek to resume negotiations with Pyongyang in some form, each naturally prioritizing its own interests. History shows repeated failures to act in concert, each time expanding North Korea’s room for maneuver. Pyongyang has always sought to drive a wedge between Tokyo and Seoul, and between the two of them and Washington.
Japan-South Korea cooperation on North Korea need not aim for complete policy alignment. Japan should pursue its own diplomacy with Pyongyang; South Korea should occupy its own space in inter-Korean relations. On that foundation, the two should share information closely and keep each other fully informed of what each prioritizes and where neither can compromise. The same applies to China: a shared understanding of when Beijing should be treated as a partner and when it should be viewed with caution. On issues of this kind, diplomatic channels matter more than defense channels.
Japan and South Korea will never adopt identical policies toward North Korea — nor should they need to. That does not mean they cannot be like-minded countries. The real question is whether they can manage their differences on North Korea and China with sufficient steadiness and dexterity. That capacity, more than any policy alignment, is what will determine whether the “like-minded” label truly fits.

articles.title: Samarkand to Host the Largest Chess Olympiad in History
articles.full_text:
The 46th World Chess Olympiad is being held in Samarkand.
On September 15 this year, the 46th World Chess Olympiad will start at the Silk Road international tourism center in the city of Samarkand. In the history of the prestigious competition, held since 1927, Central Asia will host the chess world’s largest team tournament for the first time.
The Olympiad is expected to set a new record for the number of participants and teams. A total of 398 teams will take part: 208 teams in the men’s (Open) section and 190 teams in the women’s section will compete for victory. This will break the record of 380 teams set in Budapest in 2024. The Olympiad will bring together 1,974 players, including 240 grandmasters. Together with coaches and delegation members, Samarkand will welcome more than 4,000 guests during the competition. The tournament will consist of 11 rounds and will run until 27 September.
From 10 to 18 September, Samarkand will also host the 3rd Chess Paralympiad. A total of 41 teams will take part — the highest figure in the history of the Chess Paralympiad. By comparison, 26 teams competed in Belgrade in 2023 and 34 in Astana in 2024. This year’s event will bring together 196 players, including 150 men and 46 women. It will be held over seven rounds under the Swiss system. The record scale of the Chess Paralympiad is particularly significant for the development of inclusive sport and for raising the standing of chess as an intellectual sport open to all.
Holding the competition in historic Samarkand, a city inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List and one of the key crossroads of the Great Silk Road, combines a sporting contest with a platform for cultural diplomacy and international dialogue.
According to the teams’ average rating, the United States is seeded first in the men’s (Open) section. Its line-up features Fabiano Caruana, Wesley So, Levon Aronian and Hans Niemann, who is making his Olympiad debut. Reigning champion India is seeded second and Uzbekistan third. Germany will be represented by Vincent Keymer and France by Maxime Vachier-Lagrave.
According to the teams’ average rating, India starts as the top seed in the women’s section. The Kazakhstan team includes three-time world blitz champion and Norway Chess Women 2026 winner Bibisara Assaubayeva. Ukraine’s first board will be 16-year-old European champion and woman grandmaster Anastasiya Hnatyshyn.
The line-ups of the Uzbekistan national teams reflect the emergence of a new generation of Uzbek chess. For the first time, the men’s and women’s squads will each enter three teams made up of young players. In particular, Nilufarkhon Imomkuziyeva and Khumoyun Begmurodov, both aged 16, will make their Olympiad debut. Gulrukhbegim Tokhirjonova, who played for the United States at the 2024 Olympiad in Budapest, will defend the colours of Uzbekistan this time.
FIDE World Champion Rustam Kasimdzhanov has been brought into the main men’s line-up, and Uzbekistan’s first woman grandmaster, Nafisa Muminova, has joined the women’s team as captain. In the Uzbekistan men’s team, Javokhir Sindarov (4th), Nodirbek Abdusattorov (7th), Nodirbek Yakubboev (39th) and Shamsiddin Vokhidov (61st) are among the 100 strongest players in the world rankings. The fact that Javokhir Sindarov and Nodirbek Abdusattorov are among the world’s ten strongest players clearly demonstrates the competitiveness of the Uzbek chess school. The women’s team also holds high positions in the world rankings. Afruza Khamdamova is 26th and Gulrukhbegim Tokhirjonova 80th.
The rise of Uzbek chess on the international stage is also reflected in the team rankings. Compared with 2025, the Uzbekistan men’s team has climbed 15 places in the FIDE ranking of 204 countries to take sixth place. The women’s team has climbed 17 places to take 21st.
Alongside the Olympiad, the 97th FIDE Congress will be held in Samarkand from 19 to 28 September. Leaders of more than 200 chess federations are expected to attend. The Congress will also include the election of the FIDE President.
The 46th World Chess Olympiad will be another important stage for Uzbek player Javokhir Sindarov. Eight weeks after the Olympiad ends, he will take on reigning world champion Gukesh Dommaraju for the world chess crown. Both players will be 20 years old at the start of the match, which is scheduled to be held in Geneva from 22 November to 13 December. It will be the youngest World Championship match in chess history. Notably, before their title clash both players will be defending the colours of their national teams in Samarkand: Sindarov for Uzbekistan and Gukesh for India.

These competitions will not only showcase the current strength of Uzbek chess, but will also take the country’s efforts to develop youth sport, support inclusive sport and strengthen international sports diplomacy to a new level.

articles.title: A Himalayan Flood Brings Economic Collapse to Nepal’s Border Region
articles.full_text:
The destruction of the Trishuli-Bhotekoshi corridor is a local tragedy with national economic consequences.
A drone view shows mud covering buildings and properties in Trishuli, Nuwakot District, Nepal, on Aug. 27, 2026, following devastating floods.
On August 26, a massive glacier collapse near Langtang Lirung triggered a chain of flash floods and mudslides along the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi river systems. The event has not only caused damage to what was developed there but also to what was being built in that area, including infrastructure, hydropower projects, and private businesses, primarily small and medium enterprises (SMEs). Losses are estimated at more than $5 billion, which is almost one-third of Nepal’s annual budget. 
Settlements, roads, bridges, hydropower plants, trade facilities, farmland, and human lives across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and downstream districts were swept away or buried beneath mud and boulders. Early estimates of the damage could be made using the household-level data from these locations and the data from the 2018 economic census. But that could be misleading.
The contribution to the GDP from those areas is going to be minimal when looking at the immediate numbers. However, the share could be far more significant if we factor in indirect benefits from the river systems and economic hubs in that corridor. Especially important is the opportunity cost, as Nepal was attempting to build up a vibrant trade link with China in exactly this region. 
The human toll alone is immense. More than 1,300 people are confirmed dead in Nepal, while over 4,000 people are missing. For those who survived, the loss is not limited to houses and belongings. Families have lost relatives, farmland, livestock, food stocks, shops, vehicles, savings, identity documents, and the means to earn an income. Entire local economies in the peripheral areas of the flood-hit districts have been disrupted, which has a direct impact on key sectors such as tourism and agri-businesses. 
The Trishuli-Bhotekoshi corridor is more than a river valley. It connects mountain communities to Kathmandu, national markets, tourism destinations, hydropower investments, and cross-border trade with China. Its destruction is therefore a local tragedy with national economic consequences. 
The complete destruction of the Gyirong Port border complex is especially serious. The port was Nepal’s primary trade and tourism gateway with China. At the moment, Nepal has no fully functional border crossing point with China, which has a high cost for an economy that relies on imports of raw materials and other goods from China. 
When the flood hit, more than 300 vehicles waiting at the border were swept away. About 42 kilometers of road and 41 bridges were damaged, with road and bridge repairs alone estimated to cost 15 billion rupees ($99.4 million). 
The estimated cost to repair is one thing; it’s much more difficult to calculate the cost that accumulates when the movement of local people is limited due to the absence of infrastructure, especially in a border region. Sections of the Prithvi Highway are still blocked, delaying relief operations and disrupting the transport of goods, fuel, food, and passengers. The loss of the Gyirong-Rasuwagadhi trade route will affect importers, exporters, freight companies, customs agents, drivers, hotels, warehouses, retailers, and consumers throughout Nepal. Most of the freight companies have been damaged, with their containers being completely wiped out. 
China has closed the Tatopani customs point following the complete destruction of the Rasuwagadhi border point linking Rasuwa and Gyirong. With no functional border crossing between Nepal and China at the moment, supply chains have been disrupted. This has a direct impact on customs revenue and will raise prices for consumers due to lack of supply. 
People already suffering from the price hikes due to the Iran-U.S. war, among other global events, will have to face more severe economic hardships. Local economic centers, including Syabrubesi, Betrawati, Trishuli, and Rasuwagadhi had been developing through tourism, trade, transport, agriculture, construction, and hydropower investment. Their destruction risks reversing years of local economic progress. 
The damage to Nepal’s hydropower system will have consequences beyond the immediate loss. With approximately 431 megawatts removed from the grid and another 470 MW of projects under construction affected, the disruption threatens electricity reliability just as demand is expected to rise during the dry season. In the short term, reduced domestic generation will increase reliance on electricity imports, putting additional pressure on the trade balance and increasing costs for households and businesses. 
These losses go way beyond repair costs. Nepal faces lost electricity sales, reduced export potential, lower tax revenue, job losses, increased financing risks, and weakened investor confidence. If climate risks are not incorporated into hydropower planning, lenders and investors may consider Himalayan projects more expensive and less secure. 
The estimated direct damage to Nepal’s infrastructure exceeds 200 billion rupees, or about $1.3 billion. Yet the full cost of restoring homes, schools, hospitals, roads, bridges, power systems, farmland, trade facilities, and livelihoods could reach around $8 billion.
The long-term impact is even more worrisome, as the country is again reeling under the burden of long-term rebuilding and rehabilitation. Some of the areas decimated by the flood were still rebuilding from the devastating earthquake of 2015.
Nepal cannot afford to rebuild the same infrastructure in the same vulnerable locations. Reconstruction must be financed through a green, resilient, and climate-informed approach. Roads and bridges should be rebuilt using updated flood-risk projections, with stronger foundations, safer alignments, wider river corridors, and improved drainage. Hydropower projects must account for glacier collapse, permafrost thaw, landslides, sediment flows, and glacial lake hazards – not only historical monsoon floods.
Investment in forests, wetlands, riverbanks, and degraded slopes can reduce erosion, stabilize watersheds, and protect livelihoods. Decentralized solar systems, battery storage, and local microgrids can keep health posts, schools, water systems, and emergency shelters functioning when major hydropower and transmission systems fail.
The government should consider establishing a Himalayan Climate Resilience and Recovery Financing Facility as a permanent platform for post-disaster recovery and long-term climate adaptation. Led by the Ministry of Finance in partnership with sectoral ministries, provincial and local governments, private investors, and development partners, the Facility could mobilize grants, concessional loans, insurance, guarantees, and responsibly structured private investment. It could operate through two windows: a rapid-response window to restore essential infrastructure and services after disasters, and a resilience-investment window. 
This second window can operationalize four sub-windows such as public investment, private investment, donors, and other innovative investment solutions to fund climate-resilient hydropower, safer transmission systems, watershed management, glacier monitoring, early-warning systems, and community preparedness. Public and donor resources could reduce risk for private investors through guarantees, first-loss capital, and insurance support. 
By pooling domestic and international resources, the Facility could accelerate recovery, protect public finances, and help Nepal shift from recurring emergency response toward sustained Himalayan resilience.
Nepal as a country has contributed very little to global greenhouse gas emissions, but it is suffering some of climate change’s harshest consequences. Rising temperatures are melting glaciers, weakening permafrost – the “cryospheric glue” holding mountain slopes together – and making Himalayan hazards more severe and unpredictable.
Paleo-flood studies suggest that the 2026 Trishuli event may be the largest to affect the valley in approximately 5,000 years. Boulders of this scale may have last moved during the Early Holocene Climate Optimum, about 50 centuries ago. This is a warning that present climatic shifts may be pushing the Himalayas toward prehistoric levels of hydrological instability.
High-emitting countries have benefited from carbon-intensive development for generations. They have a moral and financial responsibility to support Nepal’s recovery through rapid, predictable, and primarily grant-based climate finance. Nepal should not be pushed into deeper debt to recover from a crisis it did little to cause.
The people of Thame, Langtang, Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Chitwan cannot bear this burden alone. The people of Nepal need support not only to rebuild what was lost, but to build a safer, greener, and more resilient future.
