articles.title: Asia’s Migrant Workers Need Protection from Gulf Wars
articles.full_text:
The migrants who build, clean, drive, guard, and operate the Gulf’s economies have become the forgotten civilian casualties in its wars.
Migrant workers unload a truck in Dubai, UAE, Jan. 10, 2026.
Asian migrant workers are indispensable to the Gulf’s economy. Yet, they remain highly vulnerable and unprotected when regional conflict reaches their homes and workplaces. On February 28, after the Iranian attack on the United Arab Emirates, the first deaths included a Bangladeshi, a Pakistani, and a Nepali worker. 
Human Rights Watch reported at least 11 civilian deaths and 268 injuries across the Gulf by March 16, with migrant workers comprising most of the victims. At least 10 of those killed were foreign nationals. Some died in direct strikes; others were killed by falling debris from air defense interceptions. 
The known death toll is likely an undercount. There is no public, regionwide casualty registry that consistently records victims’ nationality, occupation, and immigration status. Nor is there a standing regional mechanism that guarantees compensation, evacuation, or income protection for migrants caught in hostilities. The people who build, clean, drive, guard, and operate the Gulf’s economies have become the forgotten civilian casualties in its wars.
Migrants make up an overwhelming share of the population in states such as the UAE and Qatar, and South Asians constitute a large part of that workforce. They work at ports, airports, construction sites, logistics hubs, energy facilities, hotels, and industrial zones – precisely the places most likely to be disrupted or targeted in a regional confrontation. During the Iran war, reporting documented workers’ fears about workplace safety, restricted access to shelter, job losses, and employers’ failure to communicate emergency plans.
For many workers, leaving the region is difficult financially and logistically. Migration to the Gulf is often financed through loans used to pay recruitment fees and travel costs. A worker who returns home abruptly may lose both income and the means to pay back that debt. The decision to remain during a conflict is therefore not always a choice between safety and work; it can be a choice between physical danger and financial collapse for an entire household.
Even for those who wish to leave, it can be difficult to do in practice. Sponsorship-based labor systems, despite reforms in several states, can still leave workers dependent on employers for documents, housing, transport, and information at the very moment mobility matters most. Current labor and compensation systems in the Gulf are designed mainly for routine occupational injuries, not missile attacks, prolonged airspace closures, or emergency evacuation. 
Some labor-sending countries attempt to provide some safeguards for their citizens. Bangladesh, for example, repatriates the bodies of deceased workers and provides support to their families. Its official migrant-insurance system can provide up to 1 million taka ($8,140) in death compensation to registered workers, alongside the Wage Earners’ Welfare Board’s grants for bereaved families. But those protections depend on registration, documentation, and successful claims processing. Undocumented workers and workers who fall outside formal recruitment channels often receive much less or nothing beyond repatriation assistance. Even where compensation is paid, a one-time benefit cannot replace the lifetime earnings of a person whose household borrowed heavily to send them abroad.
When workers are injured, stranded, or laid off during hostilities, in practice, the costs fall on the household as a family loses its main earner while retaining the migration debt that financed the journey.
This outcome is not accidental. Origin states measure the success of overseas employment through remittance flows. Recruitment intermediaries’ profit when placement costs are shifted onto workers. Destination-state employers’ benefit from a labor system that supplies workers cheaply and flexibly. None of them – the origin state’s government, the recruiters, or the employers – has a strong financial incentive to address conflict risk. The worker, who has the least bargaining power, absorbs it instead.
The region already has the institutions needed to change this. The Colombo Process brings together Asian labor-sending states, while the Abu Dhabi Dialogue includes both origin countries and major destinations in the Gulf and beyond. These forums have rightly focused on ethical recruitment, skills recognition, and reducing remittance costs. But the Iran war shows that a labor migration agenda built for peacetime is no longer sufficient.
The first step should be a conflict-contingency protocol attached to bilateral labor agreements. It should require employers and destination governments to provide multilingual emergency information, equal access to shelters, secure access to passports and identity documents, safe transport or evacuation when necessary, and continued wages when work is suspended by conflict. These are not radical demands. They are basic conditions for treating migrant workers as people with rights, not expendable labor inputs.
Second, the Abu Dhabi Dialogue should establish a pooled conflict-risk facility. It should be financed by a small employer levy in destination states, rather than by deductions from workers’ earnings or already overstretched origin-country welfare funds. The facility should cover death, serious injury, emergency repatriation, and temporary income support during conflict-related work stoppages.
Third, governments should publish clear claims rules before the next crisis. Hostile-fire deaths and injuries should be presumed covered, rather than forcing families to navigate opaque distinctions between an “accident,” a workplace incident, and an act of war. Irregular immigration status must never bar a worker from emergency shelter, medical care, evacuation, or the repatriation of remains.
Finally, the region needs a joint, publicly accessible casualty registry. A registry that records nationality, gender, occupation, cause of death or injury, and compensation status would make it harder for workers to disappear into aggregate civilian-casualty figures.
All of these measures can be accomplished through existing mechanisms, but it will be easier if Asian origin states bargain collectively rather than separately. India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka have greater leverage together than they do in parallel bilateral negotiations. A common position on conflict protection would be a practical test of whether the Colombo Process can become more than a forum for discussion.
The number of migrant workers killed in this war is small compared with the wider human toll of the conflict. But it is large enough to establish the precedent. South Asia has sent millions of people to sustain the Gulf’s growth, while assuming that the region’s security would hold. That assumption can no longer be taken for granted. The next war should not leave migrant families to carry both the debt of migration and the cost of conflict.

articles.title: Pax Silica vs WAICO: Will Central Asia Have to Pick a Side?
articles.full_text:
One clue as to how the U.S. plans to proceed might be glimpsed in how Uzbekistan progresses in following Kazakhstan into dual membership.
Kazakhstan presently sits in a unique and potentially precarious spot: It’s the only country in the world to have joined both Washington’s Pax Silica and China’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), competing AI alliances. With a Reuters report last month suggesting that the U.S. may pressure partners to pick a side, Central Asia’s – and Kazakhstan’s – multivector methods may soon be challenged. 
Astana joined Pax Silica officially on June 27, with Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev signing the relevant declaration and the joint statement on the AI Opportunity Partnership during the second Pax Silica Summit in Washington, D.C.
Less than three weeks later, Madiyev attended the World Artificial Intelligence Conference 2026, in Shanghai and became a founding member of WAICO alongside 28 other countries. 
As it stands now, Washington’s Pax Silica counts 24 countries as signatories, with Taiwan listed as a “non-signatory participant.” Beijing, meanwhile, counts 37 countries as members of WAICO, with Bangladesh taking on an “observer” status.
Pax Silica, launched in December 2025, is branded by the U.S. State Department as its “flagship effort on AI and supply chain security, advancing new economic security consensus among allies and trusted partners.” The declaration highlights supply chain resilience, particularly as it applies to the AI supply chain – everything from energy to critical mineral, manufacturing to technology and infrastructure. 
Although China is not directly named, the declaration’s references to “reducing excessive dependencies” and “forging new connections with reliable partners and suppliers committed to fair market practices” are clear dog whistles screaming Beijing. 
WAICO, meanwhile, was first proposed by China in July 2025 and came into being in July 2026. It frames itself as an international organization focused on AI governance. Whether that analogy works or not comes down to whether countries are effectively forced to pick a side.

articles.title: The Strategic Calculus of Xi Jinping’s Egypt Visit
articles.full_text:
Xi’s visit from September 1-2 was significant for both sides, though for different reasons.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi hold talks in Cairo, Egypt, Sep. 2, 2026.
As the renewed tensions in the Middle East push the region to the brink, Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Cairo couldn’t have been more precisely timed. This was the second time Xi visited Cairo – compare that to his counterpart, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, who visited Beijing eight times since assuming power in 2014. 
Xi’s visit from September 1-2 was significant for both sides, though for different reasons. For Egypt, it symbolized a broader shift among Middle Eastern states toward diversifying their foreign policy partnerships. The most obvious recent example was the Mecca Joint Deterrence Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkiye. For China, the region matters for multiple reasons, but none more than securing its trade and energy lifelines. 
The bilateral talks covered the regional conflict and its implications for maritime trade and Chinese investments in Egypt. Considering that Egypt is the second-largest recipient of U.S. military aid in the region, it is important to note how China is going to play its cards after the visit.
Xi’s visit was ostensibly meant to celebrate the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between China and Egypt. The officials claim that this meeting is aimed at tracking the implementation of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Agreement signed between both countries back in 2014. 
The visit was also accompanied by the signing of 25 bilateral agreements, covering trade, technology, military, and security. The most significant of all is the agreement that links Egypt’s Vision 2030 to China’s Belt and Road Initiative, alongside enlarging the Chinese-Egyptian economic zone at the Suez Canal. Another important development was the currency swap agreement, which allows settlements in local currencies while reducing dependency on the U.S. dollar. During past years, trade between Egypt and China has surpassed $20.7 billion, which is an indication of growing Chinese investment and confidence in Egyptian markets. 
On the diplomatic side, Egypt reiterated its commitment to the One China principle while Xi validated Cairo’s concerns about water security and rights issues over the Nile. The Chinese position on this issue was traditionally considered more pro-Ethiopian.
China’s engagement with Egypt, especially amid the Iran-U.S. war currently roiling the Middle East, has two possible goals: hedging against maritime shipping disruptions and taking advantage of growing unease among the United States’ Middle Eastern allies.
First, the ongoing conflict has exposed the vulnerability of the global oil trade, which relies on major choke points. The war that started off with the objective of denuclearizing Iran is now centered around re-opening the Strait of Hormuz, which was open prior to the war. Iran’s use of the Strait of Hormuz illustrated a broader dynamic: geographic leverage over chokepoints can offset conventional military weakness, giving smaller powers disproportionate strategic weight. 
The disruption in global energy trade is functioning as a real-time test of energy security, where China, for now, is better positioned than most. The huge oil stockpiles and diversification in oil imports have saved China in the short run, but sustained conflict in the Middle East has the potential to create disruptions domestically. The shipping disruptions have raised the importance of other maritime transit routes – including Egypt’s Suez Canal. 
The Strait of Hormuz is important for China crude and LNG exports, but equally important is the Suez Canal, which acts as the bridge to connect China to its largest export market, Europe. Egypt controls the strategically important Suez Canal, positioned at the crossroads of Africa, the Middle East, Europe, and Asia. 
Chinese investments in Egypt are concentrated in the TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone located within the Suez Canal Economic Zone. This economic zone alone hosts around 200 Chinese companies with an investment of $3.8 billion. This trade zone offers Beijing a comparatively powerful advantage in terms of logistics, as it targets global markets. While China is still absorbing the shocks brought out by the choking of the Strait of Hormuz, the Suez Canal’s role as an alternative, more insulated maritime artery becomes more valuable to China, whose exports to Europe already rely heavily on it. 
For the past two decades, Beijing has carefully observed the volatility of the Middle Eastern region, and it would be strategically negligent on the part of China if it didn’t hedge against a scenario where the Strait of Hormuz is closed. Considering this, Xi’s visit is not a coincidence but rather a calculated move, as Beijing considers an enhanced partnership with Egypt indispensable to its trade and energy security. It is natural for Beijing to secure this maritime artery, which accounts for 60 percent of its exports to Europe.       
Apart from exposing energy vulnerability, the Iran-U.S. war has exposed another uncomfortable truth about the reliability of the U.S. partnership with countries in the region. Instead of solely relying on traditional Western security umbrellas, states are now looking to diversify their external partnerships. In this scenario, there are two options: either countries make their own region-driven security architectures – like the new Mecca Joint Defense Agreement – or they look toward external powers, mainly China, which has long-term interests in the region. 
China is providing Egypt opportunities through investments, infrastructure building, and is also enhancing military and artificial intelligence cooperation. For Egypt, this is not a pivot away from the United States, but rather a realignment to achieve more strategic autonomy amidst volatility in the region.   
China-U.S. competition is unfolding in almost every domain. Pertaining to the Middle Eastern region, both powers approach issues of regional stability differently, and it is important to analyze how China is positioning itself. During his Cairo visit, Xi called for a “new security architecture” for the region, one where “interference by external forces” is opposed and the Middle Eastern countries are “masters of their own affairs.” Such a security framework, as per Xi, should be grounded in “common, comprehensive, cooperative, and sustainable security.” This idea was reciprocated by Sisi, who said Cairo was ready to cooperate with China to ease regional tensions and explore this new security architecture. 
While the U.S. approach in the region has traditionally been marked by a forward military presence, alliance obligations, and periodic direct intervention, China is offering infrastructure, investment, and trade opportunities while calling for a more non-interventionist approach, appealing to many states in the region. 
China is not in a position to replace the United States; rather, what it offers is an alternative logic of security, one that is rooted more in economic interdependence rather than security guarantees. Xi’s Cairo visit, therefore, is part of a broader strategy to increase Chinese influence in the Middle East as turmoil in the region is on the rise. Meanwhile, Egypt is trying to diversify its foreign policy so that it doesn’t rely on one major power, but rather hedges as per its own national interests. Increased partnership with China will not come at the cost of cutting off ties with the United States.

articles.title: Pakistan Takes SCO Presidency at a Crucial Time: What to Expect
articles.full_text:
As SCO chair, Pakistan can be expected to highlight new connectivity routes via Iran and Central Asia that link the Belt and Road Initiative to the Arabian Sea.
Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif (center left) with Iran’s President Dr. Masoud Pezeshkian, on the sidelines of the SCO Summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Aug. 31, 2026.
The annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) held in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, from August 31 to September 1, brought together leaders from across Central Asia as well as Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
The meeting took place amid significant geopolitical shifts in West Asia. It was the first major Eurasian multilateral gathering after the 2026 Israel-U.S. war on Iran and the subsequent Islamabad Memorandum ceasefire negotiations.
Over more than 25 years, the SCO has evolved into a platform spanning Asia, the Middle East, and Eurasia. While member states often pursue divergent priorities, the grouping has still delivered measurable benefits.
For members of developing countries, including this year’s host Kyrgyzstan, the SCO has offered a practical framework for advancing transit connectivity, improving access to larger markets, particularly China, and coordinating regional security efforts. One example is the summit’s approval for the establishment of a permanent Bishkek Center, which is expected to begin operating with a practical role in coordinating law enforcement cooperation, facilitating the exchange of operational information, and conducting joint activities. For Kyrgyzstan, this represents the creation of a lasting SCO mechanism on its territory even after the end of its presidency.
This year’s summit carried particular diplomatic weight for Iran. In the Bishkek Declaration, SCO leaders condemned military strikes on Iranian territory as violations of international law and the U.N. Charter that create serious risks to international peace and security. They also reaffirmed Iran’s right to develop and use nuclear technology for peaceful purposes without discrimination.
While the declaration refrained from explicitly naming the attackers, securing consensus among member states was itself significant. This outcome arguably represents a continuation of the SCO’s main stance on the conflict. The moderate phrasing of the Bishkek Declaration on the war on Iran likely reflected strategic restraint by key players seeking to forge common ground.
Pakistan reportedly sought to protect the stability of the Islamabad Memorandum ceasefire negotiations between Iran and the United States by avoiding explicitly naming the attackers. On the other hand, India likely aimed to protect its balanced posture toward Western partners by agreeing to a joint declaration that avoided singling out the U.S. and Israel. Similarly, Central Asian member states, which also maintain diplomatic relations with major powers, benefited from this moderated language. In this context, by focusing on core principles of sovereignty and non-aggression rather than naming specific actors, the SCO arguably demonstrated its capacity to build a functional consensus amid complex geopolitical fault lines.
For Pakistan, this consensus arrives at a crucial time. The country has assumed the rotating chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for 2026–27. The presidency is the organization’s highest rotating leadership role, which lasts one year and culminates in the host country organizing the next Heads of State summit. This means Pakistan is going to steer the forum’s agenda at a time when its international profile has grown markedly.
There are three main developments likely to shape the SCO under Pakistan’s presidency of the forum.
First, Pakistan’s policymakers now likely view their role through the lens of a country that has already made a tangible impact in West Asia, particularly through its mediatory efforts between Iran and the United States in recent months. Moreover, they increasingly see Pakistan as a responsible player and key stakeholder in regional conflict resolution. This is a perspective that is likely to shape the SCO presidency under Pakistan and bring sharper focus to practical priorities such as regional connectivity, trade facilitation, energy cooperation, and counterterrorism-related issues.
Pakistan has announced that it will host the 2027 SCO summit under the theme “Turning Vision into Action: Connectivity, Innovation and Shared Prosperity.” This suggests the country’s intention to leverage its chairmanship to prioritize shared development issues among member states.
Second, Pakistan’s assumption of the presidency is going to elevate its role from coordinating economic or ministerial agendas to chairing the SCO’s primary strategic and security discussions. In this important position, Islamabad is unlikely to use the forum to confront or vilify India, as doing so would risk making the presidency appear divisive and could undermine the organization’s credibility at a delicate time.
Instead, Pakistan is expected to prioritize developing consensus in an effort to ensure that bilateral tensions do not spill over into the SCO’s formal agenda or disrupt its proceedings. By keeping the focus on shared regional concerns rather than contentious bilateral issues, Islamabad would likely aim to protect the overall standing of the forum and avoid perceptions that the organization stalled or fractured under its leadership. That said, Pakistan is likely to use the opportunity to build consensus on issues such as river water sharing to ensure that water is not weaponized, as that would threaten regional stability.
Third, Pakistan is likely to use its presidency to advance its connectivity-hub narrative. Islamabad has already repeatedly presented the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) as a flagship project aligned with SCO goals. Under Pakistan’s chairmanship, it can be expected to expand this framing by highlighting new routes via Iran and Central Asia that link the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) to the Arabian Sea. This can allow Pakistan to showcase tangible regional benefits of SCO cooperation while reinforcing its strategic position as a key transit and logistics hub ahead of the 2027 summit in Islamabad.
A key challenge for Pakistan’s incoming presidency will be fostering institutional alignment on major regional transport routes like CPEC. India has repeatedly expressed its reservations, even opposition, to the corridor’s path through Pakistan-administered Kashmir, which may complicate Islamabad’s efforts in the coming year to reach unanimous agreement within the forum.
Moreover, persistent instability in Afghanistan and heightened Afghanistan-Pakistan border tensions could pose significant challenges to Islamabad’s chair agenda. This has the potential to derail Pakistan’s agenda on transit corridors and complicate the idea of integration of Central Asian economic routes with South Asia. At the same time, regional volatility surrounding the Iran-U.S. conflict could create additional friction.
If, against all odds, Islamabad can take this agenda forward, it would enhance Pakistan’s diplomatic standing.

articles.title: Japan and South Korea Face Off Again in the US Navy’s Frigate Search
articles.full_text:
South Korea has an industrial head start, but is Japan’s upgraded Mogami class merely a stalking horse for the Chungnam class?
Japan’s upgraded Mogami-class frigate, the New FFM (left), and South Korea’s Chungnam-class frigate
The U.S. Navy’s reported interest in foreign frigate designs has opened a new front in Japan-South Korea defense industrial competition. USNI News reported on September 1 that the White House and Navy are considering three allied designs: Japan’s upgraded Mogami class, known as the New FFM or 06FFM; South Korea’s Chungnam class; and Turkiye’s Istanbul class. Up to two ships could be built overseas before production shifts to U.S. yards.
The idea did not come from nowhere. As Naval News reported in June, the Pentagon’s fiscal year 2027 budget proposal included $1.85 billion for an effort involving foreign warship designs, with Japan and South Korea at the center of the discussion.
Japan’s top naval officer has now publicly welcomed the reported U.S. interest. Asked by The Diplomat at a September 8 press conference about the New FFM’s reported inclusion in the U.S. review, Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (MSDF) Chief of Staff Adm. Saito Akira stressed that he was not in a position to comment on individual U.S. Navy shipbuilding plans. But if the United States or other countries were considering adopting platforms used by the MSDF, he said, “We see this as reflecting a high level of trust in and appreciation for equipment that embodies the advanced technologies of our ships.”
“I am frankly pleased,” Saito said, adding that if Japan received requests for cooperation on such matters, “we would respond proactively.” 
The reported competition has encouraged a view that Seoul is the real front-runner and Japan’s New FFM merely a stalking horse. Hanwha acquired Philly Shipyard in 2024, giving a South Korean company a direct U.S. shipbuilding foothold. U.S. officials have repeatedly visited South Korean yards, and in December 2025 U.S. President Donald Trump said the Navy would work with Hanwha on a new frigate.
But that conclusion does not necessarily follow.
Trump’s remarks referred to cooperation on the U.S. Navy’s FF(X), a U.S.-designed frigate concept based on the Coast Guard’s National Security Cutter. That was not a decision to adopt South Korea’s Chungnam design. USNI News’ September 1 report described a separate review of foreign designs and identified no favorite. 
Moreover, Hanwha is not the company most closely associated with the Chungnam class. The detailed design and lead ship were handled by HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, while Hanwha Ocean and SK Oceanplant are building follow-on ships. Thus, Hanwha’s U.S. shipyard investment does not automatically translate into an advantage for the Chungnam design.
Nor has Washington’s shipbuilding outreach been limited to South Korea. Then-Navy Secretary John Phelan visited Japan in April 2025, meeting Saito and other Japanese defense officials and touring Japan Marine United. The U.S. Navy said Phelan visited JMU to learn about industry best practices and encourage investment in American shipyards. 
Asked whether Phelan or other U.S. Navy officials had previously expressed specific interest in or praise for the Mogami class or New FFM, Saito declined to disclose details, saying only that he regularly exchanges views with U.S. Navy counterparts on a broad range of issues, including defense equipment, capability enhancement, and operational cooperation.
South Korea nevertheless has some important advantages in the U.S. competition. Its major shipbuilders have substantial production capacity, while Hanwha already has a direct U.S. shipbuilding presence at a time when Washington faces serious shipbuilding delays and capacity constraints. That U.S. footprint also fits the administration’s “Finland model”: initial construction overseas followed by investment and production in the United States.
Yet Japan’s New FFM should not be dismissed. There is already a precedent for Japanese-South Korean frigate competition. In 2024, Australia identified Japan’s Mogami class and South Korea’s FFX Batch II and III, among other designs, as exemplars for its future general-purpose frigate. Canberra later narrowed the field to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Germany’s TKMS before selecting the upgraded Mogami – the New FFM – in August 2025.
Now the two Asian competitors could find themselves facing each other again in the United States, with the New FFM and South Korea’s Chungnam class – the FFX Batch III design – both reportedly under consideration.
Australia’s decision gives Japan a major naval export success with a close U.S. ally. The New FFM is expected to feature a 32-cell vertical launch system, long range, stealth-oriented design features, and reduced manning – attributes relevant to the U.S. Navy as it seeks a frigate that can relieve Arleigh Burke-class destroyers of lower-end missions.
None of this guarantees a Japanese win. Both designs would require adaptation to U.S. Navy combat systems, weapons, communications, cybersecurity, and information-security requirements. Congress also remains wary of building U.S. warships overseas. 
The better reading, then, is that South Korea has an industrial head start, not a guaranteed design victory. Hanwha’s U.S. footprint and South Korea’s shipbuilding capacity make it a formidable contender. But those factors do not prove that the Chungnam class is the Navy’s preferred frigate, nor that Japan’s New FFM is merely a stalking horse.
Washington is effectively weighing two questions: which ally can best help rebuild the U.S. shipbuilding industrial base, and which frigate design best fits the fleet. South Korea’s U.S. investments give it important advantages on the first. On the second, the competition remains very much open.
The U.S. Navy’s reported interest in foreign frigate designs has opened a new front in Japan-South Korea defense industrial competition. USNI News reported on September 1 that the White House and Navy are considering three allied designs: Japan’s upgraded Mogami class, known as the New FFM or 06FFM; South Korea’s Chungnam class; and Turkiye’s Istanbul class. Up to two ships could be built overseas before production shifts to U.S. yards.
The idea did not come from nowhere. As Naval News reported in June, the Pentagon’s fiscal year 2027 budget proposal included $1.85 billion for an effort involving foreign warship designs, with Japan and South Korea at the center of the discussion.
Japan’s top naval officer has now publicly welcomed the reported U.S. interest. Asked by The Diplomat at a September 8 press conference about the New FFM’s reported inclusion in the U.S. review, Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force (MSDF) Chief of Staff Adm. Saito Akira stressed that he was not in a position to comment on individual U.S. Navy shipbuilding plans. But if the United States or other countries were considering adopting platforms used by the MSDF, he said, “We see this as reflecting a high level of trust in and appreciation for equipment that embodies the advanced technologies of our ships.”
“I am frankly pleased,” Saito said, adding that if Japan received requests for cooperation on such matters, “we would respond proactively.” 
The reported competition has encouraged a view that Seoul is the real front-runner and Japan’s New FFM merely a stalking horse. Hanwha acquired Philly Shipyard in 2024, giving a South Korean company a direct U.S. shipbuilding foothold. U.S. officials have repeatedly visited South Korean yards, and in December 2025 U.S. President Donald Trump said the Navy would work with Hanwha on a new frigate.
But that conclusion does not necessarily follow.
Trump’s remarks referred to cooperation on the U.S. Navy’s FF(X), a U.S.-designed frigate concept based on the Coast Guard’s National Security Cutter. That was not a decision to adopt South Korea’s Chungnam design. USNI News’ September 1 report described a separate review of foreign designs and identified no favorite. 
Moreover, Hanwha is not the company most closely associated with the Chungnam class. The detailed design and lead ship were handled by HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, while Hanwha Ocean and SK Oceanplant are building follow-on ships. Thus, Hanwha’s U.S. shipyard investment does not automatically translate into an advantage for the Chungnam design.
Nor has Washington’s shipbuilding outreach been limited to South Korea. Then-Navy Secretary John Phelan visited Japan in April 2025, meeting Saito and other Japanese defense officials and touring Japan Marine United. The U.S. Navy said Phelan visited JMU to learn about industry best practices and encourage investment in American shipyards. 
Asked whether Phelan or other U.S. Navy officials had previously expressed specific interest in or praise for the Mogami class or New FFM, Saito declined to disclose details, saying only that he regularly exchanges views with U.S. Navy counterparts on a broad range of issues, including defense equipment, capability enhancement, and operational cooperation.
South Korea nevertheless has some important advantages in the U.S. competition. Its major shipbuilders have substantial production capacity, while Hanwha already has a direct U.S. shipbuilding presence at a time when Washington faces serious shipbuilding delays and capacity constraints. That U.S. footprint also fits the administration’s “Finland model”: initial construction overseas followed by investment and production in the United States.
articles.summary: South Korea has an industrial head start, but is Japan’s upgraded Mogami class merely a stalking horse for the Chungnam class?

articles.title: China’s Unity Through Erasure Should Worry Central Asia
articles.full_text:
The SCO may serve legitimate Central Asian interests, but it should not become the vehicle through which Beijing’s definitions of security, political loyalty, and ethnic identity become normalized across the Turkic world.
China’s growing efforts to increase control over the Turkic states of Central Asia was the dominant, if little discussed, outcome of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan on September 1. 
Beijing wants its relationship with the Central Asian states to be one of vassals thankful for China’s “protection” and economic integration. The recent summit produced the 25th anniversary Bishkek Declaration and 27 other documents, which claimed they would strengthen mechanisms for security, countering terrorism and organized crime, and promised new transport lines and logistics. On its face, the Central Asian states are promised infrastructure, technology and diplomatic engagement. But beneath those promises is guaranteed deeper dependence on Chinese capital, standards, and security concepts.
China successfully got Muslim-majority states (including Iran, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan) to sign onto documents clearly aimed at China’s own Turkic Muslim populations. The SCO endorsement of combatting “terrorism, separatism, and extremism” was China-sponsored and indisputably about Uyghurs. Under this pretext, the institutional capacity that enables surveillance, intelligence exchange, and political labeling of Uyghurs is being expanded.
Sadly, China’s economic leverage and coercion means the public support that these Muslim-majority states provide to Muslim communities globally is absent when it comes to China. 
The Central Asian states should ponder carefully when Beijing uses the security vocabulary noted in the Bishkek Declaration. China’s decade-long ethnic cleansing campaign in Xinjiang, also referred to as East Turkestan, demonstrates what happens when cultural difference is reclassified as a security problem. Religious behavior can be labelled extremism. Cultural autonomy can be called separatism. Overseas relationships of Uyghurs with Turkic states have tended to attract suspicion. Language, memory, and identity become objects of political management.
ASPI’s Xinjiang Data Project has documented mass detention, surveillance, forced labor and political re-education. ASPI’s Cultural Erasure research estimated that around 16,000 of Xinjiang’s 24,000 mosques had been damaged or destroyed, alongside extensive damage to Islamic shrines and other sacred sites central to regional Turkic history. Arguments that Beijing is only concerned about its “ internal affairs” are blind to China’s foreign policy.
Beijing’s formula of combating the “three evils” – terrorism, separatism, and extremism – was incorporated into the SCO establishment document signed in June 2001, and that vocabulary has been institutionalized across Eurasia.
That should matter in the Muslim-majority Turkic states of Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkiye. 
During Xi’s visit to Kyrgyzstan, Bishkek explicitly reaffirmed support for China on Xinjiang-related issues while agreeing to deepen law-enforcement, counterterrorism, and information-security cooperation. China and Uzbekistan have made similar commitments.
Uyghur, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, and other Turkic identities do not end at borders. Families, languages, religious traditions, and diaspora communities extend across the region. When governments repeat Beijing’s anti-separatist language without qualification, they risk allowing legitimate concern for fellow Turkic communities to be recast as interference or subversion.
China’s July 2026 Law on the Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress contains a provision on extraterritoriality (Article 63) that authorizes Chinese authorities to pursue organizations and individuals outside of China’s borders. 
China’s recent technological advancements increase the risks that might have been assessed in 2001 by the SCO founding nations (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan) as unlikely to cross borders. Some Chinese tech companies expanding across Central Asia have developed important capabilities within the same security ecosystem used to monitor and suppress Uyghurs and other Turkic peoples in the region.
iFLYTEK worked with China’s Ministry of Public Security on voiceprint systems and supplied voice-recognition technology used by Xinjiang police. It has since established a Central Asian presence in Tashkent offering multilingual AI services.
Technical documentation from Dahua policing systems described functions including “real-time Uyghur warnings” and identification of Uyghur attributes. Dahua disputes allegations that it intentionally designed systems for ethnic targeting. But its technology demonstrates how ostensibly neutral surveillance platforms can be adapted for ethnicity-based policing. Dahua systems are already present in Central Asian security environments.
Genomics raises an equally serious question of sovereignty. BGI has established sequencing capabilities in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan and has discussed combining AI with large-scale genomic data in Central Asia. Those laboratory platforms are likely to be connected and operate on Beijing’s cyber cloud, in collaboration with companies such as Huawei. But genomic information is permanent, sensitive, and strategically valuable. The Central Asian states should know where samples are processed, where data is stored, who can access it, and whether it can leave national jurisdiction.
The same scrutiny should apply to natural resources.
Chinese entities are expanding into geological exploration, mining, and processing across Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan. Joint surveys can give Chinese partners detailed knowledge of strategic mineral deposits long before extraction begins. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway will bring genuine commercial benefits, but it will also strengthen Beijing’s overland supply chains and reduce China’s dependence on vulnerable maritime routes.
The answer for the Central Asian SCO members is not decoupling from China as there is a genuine need for infrastructure, capital, technology, and markets to boost living standards. But blindly accepting and complying with Beijing’s demands is also not what a sovereign state should aim for. The Russian invasion of Ukraine has heightened anxiety across the former Soviet republics and encouraged Central Asian states to diversify their external relationships, including by moving closer to Beijing. But that strategic realignment should not proceed without regard to China’s human rights in general and to Xinjiang specifically. The experience of Uyghurs and other Turkic peoples under Chinese rule offers a stark warning about the political costs that can accompany deeper dependence on Beijing.
Turkic governments should distinguish violent terrorism from peaceful political advocacy, religious practice, and diaspora activity. They should scrutinize Chinese surveillance and AI systems, protect biometric and genomic data, retain sovereign control over strategic geological information, and strengthen protections against transnational repression.

articles.title: Is China Really a Cyber Threat to Taiwan?
articles.full_text:
Most people assume that China’s cyber capabilities define the totality of its threat to Taiwan, but this simply does not capture the full picture.
In July, Taiwan witnessed a first-of-its-kind intrusion – a sophisticated AI cyberattack against its government and private sector networks. The hack was suspected to have been carried out by Chinese actors. While impactful, this is not surprising and it overinflates perceptions of China’s true cyber threat to Taiwan. 
Most people assume that China’s cyber capabilities define the totality of its threat to Taiwan, but this simply does not capture the full picture. Intent and opportunity to use cyber are equally critical. A threat is properly defined as the product of an adversary’s intent, opportunity, and capability. While China’s cyber capabilities currently pose a significant threat to Taiwan’s digital sovereignty, environmental factors limit its intent and opportunity to use cyber in an existential way toward Taiwan. The threat is currently modest but can change rapidly as conditions shift.
Taiwan represents a fundamental challenge for China’s leadership, not only due to its dominance over the semiconductor market, but also due to its mere existence as a democracy made up of ethnic Chinese. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) risks losing legitimacy with its populace – and its power – if Taiwan is not incorporated back into the mainland. Thus, China has indicated it aims to integrate Taiwan back into China by 2049. 
The most likely scenario under which China would use cyber in a catastrophic way toward Taiwan would be if it were coupled with an invasion or blockade of Taiwan. Cyber is one of the many tools in the toolbox for states, and like other military actions, its goal is to induce a political outcome. A digital blockade, for instance, through a series of massive multi-sector cyberattacks, by itself would likely not be China’s first coercive option to induce reunification. A naval blockade would likely have a much more sizable and lengthy impact than a digital blockade. Unlike physical ships that cannot be moved unless sunken or moved, a cyberspace effect’s lifespan is much shorter. 
Cyber impact often takes time to generate, requiring complex access and capabilities to be developed, all the while remaining undetected. Once cyber is leveraged against a target, it can be difficult to meaningfully re-engage the target to produce sufficient follow-on impact. After the first cyber shot is fired, network and systems administrators work rapidly to identify vulnerabilities, like the access pathways and malware used. They then reconstitute their network, bringing it back online and patching any remaining known vulnerabilities. While malware can be retooled and new access vectors generated, this too can take time and slow down the offensive inertia. This is why cyber is often more impactful when coupled with other forms of statecraft, not just as a standalone instrument.
China does not currently intend to reunify with Taiwan through force. The costs associated with a kinetic invasion are estimated to be in the trillions of dollars, with impact on the global economy upwards of 10 percent of world-wide GDP. China would bear a significant portion of the costs, including long-term repercussions on its other national goals. Consequently, China has generated an alternate strategy beyond kinetic means to reunify.
That isn’t to say that China won’t take cyber actions against Taiwan. But the threat as it currently exists is not an existential one. 
Central to China’s cyber program is its emphasis on securing information superiority. Whoever controls the information environment controls the levers of power and a population’s political preferences. China utilizes cyber tools daily to gradually chip away at the will of the Taiwanese, aiming to normalize its malicious actions. According to the Taiwanese government, Chinese cyber actors attempt 2.6 million intrusions of its critical infrastructure networks every day. Over a prolonged period, China believes it can both routinely influence the Taiwanese populace to rejoin the mainland while preparing for kinetic reunification as a last-resort effort.
Polling indicates that only 5 percent of Taiwanese want to unify with the mainland. Peaceful reunification currently seems highly unplausible. While cracks are apparent in the Taiwanese political apparatus, they are not substantial enough to tip the scales in China’s favor in any meaningful way. However, Chinese leadership does not appear publicly frustrated by its slow progress in Taiwan, likely due to its long-term strategic outlook. Thus, it will likely continue its peaceful approach, unless something drastic occurs, such as a change to the United States’ “One China” policy or if Taiwan declares its independence publicly.
Taiwan’s critical infrastructure is clearly vulnerable to attack. Both technical and nontechnical security gaps in Taiwan provide China ample access vectors and freedom to traverse through Taiwan’s cyberspace, sometimes undetected. China values secrecy in its cyber operations against Taiwan and uses techniques such as “living-off-the-land” to clandestinely move from network to network and deep inside critical systems. 
Taiwan is one of the world’s most digitally connected countries which increases its cyberspace risk despite its economic upsides. Due to Taiwan’s heavy reliance on imported energy, at over 96 percent, ports like Taichung and Kaohsiung become strategic weaknesses. Impacting even one of these ports could generate downstream effects for Taiwan’s economy and societal functioning. Additional chokepoints include Taiwan’s reliance on only 15 subsea cables for its digital connectivity, as well as its heavily centralized water and electricity networks. All of these are potential targets in a major cyberattack scenario, given China’s years of posturing for conflict.
While Taiwan is clearly vulnerable from a cyberspace perspective, other factors significantly reduce China’s opportunity to threaten Taiwan existentially in cyberspace. As articulated earlier, an invasion or blockade are the only other two realistic options that would likely necessitate China using major cyber action against Taiwan. However, even a blockade may have its political limits toward accomplishing unification. While a blockade or digital blockade would present dire circumstances for Taiwan, historically, blockades have not led to countries capitulating their sovereignty. Current polling indicates that between 50 to 85 percent of Taiwanese would politically resist coercion by China’s military in an attempt for unification. Taiwan’s resolve and international backing would likely outweigh China’s prolonged blockade.
Beyond blockades, true political unification in Taiwan will require boots-on-the-ground to unite the two countries. However, there is speculation that China is not currently ready to conduct a full-scale invasion or a blockade of Taiwan. For a military invasion, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) must be able to conduct a complex inter-service amphibious landing from over 100 nautical miles away and pacify an unwilling population while securing logistics lines and staving off any counter-intervention forces. The PLA’s lack of reliable leadership, unproven joint operations, and nonexistent recent combat experience indicates it is likely not ready to conduct a full joint island attack campaign anytime soon. 
Thus, the opportunity for China to threaten Taiwan through a major cyber incident as a part of a larger coercive unification strategy in the current moment is negligible. 
China has likely caught up to the United States in cyberspace and is now a world-class cyber superpower, able to operate at speed and scale. China’s offensive cyber program will only become harder to counter in the future with the development of advanced AI models. From a capabilities perspective, China currently has the technology, pre-positioned malware, people, and technical expertise to carry out a major cyberattack against Taiwan. 
There are over 100 malicious cyber actors that operate out of China. According to former FBI Director Christopher Wray, China possesses 50 times more hackers than the FBI’s cyber professionals. China clearly invests heavily in its cyber force, likely due to its importance in its overall Taiwan and information dominance strategy. 
Beyond sheer force size, rapid advancements in AI capabilities are occurring daily and will likely give adversaries like China a first-mover advantage. China is already on the front lines of advanced AI model development, and any application to offensive cyber will completely redefine the cyber threat landscape for Taiwan. Many already predict that AI will provide cyber attackers the upper hand over cyber defenders in the short term.
There was a suspected Chinese-origin AI cyberattack of Taiwan in July. If true, this may indicate that China is making the leap from offensive cyber research and design to integration and deployment. While China has a long record of pre-positioning malware globally, AI will likely assist its cyber operators with breaking into traditionally hard-to-hack networks like air gapped industrial control systems and supervisory control and data acquisition (ICS/SCADA), defense, and government networks. Taiwan’s cyber defenses are likely not as advanced as compared to China’s capabilities, given China’s global superiority in the offensive cyberspace. 
Thus, China meets all the necessary capabilities requirements to cause Taiwan’s networks serious harm.
While China’s capabilities are formidable and amplify its potential to cause Taiwan harm, they are muted by significant environmental factors. The magnitude of threats often change, and the threat model used provides only a snapshot in time for China’s current cyber threat. It is not an eternal label. 
China will likely only be a modest threat overall temporarily. When future conditions are ripe, China will pose a much graver threat to Taiwan’s existence as a free and digitally sovereign society than it currently does. 
While one cannot predict what will happen next, Taiwan can take steps now to preserve its digital sovereignty and future as a free nation. It can  develop a whole-of-society AI Cyber Shield to offset offensive AI cyber capabilities, and train more government cyber operators and establish national cyber privateers. That includes conducting red team cyberattacks on critical infrastructure chokepoints.
Taiwan can increase societal resilience to mass cyber shock, continue civil-military joint readiness exercises, and prepare hack-back offensive plans and capabilities.
Finally, Taiwan can improve foreign partner engagement to glean best cybersecurity practices.
Taiwan may currently be in a suitable state to survive China’s low-level cyber influence campaign, but the future is much less assured. China has and continues to prepare itself for conflict to unify with Taiwan. If Taiwan does not take the appropriate steps to secure its cyberspace, a day will come when the threat becomes reality. Perhaps then China will be the ten-foot-tall cyber giant everyone presumes it to be.

The hack was suspected to have been carried out by Chinese actors. While impactful, this is not surprising and it overinflates perceptions of China’s true cyber threat to Taiwan.

articles.title: Indonesia Reopens Airports After Suspension Due to Volcanic Eruption
articles.full_text:
The eruption of Anak Krakatau, which is located on a small island in the Sunda Strait, forced the closure of eight airports, including two serving the capital Jakarta.
Lava spews from Anak Krakatau, a volcano in the Sunda Strait between the Indonesian islands of Java and Sumatra, during an eruption on Oct. 20, 2018.
Indonesia reopened five airports early this morning, after a volcanic eruption over the weekend forced them to suspend operations for two days.
Anak Krakatau, which is located on a small island in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra, began erupting late on Friday and remained active for around 25 hours.
The eruption threw up black plumes of volcanic ash that were carried by the wind over the skies of the capital, Jakarta, which lies around 150 kilometers to the east, and across Lampung province in the southern part of Sumatra.
This forced the closure of eight airports, including two servicing Jakarta. As the BBC reported, “snaking queues had formed at the departure halls in Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Monday as stranded passengers sought refunds and tried to get updates on when they would be able to fly.” Indonesian officials said yesterday that 2,961 flights were disrupted, leaving around 341,000 people stranded.
In a statement today, Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said that Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, the capital’s primary airport, resumed operations this morning after wind blew the ash away from the ⁠vicinity, Reuters reported. Four other airports, including a smaller one in Jakarta and another in the neighboring city of ​Bandung, also reopened today. Two airports remain closed, while one resumed operations yesterday.
Dudy ​told reporters that authorities would now need to confirm the airworthiness of the 178 aircraft that were at Soekarno-Hatta during ‌the closure. “Perhaps it’ll ⁠take some little extra time to prepare the planes,” he said.
Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatoa,” emerged from the sea in the 1920s in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa, which destroyed the island of Krakatau and unleashed a tsunami that killed more than 36,000 people. It has been sporadically active for much of the last decade, and an eruption in 2018 caused a devastating tsunami that killed hundreds of people and displaced tens of thousands.
On Sunday, the Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said that although the volcanic eruption has come to an apparent end, Anak Krakatau remained on alert, and further eruptions were possible.
Also yesterday, Malaysian authorities lifted a declaration of emergency in Serian, a district in the southwest of Sarawak state, that was imposed due to toxic haze from wildfires across the border in Indonesia. Sarawak, which runs along the north of the island of Borneo, is one of the areas most affected by the resulting air pollution, which has forced the closure of 647 schools across the state.

“The Federal government and the Sarawak state government will continue to closely monitor ⁠the ​situation, and residents in affected areas ​are advised to limit outdoor activities and to always comply with instructions from ​the authorities,” it added.

articles.title: Letters Targeting Kashmiri Pandits Surface on Social Media
articles.full_text:
The letters have revived memories of “hit lists” that Islamist militant groups issued in 1989-90.
An abandoned house belonging to Kashmiri Pandits in Anantnag district, Jammu and Kashmir, India.
Letters threatening Kashmiri Pandits that surfaced on social media in August have set off a wave of panic among members of the community living in Jammu and Kashmir (J&K). They have revived memories of the “hit lists” and assassinations that forced around 350,000 Pandits to flee the Kashmir valley over 36 years ago.
Three letters, all issued in the name of the United Liberation Council (ULC), said to be a front organization of the Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba, have surfaced on social media so far. The most recent letter, dated August 27, was explicitly linked to the Indian government reopening investigations into the massacre of Pandits by Islamist militants at the height of the anti-India militancy in the 1990s.
“If the SIA [State Investigation Agency of J&K] or any other agency is so eager to reopen closed cases involving migrant Pandits, they should also investigate cases like Bijebehara, Gawkadal, Sopore, Handwara, etc., where the so-called Indian mercenary security forces deliberately opened fire on innocent Kashmiris,” the letter said. “We will slaughter all those involved in these crimes no matter how much security they have.”
The first letter, dated August 7, named six Pandits working in the J&K government’s revenue department and included their cell phone numbers. It called on them to “change their ways.” The second letter, dated August 23, named six more Pandits and provided their residential addresses, including house numbers and street names. It described them as “white collar terrorists” and “traitors,” working for their “masters” in Delhi.
The letter’s contents were ominous. “Wherever you are and wherever you go, we are watching your every move,” it said. While the August 7 letter named Pandits working in the valley, the August 23 post listed Pandits in Jammu.
Kashmiri Pandits are Hindus and indigenous to the Muslim-dominated Kashmir valley. At the start of the militancy in 1989-1990, several Pandits, including Tika Lal Taploo, Neelkanth Ganjoo, Sarwanand Koul Premi and Virender Koul were assassinated. Sarla Bhat, a nurse, was abducted, raped and killed. Although militants claimed they were killed for their links to the Indian state – Taploo was a politician and Ganjoo was a high court judge—amid the rising tide of Islamism in Kashmir, it caused immense fear among the Pandits.

The Lashkar-e-Taiba and the Hizbul Mujahideen massacred 23 Pandits, including four children, at Wandhama in 1997 and another 24 Pandits, including two children, at Nadimarg in 2003.
Memories of the terror they experienced remain deeply etched in the memory of Pandits.
Soon after the second letter emerged, Dhar, who now lives in Bengaluru, spoke to The Diplomat. The JLC’s lists providing names and other identifying details of Pandits “are no different from the hit lists of 1990,” he said.
Since 2008, when former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh announced a rehabilitation package, New Delhi has promised government jobs, cash doles, accommodation and security to Pandits returning to the valley. Yet this has not been enough to convince them to return in large numbers.
Continuing attacks on Pandits in the valley – in October 2021, for example, a pharmacist who stayed back in Srinagar, J&K’s capital, in 1990, was shot dead – have kept the community on tenterhooks. The government may have provided returning Pandits with tight security but since they live in clusters, they fear they are sitting ducks for Islamist militants.
In recent months, New Delhi has reopened investigations into several high-profile murders and massacres by militant groups in Kashmir. Among the cases that have been reopened are the rape and murder of Sarla Bhat, and the massacre at Wandhama.
These investigations could serve to meet the demands of Kashmiri Pandit organizations that have been demanding justice. But also, they will reopen old wounds.
Meanwhile, this is sure to prompt Kashmiri Muslims to demand justice in incidents of mass killings by the Indian security forces. The ULC referred to this in its third letter. “It appears to be positioning itself as a guardian of Kashmiri Muslim interests. But Kashmiris, “even the Muslims, are unlikely to be impressed as they have suffered for decades, even as the militant groups operated from the safety of camps in Pakistan,” Dhar said.
When two non-Kashmiri Indian laborers working at a brick kiln in Kulgam district in the valley were shot dead on July 31, analysts pointed out that militants were hitting “soft targets” as they were not strong enough to take on India’s security forces. The targeting of Pandit civilians is yet another example of militants seeking to assert their presence by intimidating unarmed people.
Should the letters prompt Pandits to leave again, it will deal a blow to New Delhi’s efforts to normalize the situation in J&K.
Letters threatening Kashmiri Pandits that surfaced on social media in August have set off a wave of panic among members of the community living in Jammu and Kashmir (J&K). The most recent letter, dated August 27, was explicitly linked to the Indian government reopening investigations into the massacre of Pandits by Islamist militants at the height of the anti-India militancy in the 1990s.
“If the SIA [State Investigation Agency of J&K] or any other agency is so eager to reopen closed cases involving migrant Pandits, they should also investigate cases like Bijebehara, Gawkadal, Sopore, Handwara, etc., where the so-called Indian mercenary security forces deliberately opened fire on innocent Kashmiris,” the letter said. “We will slaughter all those involved in these crimes no matter how much security they have.”

articles.title: Cambodia Confirms Resumption of Joint Military Exercises With US Next Year
articles.full_text:
The move reflects the sea change that has taken place in U.S.-Cambodia relations under the second Trump administration.
U.S. Navy Adm. Steve Koehler, commander of the U.S. Pacific Fleet (center left), U.S. Charge d’Affaires to Cambodia Aleks Zittle (right), and Royal Cambodian Navy Rear Adm. Mey Dina, commander of the Ream Naval Base (center right), pose for a photo with their staff during Koehler’s visit to the base in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Aug. 7, 2026.
Cambodia’s army has confirmed that it will resume joint military exercises with the United States early next year after a decade-long suspension, the latest sign of the improving ties between the two nations.
The Royal Cambodian Army announced on Facebook on Friday that officials from the two nations had concluded an Initial Planning Conference for Exercise Angkor Sentinel 2027, which it said would be held in February of next year.
The exercise has the aim of “strengthening interoperability and disaster-response capabilities, reflecting renewed momentum in Cambodia–U.S. military cooperation and a shared commitment to strengthening defense cooperation.”
The announcement follows several high-level meetings between U.S. and Cambodian officials. These include a meeting last month between Prime Minister Hun Manet and Elbridge A. Colby, undersecretary for policy at the U.S. Department of War, during which the two discussed expanded defense cooperation.
Hun Manet said at the time that he was satisfied with the “positive momentum in Cambodia-U.S. relations” and the ongoing talks about the resumption of Angkor Sentinel, the Associated Press reported. “The joint exercises and training not only build military capability but also serve as a vital bridge to foster close friendship between the armed forces of both countries,” he added.
This was not long after Adm. Steve Koehler, commander of the U.S. Pacific Fleet, traveled to Phnom Penh for meetings with officials including Gen. Vong Pisen, the commander-in-chief of the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces, and Vice Adm. Tea Sokha, the commander of the Royal Cambodian Navy.
The visit “reaffirmed the United States’ long-term commitment to strengthening bilateral relationships and partnerships that advance a shared vision for a free and open Indo-Pacific,” the U.S. Pacific Fleet said in a statement at the time.
Angkor Sentinel was held for the first time in 2010 but was unilaterally canceled by the Cambodian government in early 2017, shortly after Cambodian troops took part for the first time in Golden Dragon, a joint military exercise with the Chinese military. The move reflected the mutually reinforcing deterioration of Phnom Penh’s relations with Washington and its growing proximity to China.
The resumption of the exercise has been anticipated by both sides for some time. It was first publicly discussed in early 2025, just prior to President Trump’s return to the White House, and has been referenced in most high-level diplomatic meetings since then. It reflects the sea change that has taken place in U.S.-Cambodia relations since the midpoint of the Biden administration, as Phnom Penh has sought to diversify its foreign relations and the U.S. has worked to pull the country out of China’s orbit.
However, the rapprochement has gained inexorable momentum since the inauguration of the second Trump administration, whose transactional mode of diplomacy has been much more to Phnom Penh’s liking. In particular, President Donald Trump’s decision to shutter USAID and cut off U.S. funding for democracy promotion efforts and media outlets like Radio Free Asia removed a key impediment to improved relations on the Cambodian side. As I noted in 2025, Cambodia’s government finally has what it has always wanted: “a relationship with the U.S. that strengthens, rather than undermines, the CPP’s hold on power.”
Last June, the U.S. government officially removed Cambodia from its arms sale blacklist, a month after an American ship docked for the first time at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base. The latter was particularly significant, given the extensive Chinese refurbishment of the base, which U.S. and Western officials feared was intended to host a permanent Chinese military presence. Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of the United States Indo-Pacific Command, described the port visit as a sign of the “strong upward trajectory” of relations between Phnom Penh and Washington.
These improvements have come even as branches of the U.S. government have come to officially recognize the extent of the Cambodian elite’s involvement in the country’s gigantic online scamming industry. According to U.S. government agencies, online scamming cost U.S. citizens at least $10 billion in 2024.

articles.title: Is BRICS Actually Benefiting India?
articles.full_text:
As India prepares to host the group’s summit, what does it want from BRICS? And what is Delhi actually getting from the group?
All eyes are on India right now. From September 12 to 13, presidents and prime ministers from Brazil, China, South Africa, Egypt, Indonesia, Russia, and more will converge on New Delhi for the 18th BRICS summit.
It’s India’s fourth time hosting BRICS, but leading the group today is a diplomatic minefield. Barely two months after Delhi took over as chair, the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, a BRICS member. Tehran then retaliated against the UAE and Saudi Arabia – also BRICS members. Now, India has to sit all three in the same room.
The U.S.-Iran war made it impossible to ignore the serious conflicts within BRICS. In a major diplomatic fail, the BRICS foreign ministers’ meeting in May, also hosted by India, ended without a joint statement. The group’s members just couldn’t agree on how to approach the crisis in West Asia. 
Some worry that the upcoming BRICS summit will also end without a joint statement. That would be a huge embarrassment for the host, India – and something Delhi is keen to avoid. 
In 2021, the last time India hosted the annual summit, BRICS was just five countries, the ones that form its name: Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.
Today, it’s an unwieldy 11-member bloc – or 10, depending on whether Saudi Arabia ever formally confirms it joined. Reaching a consensus was already tough when it was just India and China at odds within the group; now, BRICS includes rivals actively shooting at each other.
What does India get out of BRICS? And are the benefits worth the growing headache?
